About the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, as Brother Leo and the earliest Lives relate, there appeared to him a seraph, six-winged, bearing the figure of a man nailed to a cross. When the vision passed, Francis found in his own hands, feet, and side the marks of the Crucified: nail-heads of blackened flesh, and a wound in his side that often bled.

Francis bore the wounds for the two years that remained to him, hiding them beneath his habit until his death on 3 October 1226; Thomas of Celano soon recorded them, and Bonaventure set them at the heart of his great Life. His was the first stigmata recorded in the Church, and the Franciscan family has kept its memorial on 17 September ever since.

events.title: The apparition of Our Lady of La Salette
events.shortBlurb: On a mountainside in the French Alps a weeping Lady appeared to two shepherd children with a call to penance and prayer…
body: On 19 September 1846, a Saturday, two children minding cows on the mountain of La Salette, high above La Salette-Fallavaux in the diocese of Grenoble — Mélanie Calvat, a girl of fourteen, and Maximin Giraud, a boy of eleven — saw a globe of light open upon a seated woman in strange dress, her face buried in her hands, weeping.

Rising, the beautiful Lady called them to her — 'Come near, my children, be not afraid' — and gave them a message for all her people: she had long held back her Son's arm, yet men worked on the Lord's day and swore by his name; if they would not be converted, famine would come, but if they would pray, they would find mercy. To each child she entrusted a secret.

A spring began to flow where she had sat, and cures were reported. After five years of inquiry the bishop of Grenoble, Philibert de Bruillard, judged the apparition worthy of belief on 19 September 1851; a great basilica rose on the mountain, consecrated in 1879, and the Missionaries of Our Lady of La Salette were founded to spread her call to penance. She is venerated as the Reconciler of sinners.

events.title: The capture of Rome and the end of the Papal States
events.shortBlurb: Italian troops breached the walls at the Porta Pia, ending eleven centuries of papal temporal rule over Rome…
body: In July 1870 the Franco-Prussian War stripped Rome of its shield: Napoleon III recalled the French garrison, and his own empire collapsed at Sedan on 2 September. Declaring war on 10 September, the Kingdom of Italy sent General Raffaele Cadorna with some sixty thousand men against a papal army of perhaps thirteen thousand under General Hermann Kanzler.

Cadorna's guns opened at dawn on 20 September, and within hours his Bersaglieri breached the Aurelian Walls beside the Porta Pia. Pius IX, unwilling to spend lives in a hopeless cause, ordered only such resistance as honour required and then the white flag; some fifty of the Italians and nineteen of the pope's soldiers, many of them Zouaves, had fallen. A plebiscite on 2 October pronounced Rome Italian.

Thus ended the Papal States, the temporal sovereignty the popes had wielded for more than eleven centuries. Rome became the capital of Italy, and the First Vatican Council, which had defined papal infallibility that July, was suspended. Pius IX shut himself in the Vatican as its 'prisoner,' refusing the Law of Guarantees, and the Roman Question stood open until the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929.

events.title: The founding of the Order of Our Lady of Ransom
events.shortBlurb: St. Peter Nolasco founded an order vowed to ransom Christian captives from the Moors, honoured under the title of Our Lady of Ransom…
body: Thousands of Christians then languished in Moorish captivity in Spain and North Africa. Peter Nolasco, born about 1189 — by tradition a merchant settled at Barcelona — spent his patrimony ransoming them; and on the night of 1 August 1218, the order's tradition holds, the Blessed Virgin appeared to him — and to his confessor Raymond of Peñafort and King James I of Aragon — bidding him found an order for the work.

On 10 August 1218, the feast of St. Lawrence, the foundation was made in the cathedral of Barcelona: Bishop Berenguer de Palou gave the white habit, and the king granted the new brethren the arms of Aragon for their scapular. They took the name of the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy — the Mercedarians — under the patronage of Our Lady of Ransom.

Beyond the common vows each brother bound himself by a fourth: to remain, if need be, a hostage in the Moors' hands for a captive in danger of losing the faith. Gregory IX confirmed the order in 1235 under the Rule of St. Augustine. Nolasco, who died at Barcelona, was canonized in 1628, and the feast of Our Lady of Ransom on 24 September grew from the order's devotion.

events.title: The papal approval of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: Pope Paul III confirmed the new order gathered by Ignatius of Loyola, launching the Jesuits into the service of the Church…
body: On 27 September 1540 Pope Paul III issued the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae, giving formal canonical approval to the Society of Jesus. The company had begun six years earlier at Paris, where Ignatius of Loyola and six companions, students at the university, had bound themselves by vows at Montmartre on 15 August 1534.

Drawn to Rome, the companions offered themselves to the Holy Father for whatever missions he might assign, adding to the three customary vows of religion a fourth vow of special obedience to the pope in the sending of missionaries. The bull, which prudently restricted the new order to sixty members, approved it for the defense and propagation of the faith; the restriction was lifted a few years later.

The following year Ignatius was chosen the first superior general. Within a generation the Society had become a chief instrument of the Catholic reform: Francis Xavier carried the gospel to India and Japan, colleges multiplied across Europe, and Jesuit missionaries crossed to the New World. By the death of Ignatius in 1556 the order numbered about a thousand members.

events.title: St. Jerome and the Latin Vulgate
events.shortBlurb: Commissioned to set in order the rival Latin Bibles of his day, Jerome produced the Vulgate, the Church's Latin Bible for a thousand years…
body: In Jerome's day the Latin Bible was a tangle of discordant Old Latin versions — almost as many texts, he complained, as there were manuscripts. In 382 Pope Damasus charged him with setting them in order: Jerome revised the Gospels against the Greek, then at Bethlehem translated most of the Old Testament directly from the Hebrew, the 'Hebrew truth', rather than from the familiar Septuagint.

The novelty was fiercely resisted; Augustine himself feared unsettling the faithful with a Bible that departed from the Septuagint, and churches clung to the old renderings for generations. Yet by the early Middle Ages Jerome's version, copied and corrected under scholars like Alcuin at Charlemagne's court, had displaced its rivals and come to be called the Vulgate, the 'common edition' of the West.

For a thousand years it was the Bible of Latin Christendom — the text of the liturgy and the schools, and the first great book printed by Gutenberg. In 1546 the Council of Trent declared the old Vulgate the Church's authentic Latin text; the revised edition issued under Clement VIII in 1592 served until a new Vulgate was promulgated in 1979.

events.title: The death of St. Francis of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: The Poverello died at the Portiuncula near Assisi; his passing is kept by the Franciscans as the Transitus…
body: Born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182, the son of a wealthy cloth merchant, Francis as a young man renounced his inheritance to rebuild ruined churches and to live the gospel in literal poverty. The brotherhood that gathered around him, the Friars Minor, received papal approbation of its definitive rule in 1223.

Worn by austerity and a painful illness of the eyes, he had borne since September 1224 the wounds of the stigmata, imprinted upon him as he kept a fast and prayed on Mount La Verna. In his last days he added to his Canticle of the Creatures the verses in praise of "Sister Bodily Death," from whom, he sang, no living man can escape.

On the evening of 3 October 1226 he died at the Portiuncula, the chapel of Saint Mary of the Angels below Assisi, having asked to be laid naked on the bare ground as the Passion according to John was read. He was about forty-five. Pope Gregory IX canonized him on 16 July 1228; the basilica of Assisi rose over his tomb, and Franciscans keep the evening of 3 October as his Transitus.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 October

events.title: The victory of Lepanto
events.shortBlurb: The Holy League's fleet broke the Ottoman navy at Lepanto off the Greek coast; the day gave rise to the feast of the Rosary…
body: The battle was provoked by Cyprus: in 1570 the Turks seized the Venetian island, and after a long siege Famagusta fell in August 1571, its commander Bragadin flayed alive. Pius V bound Spain, Venice, and the papal states into a Holy League whose two hundred galleys and six galleasses were commanded by Don John of Austria, the Emperor Charles V's natural son; among its soldiers was Miguel de Cervantes.

On the morning of 7 October 1571 the fleets met in the Gulf of Patras, near Lepanto. In hours of close and savage fighting Cervantes was thrice wounded and lost the use of his left hand; the Turkish fleet was all but destroyed and its commander Ali Pasha slain. The League lost some eight thousand men, but freed more than ten thousand Christian captives from the Turkish oars.

In Rome, Pius V credited the deliverance to the Mother of God, invoked that day by the Rosary confraternities, and kept it with an annual feast. The victory broke the Ottoman name for invincibility at sea, yet the allies quarreled, winter closed in, and Cyprus was never retaken; two years later Venice made her own peace with the Sultan.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Holy Rosary”

events.title: The opening of the Second Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: Pope John XXIII opened the twenty-first ecumenical council before a great gathering of the world's bishops…
body: On 25 January 1959, before astonished cardinals in the basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls, John XXIII announced his intention to summon an ecumenical council — the first since Vatican I was suspended in 1870. Three years of preparation followed, as commissions of bishops and theologians from every continent drafted the schemas.

On 11 October 1962, then the feast of the Divine Motherhood of Mary, some two and a half thousand council fathers — patriarchs, cardinals, and bishops, the largest assembly in the Church's history — processed into St. Peter's for the opening Mass, while delegated observers of the Orthodox and Protestant communions looked on, a novelty for any council.

In his opening address, Gaudet Mater Ecclesia, the pope bade the Church distrust 'prophets of gloom' and prefer 'the medicine of mercy' to severity. The Council met in four autumn sessions; after John's death Paul VI carried it forward, closing it on 8 December 1965 with sixteen documents, among them constitutions on the liturgy, the Church, revelation, and the Church in the modern world.

sources.text: Vatican, Documents of the Second Vatican Council (vatican.va)

events.title: The landfall in the New World
events.shortBlurb: Columbus reached an island of the Americas, opening the way for the Christian evangelization of a continent…
body: Sailing under the patronage of the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, Christopher Columbus left Palos on 3 August 1492 with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta, and the Niña, seeking a western sea road to the Indies and the realm of the Great Khan.

At about two in the morning of 12 October 1492, after some five weeks out of sight of land, Rodrigo de Triana, a lookout on the Pinta, sighted land. The island, called Guanahani by its inhabitants, Columbus named San Salvador, Holy Saviour; going ashore, he planted the cross and took possession in the sovereigns' names, believing he had reached islands off Asia.

The landfall opened the Americas to Europe, and with the conquerors came Franciscan, Dominican, and Jesuit missionaries, who preached, baptized, and raised the Church across two continents. The faith was served also by those who resisted the conquerors' cruelty: the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos, preaching on Hispaniola in 1511, denounced the oppression of the Indians, and Bartolomé de las Casas spent his life pleading their cause at the Spanish court.

events.title: The Miracle of the Sun at Fatima
events.shortBlurb: A great crowd at Fatima reported seeing the sun spin and plunge toward the earth after the apparitions to three shepherd children…
body: Since 13 May 1917 three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, had reported apparitions of the Blessed Virgin at the Cova da Iria near Fatima in Portugal. They had foretold that in October a sign would be given so that all might believe.

On 13 October 1917 a crowd reckoned at some seventy thousand, soaked by a morning of heavy rain, filled the Cova. Numerous witnesses, skeptics among them, reported that the clouds parted and the sun appeared to spin, casting colored light over the fields, then to plunge toward the earth before resuming its place; the drenched ground and clothing were found dry.

Avelino de Almeida of the anticlerical Lisbon daily O Século described how the sun danced at noon. After a canonical inquiry the Bishop of Leiria, José Alves Correia da Silva, declared the apparitions worthy of belief on 13 October 1930. The message of Fatima, with its call to prayer, penance, the daily Rosary, and consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, became one of the most widespread devotions of the modern Church.

sources.text: Vatican, The Message of Fatima (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 2000; vatican.va)

events.title: The Gregorian calendar begins
events.shortBlurb: By decree of Pope Gregory XIII the calendar leapt from 4 October straight to 15 October to correct the drift of the seasons…
body: The Julian calendar, in use since 45 BC, ran some eleven minutes too long in each year; over fifteen centuries the error had carried the spring equinox, by which Easter is reckoned, from 21 March, where the Council of Nicaea had fixed it in 325, back toward 11 March. The Council of Trent had left the correction to the Holy See.

Acting on the plan of the Calabrian astronomer Aloysius Lilius, refined and defended by the Jesuit mathematician Christopher Clavius, Pope Gregory XIII decreed the reform in the bull Inter gravissimas, dated 24 February 1582. Ten days were cut from that year: Thursday 4 October was followed at once by Friday 15 October. Henceforth century years would be leap years only when divisible by four hundred.

Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Poland adopted the new reckoning at once; Protestant and Orthodox lands followed only over the next three centuries. Teresa of Ávila died at Alba de Tormes on the very night of the change, so that the day after her death was reckoned 15 October, the day her feast is still kept.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The Reform of the Calendar”

events.title: The election of Pope John Paul II
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose Karol Wojtyła of Kraków, the first non-Italian pope in more than four centuries…
body: Born at Wadowice in 1920, Karol Józef Wojtyła had labored in a quarry under the German occupation, studied in a clandestine seminary, and served from 1964 as Archbishop of Kraków. On 16 October 1978, in the second conclave of that year, 111 cardinals elected him on the eighth ballot to succeed John Paul I, dead after a reign of thirty-three days.

At fifty-eight he was the youngest pope since Pius IX, the first Pole to hold the office, and the first non-Italian since the Dutch Adrian VI in 1522. Taking the name John Paul II, he gave his pontificate its keynote in the homily of his inaugural Mass on 22 October: "Be not afraid."

His reign of more than twenty-six years was among the longest in the Church's history. He journeyed to more than a hundred countries, issued fourteen encyclicals, gave the Church the Catechism of 1992, and played a recognized part in the peaceful collapse of communism in eastern Europe. He died on 2 April 2005 and was canonized in 2014.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
events.shortBlurb: Constantine conquered under the sign of the Cross, opening the way to the toleration of Christianity…
body: On 28 October 312 the army of Constantine met that of his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge, where the Via Flaminia crossed the Tiber north of Rome. Maxentius held the city; Constantine had marched the length of Italy to wrest it from him.

Christian writers near the event tell of a sign given before the battle. Lactantius records that Constantine was warned in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God, the Chi-Rho monogram of Christ, on his soldiers' shields; Eusebius, writing from the emperor's own account, tells of a cross of light above the midday sun with the words "In this, conquer" — in Latin, in hoc signo vinces.

Maxentius drowned in the Tiber when the bridge of boats behind him collapsed under his fleeing army. Constantine entered Rome master of the West, and the following year, 313, agreed with his colleague Licinius at Milan upon full liberty of worship for Christians. The long age of persecution was closing, and the Church emerged from the catacombs into public life.

events.title: The election of Pope John XXIII
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose the aged Angelo Roncalli, who would surprise the world by summoning a council…
body: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli, born in 1881 at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo to a family of sharecroppers, had spent decades in the papal diplomatic service, in Bulgaria, in Turkey and Greece, and as nuncio in Paris, before being created cardinal and named Patriarch of Venice in 1953. When Pius XII died on 9 October 1958, Roncalli entered the conclave with a return ticket in his pocket.

On 28 October 1958, the fourth day of the conclave, he was elected on the eleventh ballot and took the name John XXIII, keeping his episcopal motto, Obedientia et pax. Nearly seventy-seven years old, he was widely expected to be a brief, transitional pope.

Within three months, on 25 January 1959, he astonished the Church by announcing an ecumenical council, the first in nearly ninety years. That assembly, the Second Vatican Council, opened in 1962 and reshaped Catholic life for generations. Beloved as "Good Pope John," he died on 3 June 1963 and was canonized in 2014.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope John XXIII (vatican.va)

events.title: Luther posts the Ninety-Five Theses
events.shortBlurb: At Wittenberg an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther set out ninety-five theses against the preaching of indulgences — the spark, by long tradition, of the Protestant Reformation…
body: On 31 October 1517, the vigil of All Saints, Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor of theology at Wittenberg, published ninety-five theses against the preaching of indulgences — by long tradition affixed to the door of the castle church, the university's notice board.

The occasion was the Dominican Johann Tetzel's preaching near Wittenberg of an indulgence toward the rebuilding of St. Peter's in Rome, under a commission whose proceeds were divided between Rome and Archbishop Albert of Mainz. Luther sent the theses to the archbishop; soon translated into German, they were multiplied by the press.

Examined by Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg in 1518 and pressed by Johann Eck at Leipzig in 1519, Luther came to deny the divine right of the papacy and the inerrancy of councils. The bull Exsurge Domine (1520) condemned forty-one of his propositions; Luther burned it publicly and was excommunicated in January 1521.

Refusing to recant at the Diet of Worms in April 1521, he was sheltered by his prince, Frederick the Wise, at the Wartburg, where he translated the New Testament into German. The revolt divided Western Christendom; the Church answered at the Council of Trent (1545–1563) with reform and definition of doctrine.

events.title: The Sistine Chapel ceiling unveiled
events.shortBlurb: On All Saints' Day, Michelangelo's newly completed ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was shown for the first time…
body: The chapel of the Apostolic Palace, built for Pope Sixtus IV and consecrated in 1483, received its crowning glory when his nephew Julius II commissioned Michelangelo Buonarroti in 1508 to repaint its ceiling, then a simple field of blue starred with gold.

Working on scaffolding high above the floor for some four years, largely unaided, the artist covered the vault with more than three hundred figures: nine central panels telling the story of Genesis from the creation of light to the drunkenness of Noah, and about them the prophets of Israel and the sibyls of the nations who foretold Christ, with the ancestors of Christ in the spandrels and arches.

The last scaffolding came down on the eve of All Saints in 1512, and on the feast itself, 1 November, Julius II celebrated Mass beneath the finished vault. A generation later Michelangelo returned to paint the Last Judgment above its altar, unveiled in 1541; the chapel still serves the papal liturgies and the conclaves that elect the popes.

events.title: The Lisbon earthquake
events.shortBlurb: A catastrophic earthquake struck Lisbon on All Saints' Day as the churches were full for Mass…
body: At about half past nine on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, while the churches of Lisbon were thronged for the feast, the earth shook for several minutes in one of the strongest earthquakes recorded in Europe, its magnitude later estimated at near 8.5.

The shocks brought down churches, palaces, and houses upon the worshippers; a great sea wave swept into the harbor, and fires, fed by the candles of the feast, burned for days. Some eighty-five percent of the city lay in ruins, and between thirty and sixty thousand people perished in Lisbon and the country round about.

The Marquis of Pombal, the king's chief minister, directed the relief and rebuilt the ruined center on a straight grid of earthquake-resistant streets that still stands. Falling on a holy day and levelling the churches with the devout inside them, the disaster provoked a celebrated debate across Europe on providence and evil, answered by Voltaire in his Poem on the Lisbon Disaster of 1756 and again in Candide.

events.title: The dogma of the Assumption defined
events.shortBlurb: Pope Pius XII solemnly defined that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heaven…
body: On 1 November 1950, in the midst of the Holy Year, Pope Pius XII, before an immense throng in Saint Peter's Square, solemnly defined the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary as a dogma of the Catholic faith in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus.

The definition declared it divinely revealed that "the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory." The pope had prepared the step in 1946 with the encyclical Deiparae Virginis Mariae, consulting the bishops of the whole world; nearly twelve hundred answered that the doctrine could safely be defined, and only sixteen questioned its opportuneness.

The dogma gathered up a belief attested from the earliest centuries, kept from of old in the feasts of the Dormition in the East and the Assumption in the West, and petitioned by millions of the faithful since the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854. It remains the most recent exercise of the solemn papal magisterium, and the feast of 15 August still celebrates what it declared.

sources.text: Apostolic Constitution Munificentissimus Deus, Pope Pius XII (vatican.va)

events.title: St. Odilo institutes the commemoration of all the departed
events.shortBlurb: The abbot of Cluny fixed a yearly day of prayer for all the faithful dead, the origin of All Souls' Day…
body: Toward the end of the tenth century St. Odilo, fifth abbot of Cluny, decreed that in all the monasteries of his congregation the day after All Saints should be kept as a solemn commemoration of all the faithful departed, with the office of the dead, Masses, and alms offered for their souls. The year 998 is traditionally given for the decree.

His biographer Jotsald tells the legend that moved him: a pilgrim back from the Holy Land reported an island where the groans of the tormented could be heard from the depths, and where demons raged that the prayers of Cluny's monks snatched souls from their grasp. Odilo answered by binding the whole Cluniac family to the relief of the dead.

From Cluny's hundreds of dependent priories the observance passed to other orders and dioceses; by the thirteenth century it was general in the West, and by the fourteenth Rome had entered it in her books. Thus a monastic custom became the universal All Souls' Day, fixing in the calendar the Church's most ancient instinct — to pray for her dead.

events.title: The Act of Supremacy
events.shortBlurb: The English Parliament declared King Henry VIII the Supreme Head of the Church of England, severing it from Rome…
body: On 3 November 1534 the Reformation Parliament, in the session that completed Henry VIII's quarrel with Rome, passed the Act of Supremacy, declaring the king "the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England" and annexing to the crown the honors, jurisdictions, and profits of that dignity.

The breach had been building for years. When Clement VII would not annul the king's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry wed Anne Boleyn in 1533 and had the annulment pronounced by his own archbishop, Thomas Cranmer; Parliament's Act in Restraint of Appeals had already forbidden recourse to Rome. The new act made the separation of the English Church from the Holy See a matter of statute.

A companion Treasons Act made denial of the royal supremacy a capital crime. Refusal of the oath brought the Carthusian priors to the gallows in 1535, Bishop John Fisher to the block on 22 June of that year, and the former chancellor Thomas More on 6 July; Fisher and More were canonized together in 1935, and the settlement opened long centuries of penal law against English Catholics.

events.title: The Gunpowder Plot discovered
events.shortBlurb: A conspiracy by a group of English Catholics to blow up Parliament was uncovered on the eve of its opening…
body: In the spring of 1604 Robert Catesby, a Catholic gentleman of Warwickshire despairing of relief from the penal laws, formed with Thomas Wintour, John Wright, Thomas Percy and Guy Fawkes a conspiracy to blow up King James I with the Lords and Commons at the opening of Parliament. Through Percy they hired a cellar beneath the House of Lords and stored there thirty-six barrels of gunpowder, concealed under firewood.

The plot was betrayed by an anonymous letter of 26 October 1605 warning Lord Monteagle to absent himself from the assembly. In the cellar about midnight on 4 November, Fawkes was seized guarding the powder; under torture in the Tower he named his fellows. Catesby and Percy were shot dead at Holbeche House in Staffordshire on 8 November; the survivors were tried in January 1606 and executed.

English Catholics as a body had neither part in the plot nor knowledge of it, yet they bore its penalty: new recusancy statutes followed in 1606, and for two centuries the memory of the fifth of November fed suspicion of the old religion. Parliament made the day an annual public thanksgiving, and its service remained in the Book of Common Prayer until 1859.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Leo the Great
events.shortBlurb: One of the greatest of the early popes died at Rome, leaving the faith of Chalcedon secured…
body: Leo, a Tuscan by birth, was a deacon of the Roman Church, trusted enough to be sent by the Emperor Valentinian III to Gaul to reconcile the general Aetius with the magistrate Albinus, when he was chosen pope on the death of Sixtus III. Consecrated on 29 September 440, he governed the Church for twenty-one years as Roman power collapsed in the West.

His dogmatic letter to Flavian of Constantinople, the Tome of Leo, was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 as the confession of Peter's faith, teaching one Christ in two natures. In 452 he met Attila at the Mincio near Mantua and won his withdrawal from Italy; in 455 his intercession with the Vandal Genseric spared the lives of the citizens in the sack of Rome.

Ninety-six of his sermons and 143 letters survive, marked by clarity and elevation. He died at Rome on 10 November 461 and was buried in the vestibule of St. Peter's; his remains were later moved within the basilica, where they now rest beneath the altar dedicated to him. Benedict XIV in 1754 declared him a Doctor of the Church, and with Gregory the Great he stands foremost among the popes of Christian antiquity.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Leo I (the Great)”

events.title: The Fourth Lateran Council opens
events.shortBlurb: The greatest council of the medieval West opened in Rome under Pope Innocent III…
body: Summoned by the bull Vineam Domini of April 1213, the Fourth Lateran Council opened on 11 November 1215 in the Lateran basilica, Innocent III preaching on the words 'With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you.' Some 400 bishops, more than 800 abbots and priors, and the envoys of Christian princes made it the greatest assembly of the medieval Church, reckoned the twelfth general council.

Its seventy decrees opened with the confession Firmiter, which employed the word transubstantiation for the change of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood. The twenty-first canon, Omnis utriusque sexus, bound every believer to confess to his own priest and to receive the Eucharist at least once a year at Easter; others legislated against heresy and ordered Jews and Saracens marked out by their dress.

The council further decreed the reform of the clergy, the provision of preachers for the people, and a new crusade for the deliverance of the Holy Land. Innocent died at Perugia in July 1216, but his council's canons passed into the law and life of the Church and ordered Catholic practice for centuries.

events.title: The martyrs of the Central American University
events.shortBlurb: Six Jesuit priests and two women were murdered in San Salvador during the country's civil war…
body: In the early hours of 16 November 1989, soldiers of the Atlacatl Battalion entered the campus of the Central American University in San Salvador and murdered the six Jesuits of its community: the rector Ignacio Ellacuría, Ignacio Martín-Baró, Segundo Montes, Amando López, Juan Ramón Moreno and Joaquín López y López. With them died their housekeeper Elba Ramos and her teenaged daughter Celina, who had taken shelter in the house.

The murders came five days after the start of a great guerrilla offensive, in the tenth year of the country's civil war. The Jesuits, and Ellacuría above all, had laboured for a negotiated peace and borne witness against the misery of the poor; for this they were marked as enemies, and the order to kill them was given at the head of the army.

The crime roused the world; a United Nations truth commission in 1993 laid the responsibility on the high command, and in 2020 a Spanish court sentenced the former colonel Inocente Orlando Montano to 133 years in prison for five of the murders, five of the priests having been Spanish citizens. The eight victims are honoured among the martyrs of the Church of the poor.

sources.text: Vatican / Holy See communications on the martyrs of El Salvador (vatican.va)

events.title: The bull Unam Sanctam
events.shortBlurb: Pope Boniface VIII issued his celebrated declaration on the unity of the Church and the authority of the Pope…
body: The bull crowned a bitter quarrel between Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair of France, who had taxed his clergy in defiance of the papal constitution Clericis laicos of 1296 and had dragged the bishop of Pamiers, Bernard Saisset, before a royal court. Boniface answered with the letter Ausculta fili; and on 18 November 1302, as the strife deepened, he published Unam Sanctam.

It taught that the Church is one body with one head, not two heads like a monster; that in her power are two swords, the spiritual and the temporal; and that the spiritual power may judge the earthly when it goes astray. The bull closed with the celebrated sentence declaring it altogether necessary to salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff.

Philip replied with charges of heresy and crime, and in September 1303 his agents Guillaume de Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna seized the aged pope at Anagni; rescued by the townspeople, Boniface died at Rome within the month, on 11 October 1303. The bull, which owes much to Giles of Rome, remains a classical text on the unity of the Church and the primacy of her head.

events.title: The new St. Peter's Basilica consecrated
events.shortBlurb: Pope Urban VIII consecrated the rebuilt Basilica of St. Peter in Rome, more than a century in the making…
body: On 18 November 1626, by tradition the thirteen-hundredth anniversary of the dedication of Constantine's first basilica over the Apostle's tomb, Urban VIII solemnly consecrated the new St. Peter's in the Vatican. The day is kept still in the Roman calendar as the feast of the dedication of the basilicas of Sts. Peter and Paul.

The rebuilding had begun on 18 April 1506, when Julius II laid the foundation stone to Bramante's design. Michelangelo, architect from 1547, raised the drum of the great dome, completed after his death by Giacomo della Porta and Domenico Fontana; and under Paul V, Carlo Maderno drew out the church into a Latin cross and built the facade.

The immense cost, met in part by the preaching of indulgences, had furnished the occasion of Luther's revolt a century before. As the basilica was consecrated, Bernini's bronze baldacchino was rising over the high altar and the Apostle's confessio beneath it. The greatest church of Christendom had been one hundred and twenty years in the building.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The Basilica of St. Peter”

events.title: Lumen Gentium promulgated
events.shortBlurb: The Second Vatican Council promulgated its Dogmatic Constitution on the Church…
body: On 21 November 1964, at the public sitting that closed the Second Vatican Council's third session, the Dogmatic Constitution on the Church, Lumen Gentium, was approved by 2,151 votes against 5 and promulgated by Paul VI together with the council fathers. The same day saw the promulgation of the decrees on ecumenism, Unitatis Redintegratio, and on the Eastern Catholic Churches, Orientalium Ecclesiarum.

The constitution, hammered out over two years from a schema the fathers had rejected in 1962, called the Church a mystery and a sacrament, set forth the doctrine of the People of God, taught that the bishops govern as a college with and under its head the pope, proclaimed the universal call of all the baptized to holiness, and closed with a chapter on the Mother of God.

In his discourse at the close of the sitting, Paul VI proclaimed the Blessed Virgin Mother of the Church. Lumen Gentium remains the council's central statement of what the Church is, and the soil in which its other constitutions and decrees were rooted.

sources.text: Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium (vatican.va)

events.title: The martyrdom of Blessed Miguel Pro
events.shortBlurb: A young Mexican Jesuit was shot by a firing squad, crying out his love for Christ the King…
body: Miguel Agustín Pro, born at Guadalupe in Zacatecas on 13 January 1891, entered the Jesuits in 1911 and, driven into exile by the persecution, was ordained at Enghien in Belgium in 1925. He returned to Mexico in 1926, when the laws of President Calles had silenced the churches, and ministered in secret to the faithful of Mexico City, bringing them the sacraments in disguise.

In November 1927 an attempt was made on the life of the former president Obregón by men who used a car once owned by the Pro family; Miguel and his brothers were arrested, and without trial Calles ordered him shot. He was executed on 23 November 1927 together with his brother Humberto, the government having commanded that the execution be photographed and the pictures published.

Refusing the blindfold, Pro forgave the firing squad, stretched out his arms in the form of a cross with a crucifix in one hand and a rosary in the other, and died crying 'Viva Cristo Rey' — Long live Christ the King. The photographs, published to terrorize, spread his fame instead. John Paul II beatified him on 25 September 1988, among the martyrs of the Mexican persecution.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Beatification of Blessed Miguel Agustín Pro (vatican.va)

events.title: Urban II preaches the First Crusade at Clermont
events.shortBlurb: At the Council of Clermont Pope Urban II called Christendom to aid the Eastern churches and free the holy places, and the crowd is said to have answered, “Deus vult” — God wills it…
body: The call had come from the East: at the Council of Piacenza in March 1095, envoys of the Emperor Alexios Komnenos begged help against the Turks who had overrun the Christian East. Urban II, a French pope and once a monk of Cluny, carried the summons into France; and at the close of the Council of Clermont, on 27 November 1095, he preached to a throng gathered in the fields.

He bade the knights of the West abandon their private wars and march to the aid of the Eastern Christians and the deliverance of Jerusalem, promising remission of sins to those who should take the road. Robert the Monk records that the assembly cried out 'Deus vult' — God wills it. Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, first took the cross and was named legate of the expedition.

The departure was fixed for the feast of the Assumption, 15 August 1096. So began the First Crusade: the hosts of the West took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099. Urban died at Rome a fortnight later, on 29 July, before tidings of the deliverance of the Holy City could reach him.

events.title: The apparition of the Miraculous Medal
events.shortBlurb: The Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to St. Catherine Labouré in Paris and asked that a medal be struck…
body: Catherine Labouré, a novice of the Daughters of Charity on the Rue du Bac in Paris, had first beheld the Blessed Virgin on the night of 18 July 1830. On 27 November, during evening prayer, Mary appeared, standing upon a globe with rays of light streaming from her ringed hands, while an oval frame bore the words, 'O Mary conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee.'

A voice bade her have a medal struck after this model, promising great graces to all who should wear it with confidence. Her confessor, Father Aladel, laid the matter before the Archbishop of Paris, Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen, and the first fifteen hundred medals were struck in June 1832. Spread amid the cholera then raging in France, they were so wonderfully favoured that the people called it the Miraculous Medal.

Within seven years ten million medals had gone through the world, and a canonical inquiry in 1836 vindicated both medal and seer. Catherine kept her secret until the eve of her death on 31 December 1876; she was canonized by Pius XII in 1947. The medal's invocation foreshadowed the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, proclaimed in 1854.

sources.text: Vatican biography, St. Catherine Labouré and the Miraculous Medal (vatican.va)

events.title: England reconciled to Rome
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of St. Andrew, Cardinal Reginald Pole absolved the realm of England and restored it to communion with the Holy See…
body: Twenty years after Henry VIII had cast off the Roman obedience, Cardinal Reginald Pole, of the blood royal and legate of Julius III, landed at Dover on 20 November 1554. On 30 November, the feast of St. Andrew, at Whitehall the Lords and Commons knelt before him in the presence of Queen Mary and King Philip and received absolution and restoration to the communion of the Holy See.

Parliament, which had petitioned for the reunion, repealed the statutes enacted against the Roman See since the twentieth year of Henry VIII, while Pole confirmed the new holders of the monastic lands in their possession. The old heresy laws were revived, and under them some two hundred and eighty persons, among them the bishops Latimer, Ridley and Cranmer, were burned in the years that followed.

The reunion proved brief. Mary died on 17 November 1558 and Pole, by then Archbishop of Canterbury, a few hours after her; under Elizabeth the next year the breach with Rome was reopened, and England's ancient place in the communion of Western Christendom was lost for good.

events.title: Napoleon crowned in the presence of Pius VII
events.shortBlurb: In Notre-Dame de Paris, Napoleon Bonaparte took the imperial crown and set it on his own head while Pope Pius VII looked on…
body: On 2 December 1804, in Notre-Dame de Paris, Napoleon Bonaparte was anointed and crowned Emperor of the French in the presence of Pius VII, who had journeyed from Rome for the rite. The pope had come hoping to strengthen the Concordat of 1801, which had restored the Church in France after the Revolution; he was made instead the witness of a carefully staged lesson.

When the pope had anointed emperor and empress and the prayers over the regalia were said, Napoleon lifted the crown called of Charlemagne and set it on his own head, then crowned the kneeling Joséphine — a prearranged sign that he held his authority from no hand on earth. Pius pronounced the acclamation 'Vivat imperator in aeternum', and David's great canvas has fixed the scene.

The amity did not last. In 1809 Napoleon annexed the Papal States; Pius answered with the excommunication Quum memoranda and was seized in the Quirinal, held prisoner at Savona and then at Fontainebleau, and restored to Rome only in May 1814, as the emperor fell. The captivity of the pope undid whatever the coronation had been staged to purchase.

events.title: The Council of Trent concludes
events.shortBlurb: After eighteen years and twenty-five sessions, the great reforming council of the Catholic Reformation brought its work to a close…
body: On 4 December 1563, in the cathedral of Trent, the twenty-fifth and final session of the Council of Trent concluded its work, and the presiding legate, Cardinal Giovanni Morone, declared the nineteenth ecumenical council closed. Its decrees were subscribed by 215 fathers — four legates, two cardinals, three patriarchs, twenty-five archbishops, and 167 bishops, besides abbots and generals of orders — with nineteen proxies for absent prelates.

Over its two final days the session had issued decrees on the veneration of the saints, their relics and images, on indulgences, and on the reform of religious life, and committed to the pope the completion of the catechism, the Missal, the Breviary, and the Index of forbidden books.

Pius IV confirmed the council's decrees on 26 January 1564 by the bull Benedictus Deus. Opened in 1545 to answer the Protestant Reformation, the council had defined Catholic teaching on Scripture and Tradition, original sin, justification, the seven sacraments, and the sacrifice of the Mass, and had ordered the founding of seminaries and the residence of bishops; its decrees shaped Catholic life for four centuries, until the Second Vatican Council.

events.title: St. Thomas Aquinas lays down his pen
events.shortBlurb: After a profound experience at Mass, the greatest of the scholastic theologians ceased to write, saying all he had written seemed like straw…
body: On 6 December 1273, the feast of St. Nicholas, Thomas Aquinas was celebrating Mass at Naples when a long ecstasy came upon him. From that day he laid down his pen and would write no more; the Summa Theologiae, begun at Rome eight years before, remained forever unfinished, breaking off at the ninetieth question of its third part, in the treatise on penance.

When Reginald of Piperno, his faithful companion and secretary, urged him to resume, Thomas answered: 'I can do no more; such things have been revealed to me that all I have written seems to me like straw.' He began at once to prepare his soul for death.

Summoned by Pope Gregory X to the Second Council of Lyons, he set out on foot in January 1274 but collapsed near Terracina and was carried to the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova. There, having received the Viaticum with a great act of faith in the Sacrament, he died on 7 March 1274, not yet fifty years old; John XXII canonized him in 1323.

events.title: Rome and Constantinople lift the anathemas of 1054
events.shortBlurb: On the eve of the Second Vatican Council's close, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras together erased the mutual excommunications that had divided East and West for nine centuries…
body: On 7 December 1965, in St. Peter's Basilica during a public session of the Second Vatican Council, and at the same hour in the patriarchal church of St. George in Constantinople, a common declaration of Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I was solemnly read, committing to oblivion the mutual excommunications exchanged between their sees in 1054.

Those sentences dated from July 1054, when Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, legate of Pope Leo IX, laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his followers, and a synod of Constantinople answered by anathematizing the legates in turn. Aimed at persons rather than whole churches, they had nonetheless become the standing symbol of the schism between East and West.

The gesture crowned the dialogue of charity opened by the two leaders' meeting at Jerusalem in January 1964, the first between a pope and an ecumenical patriarch in five centuries. It did not of itself restore full communion, but it removed a scandal of nine hundred years and opened the way to a new relationship between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

sources.text: Vatican, Common Declaration of Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I (1965) (vatican.va)

events.title: Pius IX defines the Immaculate Conception
events.shortBlurb: In the bull Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX solemnly defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved free from original sin from the first moment of her conception…
body: The definition was long prepared. In 1849 Pius IX, an exile at Gaeta from revolution in Rome, asked the bishops of the world by the encyclical Ubi Primum whether the doctrine could and should be defined; of the more than six hundred who answered, the great majority — 546 — urged it on.

On 8 December 1854, before a great assembly of cardinals and bishops in St. Peter's, Pius IX read the constitution Ineffabilis Deus and solemnly defined that the Blessed Virgin, 'in the first instance of her conception, by a singular privilege and grace granted by God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Saviour of the human race, was preserved exempt from all stain of original sin.'

It was the first dogma defined by a pope alone, without an ecumenical council, anticipating the definition of papal infallibility at the First Vatican Council in 1870. Four years later, in 1858, a Lady appeared to the peasant Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes and, asked her name, answered: 'I am the Immaculate Conception.'

events.title: The close of the Second Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: In St. Peter's Square, Pope Paul VI solemnly brought to an end the twenty-first ecumenical council, the largest in the Church's history…
body: On 8 December 1965, the feast of the Immaculate Conception, Pope Paul VI solemnly declared closed the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council, before a vast multitude assembled in St. Peter's Square. It was the twenty-first ecumenical council in the Church's history and by far the largest.

Opened by Pope John XXIII on 11 October 1962, the council met in four sessions over four autumns; two thousand eight hundred bishops came from every part of the world. It produced sixteen documents: four constitutions, nine decrees, and three declarations — among them Lumen Gentium on the Church, Dei Verbum on divine revelation, Sacrosanctum Concilium on the liturgy, and Gaudium et Spes on the Church in the modern world.

On the final morning the council's messages to rulers, thinkers and scientists, artists, workers, the poor and suffering, and the young were read aloud; then the fathers were sent home to carry the renewal into every diocese. No single event did more to shape Catholic life in the twentieth century.

sources.text: Vatican, Closing of the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council (1965) (vatican.va)

events.title: Luther burns the papal bull at Wittenberg
events.shortBlurb: Before a crowd outside Wittenberg, Martin Luther cast the papal bull threatening his excommunication into the flames, an open breach with Rome…
body: On 10 December 1520, outside the Elster Gate of Wittenberg, Martin Luther cast into a bonfire the bull Exsurge Domine, in which Pope Leo X had condemned forty-one propositions drawn from his writings and given him sixty days to recant or fall under excommunication. With the bull he threw into the flames volumes of the canon law, before a crowd of students and townsfolk.

The gesture was deliberate and public: Rome had ordered his books burned, and Luther now answered in kind, consigning the sentence of the Holy See itself to the flames. It amounted to an open and irrevocable repudiation of papal authority, beyond any hope of reconciliation.

On 3 January 1521 Leo X pronounced the excommunication by the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem. In April Luther stood before the Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms and refused to retract; outlawed, he was spirited away to the Wartburg by his prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony. The Reformation had passed the point of return.

events.title: Pius XI proclaims the Feast of Christ the King
events.shortBlurb: In the Holy Year encyclical Quas Primas, Pope Pius XI instituted a new feast honoring the kingship of Christ over all peoples and nations…
body: On 11 December 1925, in the closing days of the Holy Year, Pope Pius XI issued the encyclical Quas Primas and instituted a new feast in honor of the kingship of Christ, to be kept each year on the last Sunday of October.

Against the secularism of the age, which thrust religion out of public life, and the rising storms of nationalism and communism, the pope taught that Christ holds a true kingship over individuals, families, and states — a reign, he wrote, of truth and life, of holiness and grace, of justice, love, and peace — and that no society can prosper whose laws shut out the law of Christ.

Pius XI directed that on the new feast the consecration of mankind to the Sacred Heart should be renewed each year. In the calendar reform of Paul VI the solemnity was moved to the last Sunday of the liturgical year, where, as the feast of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, it now crowns the Church's year.

sources.text: Vatican, Encyclical Quas Primas of Pope Pius XI (1925) (vatican.va)

events.title: The abdication of Pope Celestine V
events.shortBlurb: Five months after his election, the hermit-pope Celestine V renounced the papacy, the first pope to resign of his own free will…
body: On 13 December 1294, at Naples, Pope Celestine V solemnly renounced the papacy after a reign of barely five months. He was Peter of Morrone, an aged hermit of the Abruzzi, who had been dragged from his mountain cell and elected on 5 July 1294, after the see of Peter had stood vacant for more than two years.

Unequal to the cares of the office and bewildered by the factions of the curia, he first issued a constitution affirming the pope's right to resign, drawn up, it was said, with the counsel of Cardinal Benedetto Caetani, and then laid down the burden, the first pope to abdicate of his own free will.

Caetani was elected in his place as Boniface VIII and, fearing the old hermit might become the tool of schismatics, kept him in custody; Celestine died at the castle of Fumone on 19 May 1296 and was canonized by Clement V in 1313. Dante placed at the gate of the Inferno the shade of him who made 'the great refusal', a verse many have read as pointing to Celestine.

events.title: The Council of Trent opens
events.shortBlurb: The great council of the Catholic Reformation began its work, defining doctrine and reforming discipline for centuries to come…
body: On 13 December 1545, in the choir of the cathedral of St. Vigilius at Trent, the nineteenth ecumenical council opened with the Mass of the Holy Ghost. Convoked by Pope Paul III after years of postponement by the bull Laetare Hierusalem of 19 November 1544, it was presided over by the cardinal legates Giovanni Maria del Monte, Marcello Cervini, and Reginald Pole.

The beginnings were small: besides the three legates there were present Cardinal Cristoforo Madruzzo, bishop of Trent, four archbishops, twenty-one bishops, and five generals of religious orders, with some forty theologians and nine canonists summoned as consultors. Few then foresaw the measure of what had been begun.

Meeting in twenty-five sessions across eighteen years, under three popes, the council answered the doctrines of the Protestant Reformation with definitions on Scripture and Tradition, original sin, justification, the seven sacraments, and the sacrifice of the Mass, and undertook a thorough reform of the clergy, decreeing the residence of bishops and the founding of seminaries in every diocese.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), General Church history

events.title: The Synod of Sutri
events.shortBlurb: A synod called by the German king Henry III swept away three rival claimants to the papacy and opened the era of reform…
body: On 20 December 1046, at Sutri, a town on the Cassian Way some thirty miles north of Rome, a synod convened under King Henry III of Germany confronted a scandal such as the Church had seldom seen: three men at once claiming the papacy — Benedict IX, Sylvester III, and Gregory VI.

Sylvester, who had been raised to the see when Benedict was driven out, was deposed and ordered into a monastery. Gregory, a devout man who had bought the office from Benedict in the hope of ending his misgovernment, confessed the simony of his purchase, pronounced himself unworthy, and stripped off the papal robes. Benedict, who had refused to appear, was declared deposed in his absence when the synod reassembled at Rome days later.

At Rome, days later, Henry presented Suidger, bishop of Bamberg, who was elected as Clement II and on Christmas Day crowned the king as emperor. Gregory VI was sent into exile in Germany, attended by his chaplain Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII. Sutri broke the hold of the Roman noble factions on the papacy and opened the age of reform.

events.title: The first recorded Christmas at Rome
events.shortBlurb: The oldest surviving record of the Church keeping the Nativity of Christ on 25 December points to the year 336 in the city of Rome…
body: The earliest firm evidence for the keeping of Christ's Nativity on 25 December comes from Rome and points to the year 336. The Chronograph of 354, an illustrated almanac compiled for a wealthy Roman Christian, preserves a list of the Church's commemorations that opens with the entry: 'eighth day before the Kalends of January, Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea.'

The calendar behind that list reflects Roman usage of about 336, so the feast was already established in the city by that date, within living memory of the persecutions. From Rome the observance of 25 December spread through the West and, in time, through much of the East, where 6 January had been the older feast of the Lord's manifestation.

Why that day was chosen, the ancients do not say. Some early Christians reckoned that the Lord died and was conceived on the same date, 25 March, and so placed his birth nine months later; others note that the feast falls where the sun begins to turn after the winter solstice, and Christ was hailed as the true Sun of Justice.

events.title: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Emperor
events.shortBlurb: On Christmas Day in St. Peter’s, Pope Leo III set a crown on the head of the Frankish king Charlemagne and hailed him Emperor, binding the fortunes of the Papacy and the West…
body: On Christmas Day of the year 800, during Mass in the basilica of St. Peter at Rome, as Charles, king of the Franks, knelt in prayer before the high altar, Pope Leo III set the imperial crown upon his head. The Romans thrice acclaimed him: 'To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor, life and victory'; and the pope did him reverence after the ancient manner.

The act crowned a year of crisis. In April 799 Leo had been assaulted in the streets of Rome by kinsmen of his predecessor Adrian I and left for dead; he escaped to Charles's camp at Paderborn and was restored to his see under Frankish protection. Two days before the coronation he had publicly sworn his innocence of the charges against him.

Einhard, the king's biographer, records that Charles afterward declared he would not have entered the church that day had he known the pope's design. Whether or not he was taken by surprise, the coronation revived the Western empire, vacant in name since 476, and bound the papacy and the Frankish monarchy in the partnership — often the struggle — that shaped medieval Christendom.

events.title: St. Francis makes the crib at Greccio
events.shortBlurb: In a hillside cave at Greccio, St. Francis of Assisi arranged the first Christmas crèche, that the birth of the Lord might be seen with the eyes…
body: At Christmas of 1223, three years before his death, Francis of Assisi kept the feast at Greccio, a village in the Rieti valley of central Italy. Wishing to set before the people's eyes the poverty of the Child born at Bethlehem, he had his friend, the nobleman Giovanni Velita, prepare a manger filled with hay, and an ox and an ass were led to the spot, as at Bethlehem.

Thomas of Celano, his first biographer, tells that Francis obtained leave of the pope, that the observance might not be thought a novelty. At midnight the brethren and the villagers gathered with candles, Mass was celebrated over the manger, and Francis, who was a deacon, sang the Gospel and preached with such tenderness on the birth of the Lord that he named him again and again 'the Babe of Bethlehem.'

Celano also records that one of those present saw in vision the figure of the Child lying lifeless in the manger, and that it stirred to life as Francis drew near and embraced it. From that night at Greccio the custom of the Christmas crib spread through the whole Church, becoming one of the most beloved devotions of Christendom.

events.title: The dedication of Hagia Sophia
events.shortBlurb: The Emperor Justinian dedicated at Constantinople the great church of Holy Wisdom, the wonder of Christian architecture for a thousand years…
body: The first church on the site, the Great Church of Constantinople, was dedicated by the Emperor Constantius II in 360; burned in the riots of 404 and rebuilt by Theodosius II in 415, it was destroyed again in the Nika revolt of January 532.

Within weeks of the fire Justinian I commissioned a new church from Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. In less than six years the church of the Holy Wisdom rose above the city, its dome, thirty metres across and ringed by forty windows, borne on pendentives so that it seemed, as Procopius wrote, to hang from heaven rather than rest on masonry.

On 27 December 537 Justinian dedicated the church; tradition holds that, entering it, he cried, 'Solomon, I have surpassed thee.' When earthquakes brought down the dome in 558, it was rebuilt by Isidore the Younger, nephew of the first architect, and the church was rededicated in 562.

For nearly a thousand years Hagia Sophia remained the cathedral of Constantinople, the seat of its patriarch and the place of imperial coronations, until the city fell to the Turks on 29 May 1453 and the great church was turned into a mosque.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Thomas Becket
events.shortBlurb: In his own cathedral at Canterbury, the archbishop Thomas Becket was cut down by four knights of King Henry II…
body: The blow was struck by four knights of the royal household — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard Brito — who had heard Henry II, in a rage at his archbishop's defiance, cry out, as tradition records the words, 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?' They crossed from Normandy and gathered at Saltwood Castle before riding on Canterbury.

In the late afternoon of 29 December 1170 they burst armed into the cathedral as the monks sang Vespers. Thomas refused to bar the doors or to flee, and near the altar of St. Benedict the knights cut him down with sword-strokes that spilled his brains upon the pavement; the clerk Edward Grim, who stood by him, was wounded in the arm.

The murderers fled to de Morville's castle of Knaresborough and, excommunicated, were sent to do penance in the Holy Land. All Christendom recoiled; Henry protested his innocence and in 1174 walked barefoot through Canterbury to be scourged by the monks at the tomb. The shrine raised over that tomb in 1220 drew pilgrims until Henry VIII plundered it in 1538 and burned the martyr's bones.

events.title: Paul VI's pilgrimage to the Holy Land
events.shortBlurb: Pope Paul VI landed at Amman and entered Jerusalem, the first pope to leave Italy in more than a century and a half and the first to come to the Holy Land since St. Peter…
body: On 4 January 1964 Pope Paul VI landed at Amman, where King Hussein of Jordan received him, and travelled on to Jerusalem, entering the Old City by the Damascus Gate. His three-day pilgrimage, announced barely a month before, was the first journey of a pope outside Italy since Pius VII had been carried off a prisoner of Napoleon in 1809, and the first ever made by air.

He had come, he said, as a pilgrim to the places where Christ had lived. He prayed at Gethsemane and along the Via Dolorosa, celebrated Mass in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and passed into Bethlehem; on 5 January he embraced Athenagoras, the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, on the Mount of Olives — the first meeting of a pope and a patriarch of Constantinople since the Council of Florence in 1438.

The journey, made while the Second Vatican Council was still in session, opened the age of the travelling papacy: nine international journeys would follow in his pontificate, from Bombay to the United Nations. The embrace with Athenagoras bore fruit two years later, when Rome and Constantinople together lifted the anathemas of 1054.

sources.text: Pope Paul VI, Apostolic Pilgrimage to the Holy Land, 4-6 January 1964 (vatican.va)

events.title: The election of Pope St. Pius V
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose the Dominican inquisitor Michele Ghislieri, who as Pius V would press the Council of Trent's reform upon the whole Church…
body: Born Antonio Ghislieri in 1504 at Bosco, near Alessandria in Piedmont, he entered the Dominicans at fourteen, taking the name Michele, and was ordained in 1528. A strict inquisitor in Lombardy, he was made bishop of Sutri in 1556, cardinal and grand inquisitor the next year, and bishop of Mondovì in 1560. On 7 January 1566, less than a month after the death of Pius IV, the cardinals elected him pope — largely, contemporaries said, through the influence of St. Charles Borromeo — and he took the name Pius V.

He was crowned on 17 January, his sixty-second birthday, and kept his white Dominican habit, whence the pope's white cassock to this day. His six years pressed the Council of Trent's decrees into practice: the Catechism of the council appeared in 1566, the reformed Roman Breviary in 1568, and the Roman Missal in 1570, which he imposed upon the whole Latin Church.
In 1570 he excommunicated Elizabeth I of England, and in 1571 the Holy League he had welded together broke the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto. He died on 1 May 1572 and was canonized by Clement XI in 1712.

events.title: The election of Pope Fabian
events.shortBlurb: A dove settling on the head of an unknown layman, as Eusebius records, marked Fabian as the Roman church's choice for its bishop…
body: After the death of Pope Anterus, who had sat barely forty days, the clergy and people of Rome assembled to choose a successor. Among them stood Fabian, a layman newly come in from the country, of whom no one had thought. In the received chronology the day was 10 January 236.

Eusebius relates that a dove suddenly descended upon Fabian's head, and that the assembly, taking the sight as a token of the Spirit's descent, chose him with one voice and set him in the chair of Peter.

His pontificate of some fourteen years fell in a lull between persecutions. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with dividing Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon; tradition sent St. Dionysius from his day to preach in Gaul; and St. Cyprian records that he condemned Privatus, a teacher of new error in Africa. He was to end as a martyr under Decius in 250.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 January

events.title: The death of St. Paulinus of Aquileia
events.shortBlurb: Charlemagne's grammarian-patriarch, hammer of the Adoptionists and apostle to the Avars, died at Aquileia…
body: Born about 726 on a farm near Friuli, Paulinus tilled his father's fields yet made himself so eminent a scholar that Charlemagne styled him in a rescript Master of Grammar and Very Venerable, bestowed an estate upon him, and raised him, against his will, to the patriarchate of Aquileia.

He stood at the emperor's side in the councils of the age — Aachen in 789, Ratisbon in 792, Frankfurt in 794 — and held his own synod at Friuli, where he vindicated the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. When Felix of Urgel taught that Christ as man was God's Son only by adoption, Paulinus refuted him in three books, and his Libellus Sacrosyllabus, approved at Frankfurt, was sent into Spain as an antidote to the spreading error.

His zeal reached beyond controversy: he preached the gospel to the pagan Carantani of Carinthia and Styria and to the Avars, and Alcuin counted him among his dearest friends. He died on 11 January, in 802 as the Catholic Encyclopedia and most modern scholars reckon, though his eighteenth-century biographer Madrisius gives 804; Aquileia now keeps his feast on 28 January.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 January

events.title: The death of St. Benedict Biscop
events.shortBlurb: The founder of Wearmouth and Jarrow, who gave England stone churches, glass windows, and books, and reared the Venerable Bede, died after three years of patient sickness…
body: Born about 628 of a noble Northumbrian family — his true name was Biscop Baducing — he served as a thegn of King Oswiu before renouncing the world at twenty-five for the first of five journeys to Rome. He took the monastic habit at Lérins, and in 668 Pope Vitalian sent him to guide Theodore of Tarsus, the new archbishop, to Canterbury.

King Ecgfrith gave him seventy hides of land at the mouth of the Wear, where in 674 he founded the monastery of St. Peter, Wearmouth, and forty more on the Tyne, where arose St. Paul's, Jarrow. From Gaul he brought masons to build in stone after the Roman fashion and glaziers, for the making of glass was then unknown in Britain; from Rome, books, relics, and pictures.

His library made possible the learning of Bede, whom he received as a boy of seven. Worn by a three-year palsy, he appointed Ceolfrith abbot of both houses and died on 12 January 690; the English Benedictines honour him as a patron of their congregation.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 January

events.title: The death of St. Sava, first Archbishop of Serbia
events.shortBlurb: The prince-monk who won autocephaly for the Serbian Church and became her first archbishop died at Tŭrnovo on his way home from the Holy Land…
body: Born Rastko, youngest son of Stefan Nemanja, the unifier of the Serbs, he fled as a youth to Mount Athos, where he was professed a monk with the name Sava. His father followed him there as the monk Simeon, and together they founded the monastery of Hilandar, still the centre of Serbian monastic life.

Returning home about 1208 to make peace between his quarrelling brothers, Sava rebuilt the Church's life in his land; in 1219, at Nicaea, Patriarch Manuel I consecrated him the first archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian Church. He organized her dioceses, formed a native clergy, gave her the Nomocanon, and crowned his brother Stephen as king.

Resigning in 1233, he set out on a second pilgrimage to the Holy Places, and on the journey home he died at Tŭrnovo, then the Bulgarian capital, on 14 January — in 1235 as most Western accounts reckon, 1236 in the Serbian tradition, which keeps his feast on 27 January by the civil reckoning. Buried in the church of the Holy Forty Martyrs, his relics were later translated to Mileševa and burned by the Turks in 1594.

events.title: The death of St. Maurus of Glanfeuil
events.shortBlurb: St. Benedict's first disciple, whom French tradition makes the apostle of Benedictine Gaul and the founder of Glanfeuil, died before the altar of St. Martin…
body: Maurus was twelve years old when, in 522, his father Equitius gave him to St. Benedict at Subiaco. He grew into the saint's coadjutor; St. Gregory the Great tells in his Dialogues how Maurus, sent at a word, walked upon the lake to draw out the drowning boy Placidus, and how Benedict afterwards called him to Monte Cassino about 528.

The French tradition, received in a Life written under the name of Faustus, tells that he came into Gaul in 543 and, by the liberality of King Theodebert, founded the great abbey of Glanfeuil on the Loire, afterwards called Saint-Maur-sur-Loire. Modern critics, Butler among them, judge that Life a pious forgery; yet the cult it served was ancient and real.

Resigning the abbacy in 581, he gave his last years to solitude, and died lying on sackcloth before the altar of St. Martin on 15 January 584. For fear of the Normans his relics were moved in 868 to Saint-Pierre-des-Fossés near Paris, which took from him the name Saint-Maur-des-Fossés; the English name Seymour descends from Saint Maur.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 January

events.title: The first Franciscan martyrs in Morocco
events.shortBlurb: Five friars sent by St. Francis to preach to the Saracens were slain by the king of Morocco with his own scimitar — the first martyrs of the new order…
body: Berard, Peter, Acursius, Adjutus, and Otto were sent by St. Francis in 1219 to preach to the Muslims of the West, while he went himself to those of the East. They preached first to the Moors of Seville, suffered much, and were banished; passing thence into Morocco, they preached Christ openly in Marrakech until the judge had them twice scourged till their ribs lay bare.
Burning oil and vinegar were poured into their wounds, and their bodies rolled over sharp stones and potsherds. At length the king, taking his scimitar, clove their heads asunder on 16 January 1220.

Their relics were ransomed and are kept in the monastery of the Holy Cross at Coimbra. There the fame of their sacrifice so moved a young Augustinian canon, Ferdinand — the future St. Anthony of Padua — that he took the Franciscan habit. Their names stand in the Roman Martyrology, and Sixtus IV canonized them in 1481, the first martyrs of the order Francis had founded eleven years before.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 January

events.title: The first Church Unity Octave
events.shortBlurb: At a poor friary in the Hudson highlands, an Episcopalian community began eight days of prayer for the reunion of Christians — the seed of the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity…
body: On 18 January 1908, then the feast of the Chair of St. Peter, Father Paul Wattson and Mother Lurana White led their little Society of the Atonement, a Franciscan community within the Episcopal Church, in the first Church Unity Octave, closing it on 25 January, the feast of the Conversion of St. Paul. The place was Graymoor, near Garrison in New York, and Wattson spread the observance through his magazine The Lamp.

The next year the friars and sisters of Graymoor were received into the Catholic Church, and Pius X gave the octave his blessing. In 1916 Benedict XV extended it, under the name of the Chair of Unity Octave, to the whole Church.

The observance outgrew its origin: since 1968 its materials have been prepared jointly with the Faith and Order commission of the World Council of Churches, and as the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity it is kept each year between the same two feasts by Christians of every communion.

sources.text: Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity (vatican.va)

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Blathmac at Iona
events.shortBlurb: The prior of Iona who would not betray the shrine of St. Columba to the Danish pirates was cut down at the morning Mass…
body: Blathmac, of Irish royal stock, gave up his patrimony for the cloister and, after governing a monastery in Ireland, came to Iona — the island St. Columba had made the lamp of the northern churches — seeking martyrdom; there he served as prior, keeping the community in the absence of its abbot Diarmait. The Northmen had burned Iona in 802 and slain sixty-eight of its monks in 806; the shrine of Columba had been solemnly restored in 818.

When the Danes came again, they found Blathmac celebrating the morning Mass. They demanded the shrine of St. Columba, with its gold and silver, and he, refusing to betray the treasures of the church, was struck down upon the altar steps. The Annals of Ulster record his martyrdom under 825; older writers placed it about 793, and the Catholic Encyclopedia about 835. The Irish calendars keep his memory on 19 January.

His life was written in Latin hexameters by Walafrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau, and so the story of his witness has been handed down. The relics of Columba were at last carried to Ireland in 849 for safety, and Iona's day as the mother house of the Gaelic church drew towards its close.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 January

events.title: The martyrdom of Pope St. Fabian
events.shortBlurb: The pope chosen under the sign of the dove was among the first to fall when the emperor Decius loosed his persecution upon the Church…
body: In the first days of 250 the emperor Decius commanded sacrifice to the gods throughout the empire, and the blow fell first upon the shepherds. Fabian, bishop of Rome for fourteen years, was seized and died a martyr on 20 January 250; whether by the sword or in prison, the sources leave uncertain.

St. Cyprian, writing to his successor Cornelius, called him an incomparable man, whose glory in death answered the purity and holiness of his life. He was buried in the catacomb of Callixtus on the Appian Way, where his grave slab, broken in pieces, still bears the Greek words: Fabian, bishop, martyr.

His death opened the first great test of the Church under a general persecution: the see of Rome stood vacant for more than a year while the storm raged, and when Cornelius was at last chosen, the question of those who had lapsed under the trial would divide the Church for a generation.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 January

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Fructuosus of Tarragona
events.shortBlurb: A bishop and his two deacons were burned alive in the amphitheatre of Tarraco, the protomartyrs of Christian Spain…
body: In the persecution of Valerian, Fructuosus, bishop of Tarraco on the Catalan coast, was taken in the night of 16 January 259 with his two deacons, Augurius and Eulogius, and kept in prison five days. On 21 January they were tried by the governor Aemilianus; the bishop confessed Christ and his office — "I am a bishop," he answered, and the governor said, "You were" — and all three were sentenced to be burned alive.

Led to the amphitheatre, the bishop refused the cup of spiced wine, for it was a Wednesday and the hour of breaking the fast had not come, and declared that he must pray for the whole Catholic Church spread through east and west. When the fire had burned through their bonds, the three knelt with outstretched arms in the form of a cross and gave up their souls.

That night the faithful gathered their ashes and laid them beneath the altar. Their acts are among the most genuine of antiquity: St. Augustine preached their praise in a sermon that survives, and the poet Prudentius sang them in his Peristephanon.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 January

events.title: The founding of Georgetown College
events.shortBlurb: On a hilltop above the Potomac, John Carroll secured the ground for the first Catholic institution of higher learning in the United States…
body: Under colonial law Catholics in America had been forbidden to conduct schools; the Revolution made a Catholic college possible. John Carroll of Maryland, a former Jesuit and from 1784 the head of the American missions, had planned such an academy with his fellow clergy since 1783, published his Proposals in 1786, and seen building begun in 1788.

On 23 January 1789 Carroll received the first deed for the hilltop property at Georgetown, above the Potomac — the date the university still keeps as its founding. In the same year he was chosen the first bishop of the United States.

The college welcomed its first student, William Gaston, in November 1791, and instruction began the following January; from 1805 it has been directed by the Society of Jesus; and in 1815 an act of Congress signed by President Madison granted its charter. It remains the oldest Catholic university in the country.

events.title: The translation of St. John Chrysostom's relics
events.shortBlurb: Thirty years after the golden-mouthed preacher died in exile, his relics came home to Constantinople in a procession of imperial repentance…
body: St. John Chrysostom had died at Comana in Pontus on 14 September 407, exiled by the court whose vices he had rebuked, his last words a doxology: Glory be to God for all things. Thirty years later his disciple Proclus, then patriarch, preached his praise in Constantinople until the people begged for the relics' return.

The emperor Theodosius II sent envoys with a silver reliquary to Comana, and, since his mother Eudoxia had driven John into exile, wrote with his own hand a letter asking the saint's forgiveness. The relics were borne to the capital with the utmost pomp, the emperor and his sister Pulcheria walking in the procession and begging pardon for the sins of their parents.
