They were laid in the Church of the Holy Apostles, the burying-place of emperors and bishops, on 27 January 438 — the day on which the Latin Church long kept his feast, while the Greeks kept 13 November. In 1204 the crusaders carried much of the treasure westward to Rome.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 January

events.title: The death of Pope Gelasius II at Cluny
events.shortBlurb: Hunted from Rome by the emperor's faction, Pope Gelasius II died in exile at Cluny after a pontificate of a single year…
body: John of Gaeta, a monk of Monte Cassino, had been made cardinal in 1088 and chancellor in 1089 by Urban II, and had served Paschal II in the same office. On 24 January 1118 the cardinals chose him pope as Gelasius II — and that very night the Frangipani, the emperor's allies in Rome, seized and maltreated him until the people broke in and set him free.

He fled to Gaeta, where he was ordained priest and consecrated bishop in March, while Henry V set up the excommunicated archbishop of Braga as the antipope Gregory VIII. From Capua that April Gelasius excommunicated the emperor and his creature, and when Rome could no longer hold him he sailed by Pisa into France.

He reached the abbey of Cluny and died there on 29 January 1119, having suffered more in one year, his contemporaries said, than any pope since the age of the martyrs. The cardinals with him chose Callixtus II in the same abbey on 2 February, and three years later the Concordat of Worms brought the long struggle over investiture towards its end.

events.title: The death of St. Aldegundis of Maubeuge
events.shortBlurb: The Merovingian princess who founded the double monastery of Maubeuge and bore slander and cancer without complaint died on 30 January…
body: Aldegundis was born about 639 in Hainault, daughter of Walbert and Bertilia, of the kindred of the Merovingian kings, and sister of St. Waldetrudis of Mons. Consecrating herself to God in her youth, she resisted every suit of marriage and received the veil from St. Amandus, bishop of Maastricht; then, about 661, she founded on the banks of the Sambre the abbey of Maubeuge, a house of nuns which she governed as its first abbess.

Her life was a hidden one of prayer, tried by violent slanders and, at the end, by a lingering cancer of the breast, whose tortures — the caustics and incisions of the surgeons — she bore, Butler says, not only with patience but with joy.

She died on 30 January, in 684 as most modern accounts reckon, though Butler, following the Bollandists, gives 660. Her relics were enshrined at Maubeuge; her name stands on this day in the martyrologies of Rabanus Maurus, Usuard, and Notker, and in the Roman Martyrology; and she is invoked as a patroness of those who suffer from cancer.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 January

events.title: The death of St. Maedoc of Ferns
events.shortBlurb: The pupil of St. David who became the first bishop of Ferns and one of the fathers of the Leinster church died on 31 January…
body: Maedoc — called also Aidan, and in the endearments of Irish speech Mogue and Maodhog — was born in Connacht about the middle of the sixth century. Passing into Wales, he lived long under the direction of the holy abbot David at Menevia, and returned to Ireland with a company of monks of eminent piety.

He founded many churches and monasteries, the chief about 598 at Ferns in the Wexford country, on land granted in the territory of the Ui Cheinnselaig, and was made its first bishop; the monastic school there became one of the glories of the Leinster church.

He died on 31 January, in 632 as Ussher reckons, though the annals are divided between 624 and 632. His feast was kept in Wales in the twelfth century, as Giraldus witnesses, and in Scotland the chronicle of Scone and the Aberdeen breviary prayed for the divine mercy through his intercession. He remains the patron of the diocese of Ferns.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 January

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Henry Morse
events.shortBlurb: Hanged at Tyburn after three banishments and four imprisonments, the plague-year priest of London gave his life for the Catholic mission to England…
body: On 1 February 1645, by the new reckoning — England still called the year 1644 — Henry Morse, a priest of the Society of Jesus, was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn under the statute that made his priesthood treason. Born at Brome in Suffolk in 1595 and bred to the law, he had been received into the Church as a young man, trained at Douai and at the English College at Rome, and ordained in 1623.

He labored first in the north of England, and made his Jesuit novitiate behind prison walls. In London during the plague years of 1636 and 1637 he ministered to the sick beside St. John Southworth, himself falling ill yet returning to his stricken flock. Thrice banished and four times imprisoned, he was seized at last in Cumberland amid the Civil War and brought to the capital for trial.
At the gallows he forgave his enemies and professed that he died for the faith alone. In 1970 Pope Paul VI canonized him among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

events.title: The death of St. Ansgar, Apostle of the North
events.shortBlurb: The Apostle of the North died at Bremen after forty years of patient mission among the Danes and the Swedes…
body: On 3 February 865 St. Ansgar died at Bremen, aged about sixty-three. Born near Amiens in 801 and a monk of Corbie and then of Corvey, he was sent by the Emperor Louis the Pious to preach to the Danes in 826, and about the years 829 to 831 he sowed the faith at Birka in Sweden.

Consecrated about 831 the first archbishop of Hamburg, with a mandate to bring Christianity to the northern peoples, he saw his city burned by Viking pirates in 845; about 849 the see of Bremen was joined to his charge, and from there he patiently rebuilt his ruined mission, ransoming captives, founding churches, and winning the confidence of kings.

His disciple and successor Rimbert wrote the Vita Anskarii, the chief record of his life, which praises his prayer and his humility above his miracles. He is honored as the Enlightener of Denmark and Sweden, and the Church keeps his feast on the day of his death.

sources.text: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii (tr. Robinson, Anskar: The Apostle of the North, 1921; public domain)

events.title: The Twenty-Six Martyrs of Japan
events.shortBlurb: On a hill above Nagasaki, twenty-six missionaries and Japanese faithful were crucified rather than renounce Christ…
body: On 5 February 1597, on the hill of Nishizaka overlooking Nagasaki, twenty-six Christians were raised on crosses and pierced with spears: six Franciscan missionaries — Spaniards, a Portuguese, and the Mexican-born Felipe de Jesús — three Japanese Jesuits, Paul Miki, John Goto, and James Kisai, and seventeen Japanese lay Franciscans, among them three boys, the youngest twelve years old.

Seized at Kyoto and Osaka by order of the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who since 1587 had forbidden the missionaries, they had their ears cropped and were marched some five hundred miles through the winter to the place of execution, that their death might terrify the most Christian city of Japan.

From his cross Paul Miki preached his last sermon, forgiving his persecutors and confessing that there is no way to salvation but the Christian way. The martyrs were beatified by Urban VIII in 1627 and canonized by Pius IX in 1862; the universal Church keeps their memory on 6 February, but Japan honors them on the day of their triumph.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Sts. Peter Baptist and Twenty-Five Companions”

events.title: The election of Pope Pius XI
events.shortBlurb: A librarian from Milan became pope and blessed the world from the loggia no pope had used since 1870…
body: On 6 February 1922, on the fourteenth ballot of the conclave that had opened four days before after the death of Benedict XV, Cardinal Achille Ratti, Archbishop of Milan, was elected pope and took the name Pius XI. Born at Desio in 1857, he had been prefect of the Ambrosian Library in Milan and then of the Vatican Library, nuncio to the reborn Poland, and a cardinal only since the previous June.

His first act was a sign read round the world: he gave the blessing Urbi et Orbi from the outer loggia of St. Peter's, which no pope had used since the loss of Rome in 1870, as if to say the self-imposed imprisonment of the Vatican would not last. Seven years later he sealed the Lateran Pacts.
His seventeen-year pontificate gave the Church the encyclicals Quadragesimo anno and Mit brennender Sorge, the feast of Christ the King, Vatican Radio, and a long roll of canonizations.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope Pius XI (vatican.va)

events.title: St. Athanasius flees into the desert
events.shortBlurb: When soldiers broke into the church of St. Theonas at the night vigil, the champion of Nicaea vanished into the desert…
body: In the night of 8 February 356, while St. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria since 328, kept a vigil with his people in the church of St. Theonas, the troops of the general Syrianus surrounded the building — more than five thousand men, the historians reckon — broke down the doors, and pressed up the nave with arrows flying.

The bishop sat upon his throne and bade the deacon intone Psalm 136, that the people might answer “for his mercy endureth for ever”; he would not stir until his flock had escaped, and then his clergy hurried him, half fainting, through the tumult. He was carried to safety among the monks of the desert, who hid him for six years and never betrayed him.

It was his third exile for the Nicene faith. The intruded George of Cappadocia took the see, but Athanasius returned under Julian in 362, outlived the enmity of four emperors, and died in 373, the unbowed confessor of the divinity of the Son.

sources.text: Gwatkin, The Arian Controversy (1914; public domain)

events.title: The execution of Mary Queen of Scots
events.shortBlurb: Condemned for the Babington plot, the captive queen went to the block at Fotheringhay professing the Catholic faith…
body: On the morning of 8 February 1587 Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots, was beheaded in the great hall of Fotheringhay Castle, after nineteen years of captivity in England. A commission of thirty-six noblemen had condemned her the previous October for complicity in the Babington plot against Queen Elizabeth, whose death warrant was signed on 1 February.

She went to the block as to a sacrifice, bearing a crucifix and a Latin book of hours; denied her chaplain, she prayed aloud in Latin and in English, forgave her enemies, and declared that she died a true Catholic. In her last letter, written six hours before to the King of France, she named as the cause of her death “the Catholic faith and the assertion of my God-given right to the English crown.”

Catholic Europe mourned her as a martyr of the faith, and her death hardened the counsels that sent the Spanish Armada the following year. Buried first at Peterborough, she was translated in 1612 by her son, King James I, to a royal tomb in Westminster Abbey.

events.title: St. John Vianney is sent to Ars
events.shortBlurb: A peasant's son who had failed his examinations was sent to a forgotten village and made it the confessional of France…
body: On 9 February 1818, a few weeks after the death of his mentor the Abbé Balley, the young priest Jean-Baptiste-Marie Vianney was appointed parish priest of Ars, a hamlet of some two hundred and thirty souls in the Dombes, north of Lyon, whose faith had grown cold since the Revolution.

Born at Dardilly in 1786 and ordained in 1815 after long struggles with Latin, he found the village so little known that, the story runs, he lost his way to it and was set right by a boy minding sheep. For more than forty years he prayed, fasted, preached against dancing and blasphemy, and reconciled sinners to God.

Ars became a place of pilgrimage: by the 1850s tens of thousands came every year, and the curé spent as many as sixteen hours a day in the confessional. He died in 1859, was canonized in 1925, and is the patron of parish priests throughout the world.

events.title: The death of Pope Pius XI
events.shortBlurb: The pope of the Lateran Pacts died on the eve of an address he meant to raise against the racial laws…
body: On 10 February 1939 Pope Pius XI died in the Vatican, aged eighty-one, on the eve of the day appointed for an address to the bishops of Italy gathered for the tenth anniversary of the Lateran Pacts — an address, it was said, in which he meant to speak plainly against the racial laws then spreading in Europe.

Born Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti at Desio in 1857 and elected in 1922, he had reigned seventeen years: he settled the Roman Question in 1929, wrote Quadragesimo anno and Mit brennender Sorge, instituted the feast of Christ the King, founded Vatican Radio, and canonized St. Thomas More and St. John Fisher together in 1935.

He was buried in the grottoes of St. Peter's, and on 2 March the cardinals chose in his place his Secretary of State, Eugenio Pacelli, who took the name Pius XII — a succession that opened on the very brink of the Second World War.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope Pius XI (vatican.va)

events.title: The birth of Vatican Radio
events.shortBlurb: Marconi built it, and a pope's voice went out for the first time to all peoples and every creature…
body: On 12 February 1931 Pope Pius XI inaugurated the Vatican Radio, the Statio Radiophonica Vaticana, built for the Holy See within the Vatican Gardens by Guglielmo Marconi, the pioneer of wireless telegraphy, and blessed the instruments that were to carry the apostolic word to peoples far away.

The first voice carried on its waves was Marconi's, announcing that the Pope's voice could now be heard “simultaneously over the entire surface of the earth”; then Pius XI himself spoke in Latin, in the message Qui arcano Dei, opening with the words of Isaiah, “Hear, O islands, and listen, O distant peoples,” and addressing “all peoples and every creature” — the first broadcast of a pope in history.

From that day the Pope's Radio has carried the Gospel, the teaching of the successors of Peter, and the news of the Church to every continent, in more than forty languages; it stands today at the heart of Vatican News, ninety-five years on.

sources.text: Vatican, “February 12, 1931, the day Vatican Radio was born” (comunicazione.va)

events.title: Galileo arrives in Rome to face the Inquisition
events.shortBlurb: Old and ailing, the astronomer reached Rome to answer for the Dialogue before the Inquisition…
body: On 13 February 1633 Galileo Galilei, in his sixty-ninth year and in poor health, reached Rome to stand trial before the Roman Inquisition, and was lodged as the guest of Francesco Niccolini, the Grand Duke's ambassador, at the Villa Medici.

Summoned the previous October after the publication of his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, he had pleaded age and infirmity; but Urban VIII was inexorable, threatening to have him brought in chains, and on 20 January the old man set out from Florence upon the weary journey.

The trial opened in April, and on 22 June he knelt in Santa Maria sopra Minerva and abjured the Copernican opinion, passing the rest of his life under guard at Arcetri, where he died in 1642. The Church has since acknowledged the wrong of his condemnation; a commission appointed by John Paul II closed its work in 1992.

events.title: The bull Pie postulatio voluntatis
events.shortBlurb: Paschal II's bull made the Hospitallers of St. John an order under the Church's own protection…
body: On 15 February 1113 Pope Paschal II issued the bull Pie postulatio voluntatis, taking the hospital of St. John in Jerusalem and its brethren under the protection of the Apostolic See, and granting them the right to choose their own superiors — the founding charter of the Order known in later ages as the Knights of Malta.

The fraternity had grown from a hospice founded by merchants of Amalfi about the year 1048, near the church of the Holy Sepulchre, to care for poor and sick pilgrims; under its first master, the Blessed Gerard, it had nursed the suffering through the siege of Jerusalem in 1099.

The original bull is treasured to this day in the National Library of Malta at Valletta. In February 2013, nine hundred years on, Benedict XVI received the knights in St. Peter's and praised nine centuries of fidelity to the Church and to “our lords the sick.”

sources.text: Benedict XVI, Address to the Order of Malta for the 900th anniversary of Pie postulatio voluntatis, 9 February 2013 (vatican.va)

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Juliana
events.shortBlurb: The martyrologies keep her name at Cumae on this day, and Gregory the Great himself sent her relics…
body: Ancient tradition holds that St. Juliana was martyred about the year 304, in the persecution of Diocletian. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum keeps her memory on 16 February at Cumae, in Campania, and both the Latin and the Greek churches honor her name.

That her cult is old is certain: St. Gregory the Great, writing to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, granted the matron Januaria's request for relics of St. Juliana for the consecration of a church on her estate. Her later acts are legend — that she was a maiden of Nicomedia who refused a heathen bridegroom, was cruelly tortured, and at last beheaded — but the veneration is genuine, and older than the story.

Her relics were treasured near Naples, and her patronage spread through the West; painters loved to show her triumph over the dragon, and the Church still names her among the virgins and martyrs of the age of persecution.

events.title: The burning of Giordano Bruno
events.shortBlurb: The philosopher of infinite worlds was burned in the Campo de' Fiori after eight years in the Inquisition's prisons…
body: On 17 February 1600 Giordano Bruno of Nola, a former Dominican friar aged fifty-two, was burned alive in the Campo de' Fiori at Rome, delivered by the Roman Inquisition to the secular arm after some eight years in its prisons.

Denounced at Venice in 1592 by his host Giovanni Mocenigo and transferred to Rome the next year, he was tried for heresies touching the faith and would not abjure. He had wandered through Europe teaching a philosophy of infinite worlds; condemned under Pope Clement VIII, he heard the sentence — tradition preserves his answer — warning his judges that perhaps they pronounced it with more fear than he received it.

In 1889 a statue was raised upon the spot, and Bruno became an emblem of free thought. The Church of our day still judges his doctrines erroneous, yet a spokesman of the Holy See has called his death a sad episode and a matter of deep regret.

events.title: The death of Fra Angelico
events.shortBlurb: The angelic friar who painted to preach died at the Minerva and lies there still…
body: On 18 February 1455 the Dominican painter Fra Giovanni da Fiesole, whom the world calls Fra Angelico, died at the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, and was buried there, where his tomb is still shown.

Born Guido di Pietro at Vicchio near Florence about 1395, he entered the Order of Preachers at Fiesole and took up the brush to preach: the Annunciation and the cells of San Marco in Florence, the San Marco altarpiece, and the chapel of Pope Nicholas V in the Vatican are his. Vasari hands down that, offered the archbishopric of Florence, he begged the pope to give it to Fra Antonino instead.

Beatified by John Paul II in 1982 and named patron of artists, he is honored on the day of his death — the “angelic friar,” who, his brethren said, never took up his pencil without first falling to his knees in prayer.

events.title: The death of Martin Luther
events.shortBlurb: The reformer died in the town of his birth, leaving a Bible in German and a Christendom divided…
body: In the early morning of 18 February 1546 Martin Luther died at Eisleben, the town of his birth, whither he had journeyed in January to arbitrate a quarrel of the counts of Mansfeld. He was sixty-two, had preached for the last time four days before, and his friend Justus Jonas was among the watchers at his bedside.

Born in 1483, an Augustinian friar ordained in 1507 and doctor of theology at Wittenberg, he had set the world alight with the Ninety-Five Theses of 1517, stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521, and in 1525 married the former nun Katharina von Bora, the mother of his six children. He died excommunicate, the author of a German Bible and of a reform that split Western Christendom.

His last scribbled note ended with the words “We are beggars, that is true.” The body was borne to Wittenberg and laid in the Castle Church on 22 February; his teaching lives on in the churches that bear his name.

events.title: The Treaty of Tolentino
events.shortBlurb: Bonaparte spared Rome, and the Pope paid with Avignon, the Legations, and thirty million francs…
body: On 19 February 1797, at Tolentino in the Marches, Pope Pius VI signed a treaty of peace with General Bonaparte. The Pope had broken the armistice of Bologna, and the French army, fresh from Rivoli and the fall of Mantua, had swept the papal troops aside and stood within reach of Rome.

The price of peace was heavy: the Pope renounced Avignon and the Venaissin, annexed by France in 1791, ceded the Legations of Bologna, Ferrara, and the Romagna, and promised thirty million francs for the Directory — besides the pictures, statues, and manuscripts already exacted by the armistice of Bologna.

It bought the papacy a year's respite. When a French general was killed in a Roman riot, the Directory answered with occupation: in February 1798 a Roman Republic was proclaimed in the city, and Pius VI, an old man, was carried into exile, dying at Valence on 29 August 1799.

events.title: The death of Pope Julius II
events.shortBlurb: The warrior pope who laid the cornerstone of St. Peter's and set Michelangelo to work is dead…
body: In the night of 20-21 February 1513 Pope Julius II died in Rome, in his seventieth year. Born Giuliano della Rovere at Albisola in 1443, a nephew of Sixtus IV, he had been elected on 1 November 1503 and reigned as the warrior pope, restoring the States of the Church by arms and by craft.

He expelled the Bentivogli from Bologna in 1506, humbled Venice by the League of Cambrai, turned the Holy League against France, and in 1512 opened the Fifth Lateran Council. He laid the cornerstone of the new St. Peter's in 1506, set Michelangelo to the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel and Raphael to the Stanze, and founded the Swiss Guard.
Michelangelo's Moses, carved for the tomb Julius had planned, still watches over him at San Pietro in Vincoli. On 9 March Giovanni de' Medici succeeded him, taking the name Leo X.

events.title: The Battle of Benevento
events.shortBlurb: On the Calore plain Manfred of Hohenstaufen fell, and the Guelph cause triumphed with Charles of Anjou…
body: On 26 February 1266, on the plain of the Calore beside Benevento, Charles of Anjou, count of Provence and brother of St. Louis IX, defeated the army of Manfred, King of Sicily, the bastard son of the Emperor Frederick II, who fell fighting on the field.

The popes Urban IV and Clement IV, long at war with the house of Hohenstaufen, had called Charles into Italy and invested him with the Sicilian crown; anointed at Rome on the Epiphany of 1266, he marched south, crossed the Garigliano by the treachery of Manfred's allies, and in one bloody afternoon broke the power of Frederick's heirs.

Dante met Manfred's soul at the gate of Purgatory, buried under a cairn of stones — before the Church had his bones cast out of her lands. Two years later, on 23 August 1268 at Tagliacozzo, Charles crushed Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, and the Angevin ruled in Naples.

events.title: The resignation of Benedict XVI takes effect
events.shortBlurb: At eight in the evening the first papal resignation in six centuries took effect, and the See of Peter fell vacant…
body: At eight o'clock in the evening of 28 February 2013 the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI took effect, and the Apostolic See fell vacant. He had declared it seventeen days before, on 11 February, in Latin, before the cardinals in consistory, pleading his failing strength of mind and body.

That last morning he took leave of the College of Cardinals in the Clementine Hall, then flew by helicopter to Castel Gandolfo, telling the crowd from the balcony that he would soon be “simply a pilgrim beginning the last leg of his pilgrimage on this earth.” At eight the Swiss Guard closed the doors of the palace and stood down.

No pope had laid down the office since Gregory XII in 1415, and none freely since St. Celestine V in 1294. The conclave that followed elected Pope Francis on 13 March; Benedict lived on in prayer at the Mater Ecclesiae monastery in the Vatican until his death on 31 December 2022.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Hilarius
events.shortBlurb: Leo the Great's legate at the Robber Synod ended his days on a leap day, and was buried by St. Lawrence…
body: Pope St. Hilarius died on 29 February 468 — a leap day — after six years, three months, and ten days upon the chair of Peter; some martyrologies place his death on 28 February, the day of his feast.

A Sardinian by birth and the trusted archdeacon of St. Leo the Great, he had been Leo's legate at the Second Council of Ephesus in 449 — the Robber Synod — where alone he protested the condemnation of Flavian and barely escaped the violence of Dioscorus' party; in thanksgiving he afterwards built at the Lateran the oratories of St. John the Baptist and St. John the Evangelist.

As pope he confirmed the faith of Chalcedon, corrected abuses in the churches of Gaul and Spain, and held in 465 the oldest Roman synod whose acts survive; he built libraries and a chapel of the Holy Cross by the Lateran, and was buried in the basilica of St. Lawrence-outside-the-Walls.

sources.text: Liber Pontificalis (tr. Loomis, The Book of the Popes, 1916; public domain)

events.title: The massacre of Vassy
events.shortBlurb: Troops of the Duke of Guise fell upon a Huguenot congregation at worship in Champagne, and the bloodshed opened France's Wars of Religion…
body: In January 1562 the regent Catherine de' Medici, seeking to hold France together, granted the Huguenots a measure of toleration by the Edict of Saint-Germain, permitting their worship outside the walled towns. Passing through Champagne on 1 March 1562, Francis, second Duke of Guise, came upon six or seven hundred Reformed Christians singing psalms in a barn at Vassy, within the town's liberties and so beyond the edict's leave.

Words were exchanged, stones flew, and the duke's men fired and charged; when the melee ended twenty-three worshippers lay dead and more than a hundred wounded — so the Catholic Encyclopedia's account, while Huguenot writers reckoned the slain far higher and named the deed a massacre.

The news raced through France. Condé and Coligny took up arms, seizing Orléans within the month, and Guise's party answered in kind: the first of the eight Wars of Religion had begun, a struggle that would burn for more than thirty years, through St. Bartholomew's Day and the League, until the Edict of Nantes closed it in 1598.

events.title: The election of Pope Pius XII
events.shortBlurb: On his sixty-third birthday Eugenio Pacelli was chosen pope in the swiftest conclave of modern times, on the eve of world war…
body: Pius XI died on 10 February 1939, and the conclave that assembled on 1 March proved the shortest of modern times. On the second day, 2 March, the cardinals chose Eugenio Pacelli on the third ballot — his sixty-third birthday — and he took the name Pius XII. He was the first cardinal Secretary of State to be elected pope since Clement IX in 1667.

Born in Rome on 2 March 1876 and ordained in 1899, Pacelli had spent his priesthood in the Holy See's diplomacy: nuncio in Munich and Berlin through the First World War and the Weimar years, cardinal in 1929, then Secretary of State, negotiating the 1933 Concordat with the German Reich and sharing in the drafting of Pius XI's protest Mit brennender Sorge.

His election was the first announced to the world by radio. Crowned on 12 March, he guided the Church through the Second World War and the age of communism that followed, defining the dogma of the Assumption in 1950, before dying at Castel Gandolfo on 9 October 1958.

events.title: The election of Pope Eugene IV
events.shortBlurb: A Venetian nephew of Gregory XII was chosen pope in the first conclave after the Great Schism, and his stormy reign saw union proclaimed with the Greeks…
body: Martin V died on 20 February 1431, and in the first conclave held since the healing of the Great Schism the cardinals chose, on 3 March 1431 — or on the fourth, as some older authorities reckon — Gabriele Condulmer of Venice, a nephew of Gregory XII made cardinal in 1408. Crowned on 11 March, he took the name Eugene IV.

His long pontificate was a running battle with the conciliar movement: he dissolved the Council of Basel at its opening in 1431, was driven from Rome into exile at Florence in 1434, and fought for years to recover his city. Yet it was Eugene who presided over the Council of Ferrara and Florence, where on 6 July 1439 the decree Laetentur Caeli proclaimed union with the Greeks.

In Florence he also consecrated, on 25 March 1436, the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore beneath Brunelleschi's new dome. Restored to Rome in 1443, he died there on 23 February 1447, having held the papacy through some of its most turbulent years.

events.title: The birth of Prince Henry the Navigator
events.shortBlurb: The Portuguese prince who sent his captains ever southward down the African coast was born at Porto, and the age of discovery had begun…
body: Henry, called the Navigator, was born at Porto on 4 March 1394, a younger son of King John I of Portugal and Philippa of Lancaster. At twenty-one he fought at the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, and from 1420 he was governor of the Order of Christ, turning its revenues to the work that filled his life: the exploration of the African coast.

Year by year his captains felt their way south — rediscovering Porto Santo in 1418 and Madeira in 1420 and settling them, passing the dreaded Cape Bojador under Gil Eanes in 1434, and reaching the Senegal and the Gambia in the 1440s. The voyages sought gold and allies against Islam — the fabled Prester John — and carried the Cross to unbaptized peoples.

Later tradition has made his retreat at Sagres a school of navigation, though historians doubt its formal existence. Henry died there on 13 November 1460; within two generations the path he opened had carried Dias to the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and da Gama to India in 1498.

events.title: The Third Lateran Council
events.shortBlurb: Alexander III gathered the Church at the Lateran to repair the schism — and fixed the two-thirds rule by which popes are chosen still…
body: Fresh from the Peace of Venice, which in 1177 had ended his eighteen-year schism with Frederick Barbarossa and a line of antipopes, Alexander III summoned the Church to the Lateran. The council opened on 5 March 1179, as Archbishop William of Tyre, our chief witness, records, with some three hundred bishops and a great body of abbots gathered about the pope.

In three sessions the fathers issued twenty-seven canons. The first reserved papal elections to the cardinals alone and required a two-thirds majority — the rule by which conclaves have been governed ever since. Others condemned the Cathar heretics of southern France and the mercenary bands then ravaging Christendom, forbade Jews and Muslims to keep Christian servants, and charged every cathedral church to maintain a schoolmaster for poor scholars.

Reckoned the eleventh ecumenical council, the Third Lateran repaired the wreckage of the schism and set the legal frame of the medieval papacy on firmer ground; thirty-six years later Innocent III would build upon it at the Fourth.

events.title: The death of Pope Celestine II
events.shortBlurb: A gentle scholar who had studied under Abelard, he reigned only five months and lifted the interdict from France…
body: Guido di Castello had sat at the feet of Peter Abelard and kept his friendship even after the master's condemnation at Sens in 1140. Made cardinal-deacon by Honorius II in 1127 and cardinal-priest of San Marco by Innocent II, whom he had served as legate in France, he was chosen pope on 26 September 1143 and consecrated on 3 October.

His brief reign was merciful: one of his first acts lifted the interdict Innocent II had laid upon France in the quarrel over the archbishopric of Bourges, restoring King Louis VII to the Church's peace. A harder contest, over the legatine rights claimed by King Roger II of Sicily, he left unsettled.

After five months and thirteen days Celestine died at Rome on 8 March 1144, at the Palladium monastery on the Palatine — of the plague then wasting Italy, says the old account — and was buried at the Lateran. His short pontificate closed quietly, while in France his old master Abelard's troubles were ending at Cluny.

events.title: The election of Pope Leo X
events.shortBlurb: A Medici deacon of thirty-seven became pope — patron of Raphael's Rome, and the pope who excommunicated Martin Luther…
body: Julius II died on 21 February 1513, and the conclave that followed chose, on 9 March, Cardinal Giovanni de' Medici, second son of Lorenzo the Magnificent; proclaimed two days later, he took the name Leo X. Made a cardinal at thirteen, he had been only a deacon: he was ordained priest on 15 March, consecrated bishop on the seventeenth, and crowned on the nineteenth — the last man not yet a priest to be elected pope.

His eight years were golden and ruinous together: the Rome of Raphael and the rising St. Peter's, and the preaching of indulgences to pay for it, which moved Martin Luther to post his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517. Leo answered with Exsurge Domine in 1520, condemning forty-one propositions, and with the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem of 3 January 1521, which excommunicated Luther.
He died on 1 December 1521, aged forty-five, leaving the papal treasury deep in debt and Christendom on the edge of its great division.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. John Ogilvie
events.shortBlurb: Scotland's only post-Reformation martyr was hanged at Glasgow Cross for refusing the king's supremacy over the Church…
body: Born about 1580 at Drumnakeith in Banffshire and raised a Calvinist, John Ogilvie was received into the Church at Louvain in 1597 and entered the Society of Jesus two years later. Ordained at Paris in 1613, he begged for the Scottish mission and returned home that November, disguised as a horse trader, to minister in secret about Glasgow.

His mission lasted less than a year. Arrested in October 1614, he was tortured by sleeplessness and pressed to own King James's supremacy in the Church, which he refused — he would acknowledge it, he said, no more than that of an old hat. Condemned for treason, he was hanged at Glasgow Cross on 10 March 1615, throwing his hidden rosary into the crowd as he died.

Out of open popular sympathy the customary quartering was spared him. Beatified in 1929, he was canonized by Paul VI on 17 October 1976 — the only post-Reformation martyr of Scotland raised to the altars.

events.title: The Triumph of Orthodoxy
events.shortBlurb: On the first Sunday of Lent in 843, after a century of iconoclasm, the holy icons came home to Hagia Sophia in triumph…
body: Twice the Church of the East had cast out the holy icons, and twice the images came home. After the Second Council of Nicaea restored them in 787, iconoclasm rose again under Leo the Armenian and the Emperor Theophilus; but at Theophilus's death his widow Theodora ruled for the child Michael III, and with Patriarch Methodios she summoned a synod at Constantinople to make peace.

On the first Sunday of Lent, 11 March 843, the whole city walked in triumph from the church of Blachernae to Hagia Sophia, and the icons were set again in their places. The synod decreed that the anniversary should be kept each year on that same Sunday — the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

With that procession a struggle of more than a century ended: no emperor ever again moved against the images. To this day the first Sunday of Great Lent keeps the victory in every church of the Byzantine rite, where the Synodikon is still read with its cries of 'Eternal Memory' for the confessors and its anathemas for the heresiarchs.

events.title: The encyclical Mit brennender Sorge
events.shortBlurb: Smuggled into the Reich and read from every Catholic pulpit on Palm Sunday, Pius XI's encyclical dared to indict the Nazi creed…
body: In the first months of 1937 the German bishops begged Pius XI for a word that could not be silenced. The answer was written in German, not Latin, with the hand of Cardinal Secretary Pacelli and of Cardinal Faulhaber of Munich in its drafting, and dated Passion Sunday, 14 March 1937: the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, 'on the situation of the Catholic Church in the German Reich'.

Copies were smuggled across the border and secretly reproduced — some three hundred thousand, pressed and typed by hand — so that on Palm Sunday, 21 March, the letter was read entire from the pulpits of every Catholic church in Germany before the Gestapo could seize a copy.

It named neither Hitler nor his party, yet it catalogued the regime's breaches of the 1933 Concordat, condemned the distortion and denial of the Christian faith, and warned against the idolatrous exaltation of race and people. Reprisals against clergy and Catholic schools sharpened in answer. Five days later, on 19 March, Pius signed its companion, Divini Redemptoris, against atheistic communism.

sources.text: Mit brennender Sorge, Pius XI, 14 March 1937 (vatican.va)

events.title: The conclave of Venice elects Pope Pius VII
events.shortBlurb: With Rome in French hands and Pius VI dead in captivity, the cardinals elected a Benedictine at Venice in the last conclave held outside Rome…
body: Pius VI died on 29 August 1799, a prisoner of the French Directory at Valence, with Rome in French hands and the papal treasures scattered. The cardinals gathered where they could: at the Benedictine abbey of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, under Austrian protection, opening their conclave on 30 November 1799 — the last conclave ever held outside Rome.

Deadlocked for three and a half months, the thirty-five electors at last united on 14 March 1800 upon Barnaba Chiaramonti, the Benedictine bishop of Imola, who took the name Pius VII. Crowned on 21 March with a makeshift tiara, he reached Rome in July.

His twenty-three years remade the Church in the new Europe: the Concordat of 1801 with Bonaparte, the coronation of Napoleon at Notre-Dame in 1804, then arrest in 1809 and five years of captivity at Savona and Fontainebleau, the return in 1814, and the restoration of the Society of Jesus by Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum on 7 August of that year. He died on 20 August 1823.

events.title: Columbus returns in triumph to Palos
events.shortBlurb: Two hundred and twenty-four days after sailing for the Indies, Columbus anchored the Niña again at Palos, and Europe learned of a new world…
body: They had sailed from Palos on 3 August 1492, after Mass, in the Santa María, the Pinta, and the Niña; on 12 October they made landfall at an island its people called Guanahani, which Columbus christened San Salvador. When the Santa María was wrecked at Christmas, he left thirty-nine men at La Navidad and turned home with the two caravels.

The return nearly killed them: a February storm parted the little ships, and Columbus sealed an account of his discovery in a barrel against the worst. The Niña reached the Tagus on 4 March 1493 and at last, on 15 March, dropped anchor again at Palos — a few hours only before the tardy Pinta — two hundred and twenty-four days after sailing.

His letter to the treasurer Santángel, printed within weeks, told Europe of a new world. On his second voyage, that September, seventeen ships carried twelve hundred men — and with Fray Buil and Fray Ramón Pane, the first missionaries — beginning the evangelization of the Americas.

events.title: Magellan sights the Philippines
events.shortBlurb: After ninety-nine days of empty ocean, Magellan's fleet raised the island of Samar, and the Gospel's road to the Philippines began…
body: Five ships under Ferdinand Magellan had cleared the strait that bears his name in November 1520 and crossed ninety-nine days of empty ocean, past the Ladrones, when at daybreak on 16 March 1521 the lookout raised a high land — the island of Zamal, which we call Samar. So Antonio Pigafetta, the expedition's chronicler, records it.

Magellan named the archipelago the Isles of St. Lazarus, watered at Homonhon, and on Easter Sunday, 31 March, his chaplain Pedro de Valderrama offered the first Mass in the Philippines at Mazaua. At Cebu the rajah Humabon and hundreds of his people received baptism in April — the seed of the faith in Asia's great Catholic nation.

Magellan himself fell at Mactan on 27 April 1521, but his Victoria sailed on under Elcano to complete the first circumnavigation in September 1522. Within fifty years Legazpi and the friars had planted the Church in the islands for good.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Gabriel Lalemant
events.shortBlurb: The young Jesuit who had begged for the hardest mission bore the fire through a long night in Huronia, one of the North American Martyrs…
body: Gabriel Lalemant, born at Paris in 1610, entered the Jesuits at twenty and spent years pleading for the hardest mission; he reached Canada only in 1646. Three years later the Iroquois war came down upon Huronia: on 16 March 1649 a war band overran the mission of St. Louis and seized Fathers Jean de Brébeuf and Lalemant.

Carried to St. Ignace, Brébeuf bore the fire for a few hours and died that same day. The tormentors kept Lalemant longer: burned from evening through the night — seared with hatchets, his eyes put out, boiling water poured over him in mockery of baptism — he died on the morning of 17 March 1649.

The mission of Sainte-Marie was abandoned and burned, and the Huron nation scattered to the winds. Lalemant, Brébeuf, and their six companions — the North American Martyrs — were canonized together by Pius XI on 29 June 1930; their feast is kept on 19 October.

events.title: The last imperial coronation in Rome
events.shortBlurb: Nicholas V crowned Frederick III of Habsburg emperor in St. Peter's — the last imperial coronation the city of Rome would ever see…
body: Frederick III of Habsburg, elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt in 1440, came down into Italy in the first weeks of 1452 for a bride and a crown. Meeting Eleanor of Portugal at Siena, he entered Rome with her on 9 March; Pope Nicholas V joined them in marriage on the sixteenth.

Three days later, on 19 March 1452, the feast of St. Joseph, Nicholas crowned Frederick emperor in St. Peter's. It was the last imperial coronation Rome would ever see: after Frederick only Charles V, in 1530 at Bologna, received the imperial crown from a pope's hands, and no emperor again from within the city.

His coronation opened the Habsburg tenure of the empire that endured, with a single gap, until Francis II laid the title down in 1806; the Concordat of Vienna of 1448, made in the same understanding, governed the Church in the German lands for nearly as long. Frederick reigned fifty-three years, the longest of any emperor.

events.title: The death of Ebbo of Reims
events.shortBlurb: The archbishop of Reims who presided over the public penance of Louis the Pious, and was twice deposed in the Carolingian civil wars, ended his days as bishop of Hildesheim…
body: Born a serf on the royal fisc and raised at the palace school, Ebbo became librarian to Louis the Pious and, in 816, archbishop of Reims. In 822 at Attigny he presided over the emperor's public penance for the blinding and death of his nephew Bernard of Italy — a spectacle of imperial humility the age never forgot.

He preached the Gospel among the Danes in the years that prepared St. Ansgar's mission; but in the wars of Louis's sons he chose Lothair's side, and at Soissons in 833 he led the bishops who deposed the emperor and imposed a second public penance. Louis's restoration brought Ebbo's fall: imprisoned, he was deposed at Thionville in 835 and shut up at Fulda.

Restored to Reims by Lothair in 840, he was driven out for good after Fontenoy; Louis the German at length made him bishop of Hildesheim, and there he died on 20 March 851. The school of manuscript painting he fostered at Reims left him a memorial in the radiant Ebbo Gospels, which still bears his name.

events.title: The suppression of the Knights Templar
events.shortBlurb: In a secret consistory at Vienne, Clement V dissolved the Order of the Temple 'by way of provision', and the Templars were no more…
body: The blow had fallen in a single dawn: on Friday, 13 October 1307, every Templar in France was seized at King Philip's command, and confessions of blasphemy and heresy were wrung from many by torture. Clement V, after years of inquiry, summoned the Council of Vienne in October 1311 to judge the Order.

The fathers leaned toward hearing the Templars' defense, but the king descended on Vienne in person. On the Wednesday of Holy Week, 22 March 1312, in a secret consistory, Clement suppressed the Order — not by definitive sentence upon its guilt, but 'by way of provision', as the bull Vox in excelso declares, published in the council's second session on 3 April.

By Ad providam of 2 May the Templars' goods passed chiefly to the Hospitallers; the last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, held a prisoner, was burned at Paris on 18 March 1314. The Chinon parchment, found in the Vatican archives, records that the pope had absolved the Order's leaders — the suppression stood as policy, not as judgment.

events.title: The death of Pope Julius III
events.shortBlurb: The cardinal who had opened the Council of Trent became its restorer as pope, and died as England returned to Rome…
body: Giovanni Maria del Monte had stood at the Council of Trent's cradle: made a cardinal by Paul III in 1536, he was first of the three legates who opened the council on 13 December 1545. Elected pope on 7 February 1550 after ten weeks of conclave, against the emperor's wishes, he took the name Julius III.

He kept the jubilee of 1550, confirmed the young Society of Jesus by Exposcit debitum, and founded the Collegium Germanicum in 1552 to form priests for the embattled German Church. At the emperor's urging he called the fathers back to Trent in May 1551, where they defined the doctrine of the Eucharist, penance, and anointing — until war scattered them again within a year.

His eyes reached also to England: when Mary Tudor came to the throne he sent Cardinal Pole home as legate, and in November 1554 the realm was reconciled to Rome. Worn by gout, Julius died at Rome on 23 March 1555; his Villa Giulia still witnesses the gentler side of his reign.

events.title: The coronation of Conrad II
events.shortBlurb: On Easter Sunday 1027, John XIX crowned Conrad II emperor in Old St. Peter's, with Cnut and the king of Burgundy looking on…
body: The Salian century began with a crown: Conrad, first of his line, elected king in September 1024 when Henry II died childless, came down into Italy in 1026, took the Iron Crown of the Lombards at Milan, and reached Rome for Easter.

On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1027, Pope John XIX crowned him emperor in Old St. Peter's, and his queen Gisela empress. Kings stood about the altar — Cnut of England and Denmark, then a pilgrim in Rome, and Rudolph III of Burgundy — with some seventy prelates, the archbishops of Cologne, Mainz, Trier, Magdeburg, Salzburg, Milan, and Ravenna; the solemnities lasted seven days, troubled by a precedence quarrel between Milan and Ravenna that Conrad settled for Milan.

So began the Salian emperors — Conrad II, Henry III, Henry IV, Henry V — whose hundred years carried both the Church's reform and the investiture struggle. Cnut wrote home to his English people of the honor shown him there, a letter that survives.

events.title: The encyclical Populorum progressio
events.shortBlurb: Paul VI's Easter encyclical summoned the rich nations to the service of the poor, declaring that development is the new name for peace…
body: On Easter Sunday, 26 March 1967, Paul VI signed the encyclical Populorum progressio, 'on the development of peoples' — the fruit of his journeys to India and to the United Nations, and of the Council's teaching in Gaudium et spes.

The letter took the world's measure: a gulf widening between rich nations and poor, commerce that rewarded the strong, and peoples whose hunger for bread was also a hunger for dignity. 'Development', the pope declared, 'is the new name for peace' — and he asked the wealthy nations for aid without domination, fair prices for poor countries' goods, and a world fund fed from what the rich count superfluous.

John Paul II marked its twentieth year with Sollicitudo rei socialis in 1987, and the Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace was established in its wake. Its principle — that the Church owes service to the whole human family and not to souls alone — has framed every later social encyclical, down to Caritas in veritate in 2009.

events.title: The death of Pope Stephen IX
events.shortBlurb: The legate of Hagia Sophia in 1054 and a reforming pope of eight months, he died at Florence while the factions plotted his succession…
body: Frederick of Lorraine, brother of Duke Godfrey the Bearded, had been archdeacon at Liège when Leo IX drew him to Rome and made him chancellor. In 1054 he stood with the two other legates who laid the bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius upon the altar of Hagia Sophia — the act remembered as the opening of the East–West schism.

Made abbot of Monte Cassino and cardinal by Victor II, he was chosen pope at the beginning of August 1057, five days after Victor's death, and took the name Stephen IX. His eight months pressed the reform of the clergy against simony and unlawful marriage, while with his brother he planned to drive the Normans from the south.

Setting out toward Tuscany, he died at Florence on 29 March 1058, having first forbidden the Romans, under pain of his curse, to elect a successor before Hildebrand's return from Germany. The Tusculan nobles ignored him and crowned Benedict X within days — and Hildebrand's party answered with Nicholas II, in whose reign papal elections passed to the cardinals.

events.title: The Sicilian Vespers
events.shortBlurb: A quarrel at the church of the Holy Spirit on Easter Monday set Sicily ablaze and broke the Angevin empire of the Mediterranean…
body: Charles of Anjou, the papacy's champion, had taken the Hohenstaufen kingdom of the Two Sicilies at Benevento and Tagliacozzo, and his French officials ruled it harshly. On Easter Monday, 30 March 1282 — some older accounts say the Tuesday — at the hour of vespers, a quarrel outside Palermo's church of the Holy Spirit, where tradition says a French sergeant insulted a Sicilian bride, set the city alight.

'Death to the French!' ran through Palermo, and through the island: for six weeks the rising hunted the Angevins down — thousands perished, and suspects were tried by the word ciciri, which French tongues could not pronounce.

The Sicilians called in Peter III of Aragon, who landed at Trapani that summer; Pope Martin IV excommunicated him and preached a crusade for Aragon, but the Angevin cause was broken. The War of the Vespers burned on to the Peace of Caltabellotta in 1302, which parted Sicily to Aragon from Naples to Anjou — and Charles's dream of a Mediterranean empire died at Palermo.

events.title: The death of Eleanor of Aquitaine
events.shortBlurb: Queen of France and then of England, a crusader's wife and a crusader's mother, she died among the nuns of Fontevraud…
body: On 1 April 1204 — some accounts give the last day of March — Eleanor of Aquitaine died at the abbey of Fontevraud, where she had withdrawn and taken the veil in her last years, aged about eighty-two. Born about 1122, she was the daughter and sole heir of Duke William X of Aquitaine, whom she succeeded in 1137, the greatest heiress of western Christendom.

Married first to Louis VII of France, she went with him on the Second Crusade in 1147; the marriage annulled in 1152, she wed Henry of Anjou and was crowned with him as queen of England in 1154. Mother of ten children, among them Richard the Lionheart and King John, she was imprisoned by Henry for backing her sons' revolt from 1173 to 1189, then ruled England while Richard crusaded and toiled to raise his ransom.

In 1200, near eighty, she crossed the Pyrenees to fetch her granddaughter Blanche of Castile as bride for the French heir. She was buried in the abbey church of Fontevraud beside Henry II and, later, Richard I; her painted effigy still lies there, an open book in her hands.

events.title: The coronation of St. Edward the Confessor
events.shortBlurb: On Easter Day 1043 Edward, son of Æthelred and Emma, was crowned at Winchester, the last sainted king of the old English line…
body: On Easter Day, 3 April 1043, Edward — called the Confessor — was crowned king of the English in the Old Minster at Winchester. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that he was consecrated 'early on Easter-day, with much pomp,' Easter falling that year on 3 April, by Eadsige, archbishop of Canterbury, assisted by Ælfric of York.

Son of King Æthelred the Unready and Emma of Normandy, Edward had passed some twenty-five years in Norman exile before being recalled in 1041, and he succeeded his half-brother Harthacnut, the last of the Danish kings, who died in June 1042. The choice of Winchester, the ancient royal city and the seat of his mother Emma, proclaimed the restored house of Cerdic after a generation of Danish rule.

His reign of twenty-three years raised his great church, Westminster Abbey, consecrated on 28 December 1065, days before his death on 5 January 1066. Miracles were reported at his tomb; Alexander III canonized him in 1161, and for centuries he was venerated as a patron of English kings.

events.title: The death of Pope Nicholas IV
events.shortBlurb: The first Franciscan pope died in Rome, and the Chair of Peter then stood vacant for more than two years…
body: On 4 April 1292 Pope Nicholas IV died in Rome. Born Girolamo Masci near Ascoli Piceno about 1227, he had entered the Franciscan Order young, succeeded St. Bonaventure as its minister general in 1274, and served as legate to the Greeks before his election on 22 February 1288 — the first Franciscan to occupy the Chair of Peter.

His four years' reign was busy: he crowned Charles II of Anjou king of Sicily in May 1289, and in the same year dispatched the Franciscan John of Montecorvino to the court of the Great Khan, who would plant the Church's first mission at Khanbaliq, the modern Peking. In Rome he adorned Santa Maria Maggiore, where his kneeling portrait survives in the apse mosaic.

His death opened one of the longest vacancies of the medieval Church, surpassed in that age only by the deadlock that had chosen Gregory X: the cardinals wrangled two years, three months, and two days before electing, on 5 July 1294, the hermit Pietro da Morrone as Celestine V — the last election held outside conclave. Celestine's few troubled months and his abdication led straight to Boniface VIII, and in time to Avignon.

events.title: The Battle on the Ice
events.shortBlurb: On the frozen Lake Peipus, Alexander Nevsky broke the crusader advance into the Russian lands…
body: On 5 April 1242 Prince Alexander of Novgorod — called Nevsky, 'of the Neva,' for his victory over the Swedes on that river in July 1240 — met the knights of the Livonian crusade on the frozen surface of Lake Peipus and routed them.

The Livonian Order, a military order sanctioned by the popes for the conversion of the Baltic peoples, had taken Pskov that winter and pressed toward Novgorod itself. Alexander, recalled by the citizens who had lately driven him out, recovered Pskov and advanced into Livonia; in the peace that followed, the knights renounced all their conquests. Later chronicles told of the spring ice breaking beneath the heavily armed knights — a detail the older sources do not confirm.

The battle fixed for centuries the frontier between the Latin West and the Orthodox East. Alexander, prince of Vladimir from 1252, judged submission to the Mongol khans safer than alliance with Rome, and rebuffed the papal envoys who sought to draw him into union. Canonized by the Russian Church in 1547, he remains its soldier-saint — his memory a monument of the estrangement of East and West in the crusading age.

events.title: The death of Raphael
events.shortBlurb: Raffaello Sanzio of Urbino, painter of the School of Athens and the Sistine Madonna, died on Good Friday at thirty-seven…
body: On Good Friday, 6 April 1520, Raphael died in Rome after a brief fever, aged thirty-seven — born, tradition holds, on the same day in 1483 at Urbino. His body lay in state in his studio beside his last, unfinished canvas, the Transfiguration, and all Rome mourned the 'divine painter.'

Summoned to Rome by Julius II about 1508, he had frescoed the Stanze of the Vatican — the School of Athens and the Disputà among them — painted the Sistine Madonna and the Galatea, and on Bramante's death in 1514 been made chief architect of the new St. Peter's then rising.

He was buried, as he had asked, in the Pantheon, the ancient temple become the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, where his tomb still bears Cardinal Bembo's epitaph: here lies Raphael; while he lived, great Nature feared to be outdone, and when he died, she feared to die herself.

events.title: The death of El Greco
events.shortBlurb: Doménikos Theotokópoulos, 'the Greek' of Toledo, painter of The Burial of the Count of Orgaz, died among his canvases…
body: On 7 April 1614 Doménikos Theotokópoulos — El Greco, 'the Greek' — died at Toledo, aged seventy-two, and was laid in the convent of Santo Domingo el Antiguo, where some of his first great Spanish altarpieces had stood.

Born in 1541 at Candia in Crete, then a Venetian possession, he was trained as an icon painter of the Byzantine school before passing to Venice, where he drank in Titian and Tintoretto, and to Rome. In 1577 he came to Spain and settled at Toledo, the city he made his own and painted as none has since.

There he produced The Disrobing of Christ for the cathedral sacristy, The Burial of the Count of Orgaz for the church of Santo Tomé (1586–88), and the Adoration of the Shepherds he destined for his own tomb. Philip II, displeased with his Martyrdom of St. Maurice, gave him no further commissions; the churches and convents of Toledo employed him to the end. His flame-limned saints, long dismissed, now seem the very image of the spirit of Catholic Spain.

events.title: The Battle of Legnica
events.shortBlurb: Henry the Pious of Silesia, the son of St. Hedwig, fell defending Christendom against the Mongol storm…
body: On 9 April 1241, at Legnickie Pole — the Field of Legnica, German Wahlstatt — Duke Henry II of Silesia, called the Pious, fell fighting the Mongol host that had swept into Poland that spring.

The invaders, a flank army of Batu Khan's great western campaign, had crushed the knights of Little Poland at Chmielnik on 18 March and burned Kraków. Henry, son of St. Hedwig of Silesia, gathered what forces he could — Silesian and Polish knights, with brethren of the military orders — and met the horde near Legnica; two days later the main Mongol army shattered the Hungarians at Mohi on 11 April.

The victors struck Henry's head upon a spear and bore it before the walls of Legnica; tradition relates that his body was known by a deformity of one foot, and it was buried at Wrocław in the church of St. Vincent he had founded. His mother, the hagiographers tell, had foreseen his death in a vision. Within the year the Mongols withdrew from Europe on the death of the Great Khan Ögedei, and the West accounted itself delivered.

events.title: The death of St. Magdalene of Canossa
events.shortBlurb: The Veronese marchioness who traded her palace for the slums died among her Daughters in Passion Week…
body: On 10 April 1835, the Friday of Passion Week, St. Magdalene of Canossa died at Verona, aged sixty-one, surrounded by her Daughters.

Born on 1 March 1774 to the marquesses of Canossa, she lost her father at five and was left behind by her mother's remarriage; drawn to the cloister yet convinced that God asked her for the streets, she left the family palace in 1808 for the poor San Zeno quarter and founded the Daughters of Charity — teaching poor girls, catechizing, nursing the sick — and later the Sons of Charity at Venice in 1831. Pope Leo XII approved the institute's Rule on 23 December 1828.

Her houses had spread to Venice, Milan, Bergamo, and Trent before her death; the Canossian family she planted now serves in some thirty countries. Pius XII beatified her in 1941, and John Paul II canonized her on 2 October 1988, holding her up as a prophet of charity.

sources.text: Vatican Radio, “St. Magdalen of Canossa (1774–1835): Her Canonization”

events.title: The Battle of Adrianople (1205)
events.shortBlurb: A year after the sack of Constantinople, the Latin emperor Baldwin fell captive to the Bulgarians…
body: On 14 April 1205, almost a year to the day after the Fourth Crusade stormed Constantinople, the new Latin Empire suffered its mortal wound: before Adrianople the crusader host was destroyed by Kaloyan, tsar of the Bulgarians, and the emperor Baldwin I was taken alive.

The Greeks of Thrace, rising against Latin rule, had called Kaloyan in; Baldwin besieged Adrianople in March 1205 with Louis of Blois and the aged Doge Enrico Dandolo. Kaloyan's Cuman light horse, feigning flight, drew the armored knights into an ambush; Louis of Blois was slain, and the emperor was dragged into captivity at Tarnovo, where he died. Dandolo led the remnant home.

Baldwin's brother Henry succeeded to a diminished empire that lingered until 1261. Kaloyan, by a strange turn, had months before received a royal crown from a legate of Pope Innocent III, whom he professed to call father — yet the battle sealed what the sack had begun: between the Greek East and the Latin West the breach was past healing.

events.title: The birth of Leonardo da Vinci
events.shortBlurb: In the Tuscan hill town of Vinci was born the painter of the Last Supper…
body: On 15 April 1452 Leonardo was born at Anchiano, a hamlet beneath the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, the natural son of Ser Piero da Vinci, a notary, and a country girl, Caterina; his grandfather Ser Antonio recorded the birth — a grandson born on 15 April, a Saturday, in the third hour of the night — and the child was baptized by the priest Piero di Bartolomeo.

Raised in his father's house, he was apprenticed about 1466 to Verrocchio in Florence, where, the old writers say, the pupil painted an angel so well that the master laid down his brush. In Milan under Ludovico Sforza he painted the Virgin of the Rocks and, for the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, the Last Supper (about 1495–98), the most meditated sacred image of the Renaissance.

Painter, sculptor, engineer, and anatomist, he filled his notebooks with everything from the flight of birds to the child in the womb; he died at Amboise in France on 2 May 1519. His Annunciation and his St. John the Baptist remain among the Church's quiet sermons in paint.

events.title: The fire of Notre-Dame
events.shortBlurb: Flames took the spire and the medieval roof of Paris's cathedral, and the world watched the mother church of France burn…
body: On the evening of 15 April 2019, the Monday of Holy Week, fire broke out beneath the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris, the cathedral begun in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and completed in the following century.

Before the eyes of the world the nineteenth-century spire of Viollet-le-Duc (1859) fell through the vaulting, and the medieval oak roof the Parisians called 'the forest' burned away. The stone vaults held, sparing the interior: the great rose windows, the organ, and the altar cross survived, and the cathedral's chaplain, Fr. Jean-Marc Fournier, bore the Crown of Thorns and the Blessed Sacrament to safety. The cause was judged accidental, bound up with the restoration works then on the spire.

Pope Francis, writing the next day to Archbishop Michel Aupetit of Paris, mourned the wound to 'the architectural jewel of a collective memory' and praised the firefighters' courage. France vowed to rebuild; hundreds of millions of euros were pledged within days, and on 7 December 2024 the restored cathedral was solemnly reopened, its first Mass following on 8 December.

sources.text: Message of the Holy Father to the Archbishop of Paris for the fire in the Cathedral of Notre Dame (Holy See Press Office, 16 April 2019)

events.title: The death of St. Benedict Joseph Labre
events.shortBlurb: The beggar-pilgrim of Europe's shrines died in Rome in Holy Week, and the poor proclaimed him a saint…
body: On 16 April 1783, in Holy Week, Benedict Joseph Labre died in Rome, aged thirty-five; he was buried in the church of Santa Maria ai Monti, where he had so often knelt, and the Roman poor at once proclaimed him a saint.

Born on 26 March 1748 at Amettes in the diocese of Boulogne, the eldest of fifteen children, he sought admission among the Trappists and the Carthusians and was refused; instead he took the road as a pilgrim and a beggar, visiting on foot the great shrines of Christendom — Rome and Loreto, Assisi, Naples, Bari, Einsiedeln, Paray-le-Monial, Compostela — content to be despised for Christ.

From 1774 he made Rome his home, sleeping in the ruins of the Colosseum and spending his days before the Blessed Sacrament wherever the Forty Hours was kept; the Romans called him the saint of the Forty Hours. Wonders were told of him in life, and within months of his death more than a hundred cures were laid to his intercession. Pius IX beatified him in 1860; Leo XIII canonized him on 8 December 1881; he is the patron of pilgrims, of beggars, and of the homeless.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 April

events.title: The Capitulations of Santa Fe
events.shortBlurb: In the camp of conquered Granada the Catholic Monarchs signed the contract that sent Columbus west…
body: On 17 April 1492, at Santa Fe beside newly fallen Granada, Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile signed the first of two agreements with Christopher Columbus — remembered as the Capitulations of Santa Fe — commissioning him to sail west into the Ocean Sea; the second followed on 30 April.

Granada, the last Muslim kingdom of Spain, had surrendered on 2 January. Columbus, whose project had been refused for years, was departing in despair when the queen's officers recalled him; tradition says a messenger overtook him at the bridge of Pinos. The capitulations named him Admiral of the Ocean Sea, viceroy and governor of whatever lands he should find, with a tenth of their revenues — all hereditary in his family.

The enterprise was framed from the first in the language of faith: the sovereigns' letters, and Columbus's own journal, set before God the hope of extending the holy Christian faith among the peoples to be found. He sailed from Palos on 3 August and made landfall on 12 October 1492; the friars who followed, Fray Bernardo Buil first among them, planted the Church in the New World.

events.title: The execution of Elizabeth Barton
events.shortBlurb: The Holy Maid of Kent, whose visions condemned the king's divorce, was hanged at Tyburn without trial…
body: On 20 April 1534 Elizabeth Barton, the Benedictine nun called the Holy Maid of Kent, was drawn from the Tower to Tyburn and hanged for treason, with five companions — her confessor Edward Bocking, her parish priest Richard Masters, and the Observant friars Richard Risby and Hugh Rich among them — condemned not by any jury but by act of Parliament.

A servant at Aldington in Kent, she had fallen into trances in 1525, and her revelations, judged sincere by a commission of Archbishop Warham, made her famous; professed at St. Sepulchre's, Canterbury, she was consulted by the great, Bishop Fisher and Sir Thomas More among them. When Henry VIII put aside Catherine of Aragon for Anne Boleyn, the Maid prophesied that the king would die a villain's death and lose his realm within a month.

Cromwell broke her circle in 1533, and she was attainted by statute, about twenty-eight years old. On the scaffold, the chronicle relates, she owned herself the cause of her companions' deaths, 'and yet not so much to be blamed, considering that I was a simple woman.' Their heads were set on London Bridge and the gates of the city.

events.title: The death of Pope Clement V
events.shortBlurb: Thirty-three days after Jacques de Molay's burning, the pope who suppressed the Templars died at Roquemaure…
body: On 20 April 1314 Pope Clement V died at Roquemaure on the Rhône — thirty-three days after the last Grand Master of the Temple, Jacques de Molay, had gone to the stake in Paris. Later chroniclers told how Molay, from the flames, summoned pope and king to answer before God's tribunal within the year; the tale is not in the earliest witnesses, but Philip the Fair indeed followed Clement to the grave that November.

Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, had been elected on 5 June 1305, after a conclave of eleven months, and crowned at Lyon; he never entered Italy, and in 1309 he settled the papal court at Avignon, beginning the seventy years' sojourn of the papacy on French soil.

Under the shadow of the French king he convened the Council of Vienne (1311–12), which suppressed the Order of the Temple by the bull Vox in excelso of 22 March 1312 and gave its goods to the Hospitallers; his constitutions, the Clementinae, issued by his successor, stood in the law of the Church for centuries. After his death the cardinals wrangled more than two years before choosing John XXII in August 1316.

events.title: The death of Peter Abelard
events.shortBlurb: The brilliant, storm-tossed master of the Paris schools died a monk of Cluny, reconciled at last…
body: On 21 April 1142 Peter Abelard died at the Cluniac priory of Saint-Marcel near Chalon-sur-Saône, aged about sixty-three, wearing the habit of a monk of Cluny.

Born in 1079 at Le Pallet near Nantes, he had renounced his inheritance for the schools and become the most acclaimed master in Christendom, drawing thousands to his lectures at Paris and on Mont-Sainte-Geneviève. His love for Héloïse, niece of the canon Fulbert — the secret marriage, his mutilation at her kinsmen's hands — is among the most famous of medieval tragedies; both took the religious life.

His Theologia was condemned at Soissons in 1121, and again at the Council of Sens in 1141, where St. Bernard of Clairvaux was his relentless accuser. Setting out for Rome to appeal, he stopped at Cluny, where the abbot Peter the Venerable kept him, made his peace with Bernard, and won him rest. His body Peter the Venerable sent to Héloïse at the Paraclete, with a letter calling him a philosopher of Christ; their remains were laid side by side in Père Lachaise, Paris, in 1817.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Adalbert of Prague
events.shortBlurb: Bishop Vojtěch, apostle of the Prussians, was cut down on the Baltic shore, and Poland gained its first patron…
body: On 23 April 997 Adalbert of Prague — Vojtěch in his own Bohemian tongue — was martyred among the pagan Prussians on the Baltic coast, struck down by a heathen band after he had preached and offered the Mass; his companions were spared to carry the tale back to Poland.

Of the princely Slavník clan, he had taken the name Adalbert from the archbishop of Magdeburg who taught him. Made bishop of Prague in 982, he twice fled the violence of his own half-Christian city for the peace of a Roman cloister, founded Břevnov, the first Benedictine house of Bohemia, in 993, and was twice sent back to his see — until, released at last, he went to the court of Bolesław the Brave, and thence by sea to convert the Prussians, with his half-brother Gaudentius and the priest Benedict.

Bolesław ransomed the martyr's body for its weight in gold and laid it in Gniezno cathedral, where the Emperor Otto III came on pilgrimage in the year 1000. Canonized about 999, Adalbert became patron of Poland, Bohemia, and Prussia; and his friend Bruno of Querfurt, who wrote his Life, followed him to martyrdom among the same people in 1009.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 April

events.title: The attack on Pope Leo III
events.shortBlurb: Assailants of the late pope's kindred fell upon Leo III in the procession of the Greater Litanies…
body: On 25 April 799, as Pope Leo III rode in the procession of the Greater Litanies toward the Flaminian Gate, armed men of the late Pope Hadrian I's kindred set upon him, dashed him to the ground, and strove to tear out his eyes and his tongue, leaving him bleeding in the street.

Leo, a Roman of humble birth, cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna, had been elected on 26 December 795, the very day of Hadrian's burial, and had sought Charlemagne's friendship from the first, sending him the keys of St. Peter's confession and the standard of the city. His enemies accused him to the Frankish king; held in the monastery of St. Erasmus on the Caelian, he recovered the use of his eyes and tongue — in what the old biographies relate as miraculous — escaped, and made his way to Charlemagne at Paderborn, who received him with the highest honor.

Restored to Rome in November 799 under Frankish guard, he purged himself by oath of his accusers' charges on 23 December 800; two days later, at Mass on Christmas Day, he crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans — an act that remade the map of Europe and bound the papacy to the West.

events.title: The Pazzi conspiracy
events.shortBlurb: At High Mass in Florence's cathedral, daggers fell upon the Medici brothers…
body: On Sunday, 26 April 1478, at High Mass in Florence's cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, the conspirators of the Pazzi family struck: Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed to death on the cathedral floor — nineteen wounds, the record runs — while his brother Lorenzo, wounded, beat back his attackers and escaped into the sacristy.

The plot had been woven around Girolamo Riario, nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, with Francesco Salviati, archbishop of Pisa, and the Pazzi, papal bankers and rivals of the Medici; the king of Naples was privy to it, and the tradition relates that the blow was timed for the elevation of the Host, when heads would be bowed. But the city rose for the Medici: the archbishop was hanged from the windows of the Signoria in his very cassock, and Jacopo de' Pazzi was put to death within days.

Sixtus IV answered with an interdict on Florence and the excommunication of Lorenzo, and war followed with Naples, until Lorenzo's bold journey to King Ferrante in the winter of 1479–80 made the peace. The sacrilege at the altar shocked even a violent age, and the Pazzi name became a byword for treachery.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Peter Chanel
events.shortBlurb: The Marist whom Futuna called 'the man with the kind heart' became Oceania's first martyr…
body: On 28 April 1841 Pierre Louis Marie Chanel, priest of the Society of Mary, was clubbed to death on the island of Futuna by warriors sent by King Niuliki — the protomartyr of Oceania.

Born in 1803 at Cuet in the diocese of Belley, a shepherd's son, he was ordained in 1827 and revived the derelict parish of Crozet before joining Fr. Jean-Claude Colin's new Marist congregation; professed in September 1836, he sailed that Christmas Eve as superior of the first Marist band to the South Seas, landing on Futuna on 8 November 1837 with Brother Marie-Nizier Delorme.

Three years of hunger, fevers, and slow patience won him the islanders' name of 'the man with the kind heart,' and a few converts; but when the king's own son Meitala sought baptism, Niuliki, fearing the new faith, sent his son-in-law Musumusu to kill the missionary. Within two years nearly the whole island had asked for baptism. Pius XII canonized him on 12 June 1954, and he is honored as the patron of Oceania.

events.title: The death of St. Marie of the Incarnation
events.shortBlurb: The widowed mother who crossed the ocean to found the Ursulines of Quebec died among her daughters in New France…
body: On 30 April 1672 Marie Guyart — in religion Marie of the Incarnation — died at Quebec, aged seventy-two, first superior of the Ursulines of New France, and was buried in the monastery she had raised.

Born at Tours on 28 October 1599, she was married at seventeen and widowed at nineteen with an infant son; after years managing a brother-in-law's business she entered the Ursulines in 1631, and in 1639, answering a call she had long heard in prayer, sailed with Madame de la Peltrie for Canada, landing at Quebec in the summer of 1639.

In the wooden town of the fledgling colony she opened the first school for girls in North America, taught French and Indian children alike, composed catechisms and word-lists in the Huron and Algonquin tongues, and wrote thousands of letters that are a chronicle of New France. Her son Claude, left behind in France, became a Benedictine and wrote her Life. Long venerated, she was numbered among the saints by Pope Francis in 2014, together with François de Laval, Quebec's first bishop.

events.title: John Knox returns to Scotland
events.shortBlurb: The Genevan exile came home to a regency torn over religion, and within fifteen months Scotland had abolished the Mass and the pope's authority…
body: On 2 May 1559 John Knox landed in Scotland, called home by the Protestant lords of the Congregation to a kingdom governed by the regent Mary of Guise for her young daughter, Mary Queen of Scots. Born at Haddington between 1505 and 1515, he had been a galley slave of the French, a chaplain in Edward VI's England, and lastly pastor of the English congregation at Geneva.

Nine days later he preached at Perth in the parish kirk of St. John, and the sermon kindled what he had perhaps not willed: the casting down of the town churches and the wrecking of the religious houses round about. The regent marched and the Congregation armed, and that summer St. Andrews and the coast towns of Fife were purged of images and altars — destruction that ran ahead of Knox himself and, in places, to his grief.

The quarrel was decided the next year. Mary of Guise died in June 1560; by the Treaty of Edinburgh the French and English soldiers alike went home; and in August the Scottish Parliament abolished the Mass, renounced the jurisdiction of Rome, and adopted the Confession of Faith framed chiefly by Knox. The Kirk that rose from that settlement he governed until his death at Edinburgh on 24 November 1572.

sources.text: Walker, A History of the Christian Church (1918), the Scottish Reformation (public domain)

events.title: The Second Council of Constantinople opens
