events.shortBlurb: Justinian summoned the fifth ecumenical council to condemn the Three Chapters, and Pope Vigilius, a prisoner in all but name, refused to attend…
body: On 5 May 553 the Second Council of Constantinople, reckoned the fifth ecumenical council, opened in the imperial city, called together by the Emperor Justinian. Nearly all its fathers were bishops of the East — only six came out of the Latin West, and those Africans; the presidency fell to Eutychius, patriarch of the city.

At issue were the Three Chapters: the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus against St. Cyril of Alexandria, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa. Pope Vigilius, detained in Constantinople since 547, had once condemned the chapters in his Judicatum of 548 and then withdrawn it under Western protest; he would not sit in a council where Eastern prelates so outnumbered his own.

In eight sessions the bishops heard the chapters read and, on 2 June, the 165 present condemned them in fourteen anathemas, while Justinian struck the pope's name from the diptychs. Vigilius, exiled for a season, yielded at last and condemned the chapters himself, in December 553 and again in February 554; but the West was slow to follow — Milan and Aquileia broke communion with Rome, and the schism of Aquileia endured nearly to the year 700.

events.title: The relics of St. Nicholas are carried to Bari
events.shortBlurb: Sailors of Bari bore off the bones of St. Nicholas from Turkish-held Myra, and the wonder-working bishop of Lycia came to rest beside the Adriatic…
body: On 9 May 1087 the relics of St. Nicholas, bishop of Myra, were brought ashore at Bari in Apulia. Sixteen years after Manzikert, with Lycia passing under the Seljuk Turks, merchants and sailors of Bari — the city's tradition reckons sixty-two of them — had sailed to Myra, forced open the saint's tomb despite the protests of its Greek guardians, and carried off the bones.

Of Nicholas himself history can affirm little beyond his bishopric in fourth-century Lycia and his death on a 6 December; yet his cult was already ancient, for Justinian had built a church in his honor at Constantinople in the sixth century, and his relics were famed for the sweet-scented 'manna' they were said to distil — a marvel still pointed out at Bari.

The new basilica of San Nicola rose to receive the treasure, and in 1089 Pope Urban II himself laid the relics beneath the altar of its crypt. From that translation flowered the Western devotion to the bishop who became patron of mariners, merchants, and children — and, by way of the Dutch Sinterklaas, the distant ancestor of Santa Claus. Bari keeps the feast of the translation every year on 9 May.

events.title: Paul VI and Shenouda III sign a common declaration
events.shortBlurb: For the first time since Chalcedon a pope of Rome and a pope of Alexandria met face to face, and together confessed one faith in Christ…
body: On 10 May 1973, at the Vatican, Paul VI, Bishop of Rome and Pope of the Catholic Church, and Shenouda III, Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the See of St. Mark, signed a Common Declaration — the first meeting of the heads of the Roman and Coptic Churches since the division that followed the Council of Chalcedon in 451. The way had been prepared in 1968, when Paul VI returned the relics of St. Mark to Egypt.

At the heart of the declaration stood a common confession of Christ: 'perfect God with respect to His divinity, perfect man with respect to His humanity,' the two natures united 'without mingling, without commixtion, without confusion, without alteration, without division, without separation' — His divinity never parted from His humanity 'for an instant, not for the twinkling of an eye.'

The declaration set up a joint commission to study tradition, liturgy, and theology, and renounced all proselytism between the Churches. Its fruit has ripened slowly: in 2013 Pope Francis and Pope Tawadros II made 10 May a yearly day of Catholic-Coptic friendship, and on the fiftieth anniversary, in 2023, Francis inscribed the twenty-one Coptic martyrs of Libya in the Roman Martyrology.

sources.text: Common Declaration of Paul VI and Shenouda III, 10 May 1973 (vatican.va)

events.title: The dedication of Constantinople
events.shortBlurb: Constantine solemnly inaugurated his New Rome on the Bosphorus, and for eleven centuries it stood as the capital of Christian empire in the East…
body: On 11 May 330 Constantine the Great solemnly dedicated his new capital on the site of ancient Byzantium, the colony that Megarian Greeks under Byzas had planted beside the Bosphorus nearly a thousand years before. The city had received its founder's name as early as the end of 324, but only with the inauguration of 330 did the court and government settle there for good.

The New Rome was made in the old Rome's image: it rose upon seven hills and was divided into fourteen regions, and it received a senate house, forums, a capitol, and circuses of its own. Among its new churches the emperor built that of the Holy Apostles, destined to be the burial-place of the emperors, while the statues of the ancient world were gathered from every province to adorn its streets.

The dedication fixed the axis of Christendom for a millennium. The bishop of the new capital was ranked next after the bishop of Rome by the council of 381, and the city became the seat of four ecumenical councils and the fortress of the Christian East — until, on 29 May 1453, almost exactly eleven centuries after its dedication, it fell to the Turks.

events.title: The Martyrs of Otranto are canonized
events.shortBlurb: Pope Francis raised to the altars some eight hundred men of Otranto who in 1480 chose death rather than deny Christ…
body: On 12 May 2013, in St. Peter's Square, Pope Francis celebrated the first canonizations of his pontificate, raising to the altars Antonio Primaldo and his companions, the Martyrs of Otranto — some eight hundred men of that Apulian city who in 1480 had refused to renounce their faith.

In the summer of 1480 an Ottoman army under Gedik Ahmet Pasha had stormed Otranto after a siege of a fortnight and sacked it. The surviving men were offered their lives if they would abandon their religion; led, it is said, by Primaldo, a tailor of the city, they refused, and on 14 August 1480 they were beheaded one by one on the hill of Minerva outside the walls. Their remains are venerated to this day in Otranto's cathedral, and Clement XIV had confirmed their cult in 1771.

Beside the martyrs the Pope canonized two religious women of the New World: St. Laura Montoya of Colombia, missionary mother of the indigenous peoples, and St. María Guadalupe García Zavala of Mexico, foundress of the Handmaids of St. Margaret Mary and the Poor. The Ottoman bridgehead in Italy did not long outlive the martyrs: Mehmed II died in May 1481, and Otranto was retaken that September.

sources.text: Pope Francis, Homily at the Canonization Mass, 12 May 2013 (vatican.va)

events.title: The assassination of Henry IV of France
events.shortBlurb: The king who had judged Paris worth a Mass and given France the Edict of Nantes was stabbed in his coach by a Catholic zealot…
body: On 14 May 1610 Henry IV, the first Bourbon king of France, was assassinated in the Rue de la Ferronnerie in Paris, stabbed by François Ravaillac as his coach halted in the press of traffic for the coronation festivities of his queen, Marie de' Medici, crowned the day before at Saint-Denis. He was fifty-six years old, and had escaped a dozen earlier attempts upon his life.

Born at Pau in Béarn in 1553, Henry of Navarre had led the Huguenot party through the Wars of Religion and inherited the crown in 1589. When Paris would not open its gates to a Protestant, he was received into the Catholic Church at Saint-Denis on 25 July 1593 — 'Paris is well worth a Mass,' as the saying ascribed to him runs — was crowned at Chartres the following February, and was absolved by Clement VIII in 1595.

His reign healed what sixty years of war had torn: the Edict of Nantes in 1598 granted the Huguenots liberty of conscience and a measure of public worship, and the king who wished every peasant a chicken in his pot restored the kingdom's fortunes with his minister Sully. His death left the throne to a child of eight, Louis XIII, with the queen-mother as regent.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Henry IV” (King of France and Navarre)
Encyclopædia Britannica (11th ed., 1911), “Henry IV of France” (public domain)

events.title: Napoleon annexes the Papal States
events.shortBlurb: From Schönbrunn the emperor decreed the Patrimony of St. Peter part of France; Pius VII answered with excommunication, and was taken prisoner…
body: On 17 May 1809, from the palace of Schönbrunn in a Vienna his armies had just taken, Napoleon issued two decrees declaring the States of the Church annexed to the French Empire — reproaching the popes, as the decrees ran, for the ill use they had made of the gift of Charlemagne, his 'august predecessor.' Rome itself was named the second city of the Empire.

The blow had been long in falling. General Miollis had occupied Rome with ten thousand men in February 1808, and a decree of that April had already shorn away Urbino, Ancona, Macerata, and Camerino. On 10 June 1809 the French hauled down the pontifical flag over the castle of Sant'Angelo, and Pius VII answered by having Rome placarded with the bull Quum memoranda, excommunicating the violators of the Patrimony of St. Peter — the emperor not named, but meant.

Napoleon's reply came within the month: in the night of 5–6 July General Radet entered the Quirinal, arrested the pope and Cardinal Pacca, his secretary of state, and drove them from Rome at four in the morning. Pius VII was held at Savona and later at Fontainebleau until 1814, when he returned to Rome, and the Congress of Vienna restored the Papal States.

events.title: Sts. John Fisher and Thomas More are canonized
events.shortBlurb: Four hundred years after they laid down their lives for the unity of the Church, the bishop and the chancellor were declared saints…
body: On 19 May 1935, in St. Peter's Basilica, Pius XI canonized John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, and Sir Thomas More, sometime Lord Chancellor of England — the fourth centenary of the year in which both had died for their refusal of the royal supremacy over the Church.

Fisher, the only one of the English bishops who would not bend to Henry VIII, had been named cardinal while he lay in the Tower and was beheaded on Tower Hill on 22 June 1535; More, who had resigned the chancellorship in 1532 rather than countenance the king's course, followed him to the scaffold on 6 July, declaring that he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Leo XIII had beatified them on 29 December 1886, More with fifty-three fellow martyrs of England and Wales, Fisher among them.

The canonizations of 1935, sought by a great petition of English Catholics, crowned the long vindication of the two men: their names were joined ever after, kept together on 22 June, the day of Fisher's martyrdom. In the year 2000 John Paul II proclaimed St. Thomas More the heavenly patron of statesmen and politicians.

sources.text: John Paul II, Apostolic Letter proclaiming St. Thomas More Patron of Statesmen and Politicians (vatican.va)

events.title: The 'Earthquake Synod' condemns Wyclif's propositions
events.shortBlurb: While London trembled, Archbishop Courtenay's council at Blackfriars judged twenty-four propositions of John Wyclif heretical or erroneous…
body: On 21 May 1382, as an earthquake shook London, the synod that William Courtenay, the new Archbishop of Canterbury, had summoned to the Blackfriars convent judged twenty-four propositions drawn from the teaching of John Wyclif: ten it pronounced heretical, and fourteen erroneous. The tremor gave the assembly its name in English history — the Earthquake Synod.

Among the condemned articles were Wyclif's denial of the corporeal presence of Christ in the sacrament — he had attacked Transubstantiation from 1380, calling the consecrated Host 'an effectual sign' — with assertions that oral confession is not necessary to one prepared for death, and that England need acknowledge no pope. Courtenay read the earthquake as a token of heaven's favor; Wyclif, who was not present, answered that the earth had trembled, as at Christ's passion, because the friars had there put heresy upon Christ.

Oxford's doctors had condemned his eucharistic teaching the year before; the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, though he disowned it, had been laid at his door. Wyclif himself was suffered to retire to Lutterworth, where he died on 31 December 1384 — but the Council of Constance in 1415 ordered his bones cast out, which was done in 1428, and his Lollards were driven underground.

sources.text: Schaff, History of the Christian Church, Vol. VI: The Middle Ages (public domain)

events.title: Leo XIII canonizes John Baptist de La Salle and Rita of Cascia
events.shortBlurb: In one ceremony the aged pope raised the founder of the Christian Brothers and the Umbrian widow invoked in impossible causes…
body: On 24 May 1900 Leo XIII solemnly canonized, in one ceremony, two saints of very different worlds: John Baptist de La Salle, founder of the Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, and Rita of Cascia, the Augustinian nun venerated in Spain as La Santa de los impossibiles — the saint of impossible causes.

La Salle, a canon of Reims who had exchanged the cathedral close for the unpaid schoolrooms of the poor, founded his institute in 1680 and died at Rouen in 1719; declared venerable in 1840, he was beatified in 1888. His Brothers, bound by vow to teach the poor gratuitously, numbered more than ten thousand within two generations, and in 1950 Pius XII proclaimed their founder the patron of all teachers of youth.

Rita, born at Roccaporena in the diocese of Spoleto, had been for eighteen years the wife of a violent husband, and a mother who prayed her twin sons out of the blood-feud that took their father, before the Augustinians of Cascia received the widow among them; she died in their cloister, bearing on her forehead the wound of a thorn of the Crucifix. Urban VIII permitted her Mass and Office in 1637; her feast is kept on 22 May.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools”

events.title: The death of the Venerable Bede
events.shortBlurb: With the last sentence of his English St. John dictated, the father of English history died on the floor of his cell, singing the Gloria…
body: On Ascension Day, 26 May 735, the Venerable Bede died in his cell at Jarrow in Northumbria, in about his sixty-second year, in the evening after the festival procession. The account of his last hours was written by his disciple Cuthbert to the priest Cuthwin.

All that day he had gone on dictating his translation of the Gospel of St. John into English. In the evening the boy Wilbert, who wrote at his word, said: 'There is still one sentence, dear master, which is not written down.' When it was supplied, 'It is finished,' Bede answered; 'take my head in thy hands.' And so, singing 'Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost,' he breathed his last upon the floor of his cell.

Born about 673, he had been given at seven years old to Abbot Benedict Biscop at Wearmouth, and passed his whole life in the twin monastery — deacon at nineteen, priest at thirty. 'It was ever my delight,' he wrote, 'to learn or teach or write,' and his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, finished in 731, remains the foundation of our knowledge of early England. In 1899 Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church.

events.title: The execution of Blessed Margaret Pole
events.shortBlurb: The last of the Plantagenets, mother of a cardinal and once governess to Princess Mary, was beheaded within the Tower at sixty-seven…
body: On 27 May 1541 — the ambassador de Marillac gives the 28th — Blessed Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury, was beheaded within the Tower of London. Told that morning that she was to die within the hour, she answered that no crime had been imputed to her; a clumsy novice headsman did the work.

She was the daughter of George, Duke of Clarence, brother of Edward IV, and of Isabel Neville, the Kingmaker's daughter; her brother the Earl of Warwick, the last male Plantagenet, had paid for his blood with his life in 1499. Henry VIII had restored her honor and lands, called her the saintliest woman in England, and made her governess to the Princess Mary. But her son Reginald — later cardinal, and the last Catholic Archbishop of Canterbury — denounced the king's proceedings from abroad, and the royal anger fell on the hostages at home.

Her sons were arrested in November 1538, and the elder, Lord Montagu, executed within months; the countess herself was attainted in 1539, on a charge resting, among other things, on a silk tunic embroidered with the Five Wounds found in her coffer. Nearly two years she lay in the Tower, until a rising in Yorkshire sealed her fate. Leo XIII declared her blessed, a martyr, on 29 December 1886.

events.title: The death of St. Germain of Paris
events.shortBlurb: The abbot-bishop who cowed Merovingian kings and excommunicated one of them died in the city he had served for twenty years…
body: On 28 May 576 St. Germain, bishop of Paris, died in his city, and his feast is kept on that day. Born near Autun about 496, he was abbot of Saint-Symphorien when, happening to be in Paris at the death of Bishop Eusebius in 555, King Childebert I kept him there and, with the consent of clergy and people, he was consecrated to the vacant see.

For two decades he labored to bridle the licence of the Frankish court: he won the worldly Childebert to a Christian life, healed him of a grievous sickness at the palace of Celles, and dedicated the king's new church of St. Vincent on 23 December 558, the very day of Childebert's death — the church that would one day bear Germain's own name, Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He sat in the Third and Fourth Councils of Paris and the Second of Tours, and when King Charibert's wickedness passed all bounds, Germain excommunicated him.

His last years were spent in a losing work of peace among Childebert's warring heirs: he wrote to Queen Brunehaut pleading that she stay the strife between her husband Sigebert and Chilperic, but Sigebert was murdered on the way at Vitry in 575, and Germain died the following spring, before peace returned. In 754 his relics were borne into the abbey church in the presence of Pepin and of Charlemagne, then a child of seven.

events.title: The death of St. Ferdinand III of Castile
events.shortBlurb: The king who had taken Córdoba and Seville from the Moors and turned their great mosques into cathedrals died in his city of Seville…
body: On 30 May 1252 St. Ferdinand III, king of Castile and León, died at Seville, the city he had won for Christendom four years before; the Franciscans keep his feast on this day. He was buried in Seville's great cathedral before the image of the Blessed Virgin, clothed at his own request in the habit of the Third Order of St. Francis, and his body is said to remain incorrupt.

Born near Salamanca, the son of Alfonso IX of León and of Berengaria of Castile — and so the first cousin of St. Louis IX of France — he became king of Castile in 1217 by his mother's renunciation and of León in 1230, joining the two crowns for good. The highest aims of his life, says the old account, were the propagation of the faith and the liberation of Spain: he took Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248, the greatest joys of his life, and made their great mosques cathedrals of Our Lady; at his death only Granada and Alicante remained in Moorish hands.

In the conquered towns he founded bishoprics and re-established Catholic worship, built churches, monasteries, and hospitals, and gave Spain the University of Salamanca. In camp he lived, it was said, like a religious in the cloister — fasting strictly, wearing a rough hairshirt, and spending the nights before battle in prayer. Clement X canonized him in 1671.

events.title: The Roman catacombs are rediscovered
events.shortBlurb: Diggers in a pozzolana quarry on the Via Salaria broke into a buried Christian cemetery, and Christian archaeology was born…
body: On 31 May 1578 — the date Bosio recorded and De Rossi followed, though the Roman news-sheets noted the find that June — laborers digging pozzolana on the Via Salaria broke through into a subterranean cemetery adorned with Christian paintings, Greek and Latin inscriptions, and sculptured sarcophagi. 'In that day,' wrote De Rossi, 'was born the name and the knowledge of Roma Sotterranea.'

The catacombs had never wholly been forgotten — the written sources spoke of them — but their miles of galleries had long been lost to sight. The newly opened cemetery, ascribed then to St. Priscilla, soon collapsed again under the diggers' picks; it is reckoned now the nameless cemetery of the Via Anapo. But the chase was lit: Antonio Bosio, 'the Columbus of this subterranean world,' spent his life exploring the tombs, and his Roma Sotterranea appeared at Rome in 1632, after his death.

The discovery stirred Catholic Rome. St. Philip Neri and St. Charles Borromeo spent whole nights in prayer among these ruins of the age of martyrs, as St. Jerome had prayed among the caves of Bethlehem. Two centuries later Giovanni Battista de Rossi resumed Bosio's work, and the study of the catacombs — their inscriptions, paintings, and sarcophagi — grew into the discipline of Christian archaeology.

sources.text: Schaff, History of the Christian Church, Vol. II: Ante-Nicene Christianity (public domain)

events.title: The martyrdom of Bl. John Story
events.shortBlurb: An Oxford lawyer and layman was hanged at Tyburn for defying the Elizabethan religious settlement…
body: John Story, born in 1504, was educated at Oxford, where he lectured in civil law and presided over Broadgates Hall, the house that became Pembroke College, from 1537 to 1539. Entering Parliament in 1547, he spoke boldly against the Bill of Uniformity under Edward VI and was imprisoned for it, then withdrew with his family to Louvain.

Under Queen Mary he returned and served as chancellor to Bishop Bonner of London; under Elizabeth he opposed the Bill of Supremacy in Parliament and was committed to the Fleet in May 1560. Escaping, and again escaping the Marshalsea in 1563, he fled to Antwerp, renounced his English allegiance, and became a Spanish subject.

In 1570 he was decoyed aboard an English ship at Antwerp and carried prisoner to the Tower. His plea of Spanish allegiance availed nothing: condemned for treason, he was hanged at Tyburn on 1 June 1571. Leo XIII beatified him in 1886 among the martyrs of England and Wales.

events.title: The Vandals sack Rome
events.shortBlurb: Genseric's Vandals plundered Rome for a fortnight, while Pope Leo the Great won a promise to spare lives and buildings…
body: When the Emperor Valentinian III was murdered in March 455, the usurper Petronius Maximus seized the throne and broke the betrothal that bound the imperial house to the Vandal king Genseric. Declaring his treaty void, Genseric sailed from Carthage with a great fleet and landed at the mouth of the Tiber; Maximus, fleeing the city, was torn to pieces by the Roman mob.

The chronicler Prosper of Aquitaine relates that Pope Leo I went out to meet the invader and obtained his promise that the city would not be burned nor its people slain. On 2 June 455 the gates were opened, and the Vandals and Moors plundered Rome for fourteen days, carrying off its treasures, together with the widowed empress Licinia Eudoxia and her daughters Eudocia and Placidia.

The sack, gentler than its later legend, nonetheless gave the language a word: in 1794 Bishop Grégoire coined 'vandalism' for the destruction of art. Leo's intercession before Genseric stands with his earlier turning of Attila as the glory of his pontificate.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Leo I (the Great)”
Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (public domain)

events.title: Lothair III is crowned emperor at the Lateran
events.shortBlurb: Amid a papal schism, Innocent II crowned the Saxon king emperor in St. John Lateran, for the antipope held St. Peter's…
body: The double election of 1130 had split the Church between Innocent II and Anacletus II. Anacletus held Rome, while Innocent, championed by Bernard of Clairvaux, was acknowledged in France, England, and Germany, and won the support of King Lothair of Süpplingenburg, whom he met at Liège in 1131.

Lothair crossed the Alps in 1132 with a modest army to seat Innocent in Rome and receive the imperial crown from him. In April 1133 they entered the city, but Anacletus held the Leonine City and the castle of St. Angelo, so St. Peter's could not be used.

On 4 June 1133 Innocent crowned Lothair emperor in the church of the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral. Days later the pope granted the new emperor his canonical rights and invested him with the vast inheritance of the Countess Matilda of Tuscany as a papal fief. The schism outlasted them both and ended only with Anacletus's death in 1138.

events.title: St. Louis takes Damietta
events.shortBlurb: At the opening of the Seventh Crusade, the sainted King of France took the gateway to Egypt almost without a blow…
body: Struck by a grievous illness in 1244, Louis IX of France vowed to take the cross, and the fall of Jerusalem to the Khwarezmians that year fixed his purpose. He sailed from Aigues-Mortes in August 1248, wintered in Cyprus, and steered for Egypt, reckoning its wealth the key to the Holy Land.

The crusaders landed before Damietta in the first days of June 1249, and the city, abandoned by its defenders, fell to them on 6 June — the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 7 June — almost without resistance. With the timber of twenty-four captured trebuchets Louis built a stockade for the whole camp, and set a Latin archbishop over the city.

The Nile flood held the army at Damietta for six months. When at last it marched on Cairo, pride and the river undid it: Robert of Artois was killed in the streets of Mansurah, and in April 1250 the king himself was taken prisoner, to be freed only on surrendering Damietta and paying a heavy ransom.

events.title: The death of Frederick Barbarossa
events.shortBlurb: The emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned in a Cilician river on the road to the Holy Land, breaking the greatest host of the Third Crusade…
body: Frederick I, called Barbarossa from his red beard, was elected King of the Romans in 1152 and crowned emperor at Rome in 1155. His long reign was spent in contention with the papacy of Alexander III, until defeat by the Lombard League at Legnano in 1176 brought him to the Peace of Venice the following year.

In the spring of 1188 the aged emperor took the cross at the Diet of Mainz, and on 11 May 1189 he set out for Palestine at the head of a mighty army, marching overland through Hungary and the Balkans and defeating the Seljuk Turks at Iconium in May 1190.

On 10 June 1190, crossing the River Saleph in Cilicia, he was swept from his horse and drowned. Grief and leaderlessness scattered his host: many turned home, and only a remnant reached the siege of Acre. Later legend refused his death, and placed him sleeping in the Kyffhäuser mountain, awaiting his country's hour of need.

sources.text: Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (public domain)

events.title: The consecration of Saint-Denis, the first Gothic church
events.shortBlurb: Abbot Suger's rebuilt abbey church was consecrated before the King of France — the morning of Gothic architecture…
body: The abbey of Saint-Denis, north of Paris, guarded the tomb of the third-century martyr and first bishop of the city, and had been the burial place of French kings since before Pepin the Short was anointed there by Pope Stephen II in 754. Its abbot from 1122, Suger, was counselor to two kings and would rule France as regent while Louis VII went on crusade.

Determined that the old Romanesque church was too dark and low for so royal a house of God, Suger rebuilt it, beginning about 1135 with the west front and finishing with a new choir — a ring of chapels, pointed arches and ribbed vaults, and walls opened to the 'wonderful and uninterrupted light' of stained glass.

On 11 June 1144 the new church was consecrated in the presence of King Louis VII, an occasion Suger recorded in his little book on the consecration of the church of St. Denis. The Catholic Encyclopedia marks his church as the beginning of the Gothic tendency in architecture; from it the style of the great cathedrals spread across Christendom.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Leo III
events.shortBlurb: The pope who crowned Charlemagne on Christmas Day 800 died after a pontificate of more than twenty years…
body: Leo, a Roman of the papal treasury, was elected on 26 December 795, the very day his predecessor Adrian I was buried, and consecrated the next day. At once he sent Charlemagne, King of the Franks, the keys of the Confession of St. Peter and the banner of the city of Rome, acknowledging him as the Church's protector.

On 25 April 799, in the procession of the Greater Litanies, partisans of Adrian's house set upon Leo and sought to put out his eyes and tongue; tradition holds that both were miraculously restored. He fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn, and when the king came to Rome the next year, Leo purged himself of his enemies' charges by a solemn oath in St. Peter's.

Two days later, at Mass on Christmas Day 800, Leo set the imperial crown on Charlemagne's head, reviving the empire in the West. He died on 12 June 816 and was buried in St. Peter's; he was canonized in 1673, and his feast is kept on the day of his death.

events.title: The death of John III Sobieski, the savior of Vienna
events.shortBlurb: The King of Poland who broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683 died at his beloved palace of Wilanów…
body: Born at Olesko in 1629, John Sobieski rose through wars against the Cossacks and the Turks, and his victory at Chocim in 1673 carried him the next year to the elective throne of Poland. In 1683 he bound himself by treaty to the Emperor Leopold I against the Ottoman power.

That summer the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa marched on Vienna with a vast host, and Sobieski hastened to the relief, joined by imperial and German contingents under his command. On 11 September 1683 he stood on the heights of the Kahlenberg above the city, and the next day, having heard Mass in the morning, he gave battle and routed the Turks in one of history's great cavalry charges. 'Vienna and Christendom saved,' the Catholic Encyclopedia sums it up; the king sent the captured Standard of the Prophet to the pope.

His later years brought fruitless campaigns in Hungary and bitter quarrels among his own family and nobles. He died at his palace of Wilanów on 17 June 1696 and was buried in Wawel Cathedral at Kraków.

events.title: The Battle of Civitate
events.shortBlurb: The Normans of Apulia shattered the pope's army and took St. Leo IX prisoner — a defeat that shaped the schism of 1054…
body: Leo IX, pope from 1049 and a kinsman of the Emperor Henry III, watched the Normans of southern Italy grow from pilgrims' protectors into oppressors of the land. When promised German help failed him, he raised what forces he could among the Italian princes and marched south, hoping to join the Greek general Argyrus.

The Normans under Humphrey of Hauteville, with Robert Guiscard and Richard of Aversa, cut off the papal army at Civitate near the Fortore. There, on 18 June 1053 — some accounts name the 17th — they defeated first the Greeks and then the pope's host, and Leo gave himself up to his conquerors, who knelt, the chroniclers relate, to beg his pardon.

The pope was held honorably at Benevento for some nine months and died in April 1054. The defeat bore strange fruit: Norman power in the south would soon be legitimized as a papal fief, while Leo's chancellor Humbert went as legate to Constantinople, where the mutual excommunications of 1054 fixed the schism of East and West.

events.title: The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.shortBlurb: Aetius and the Visigoths broke Attila's host in Gaul — the day the 'scourge of God' was turned back from the West…
body: In 451 Attila, king of the Huns, whom men called the scourge of God, swept into Gaul with a countless host, crossed the Rhine, and laid siege to Orléans. The Roman general Aetius gathered a coalition — Romans, Visigoths under their king Theodoric, Franks, Burgundians, and Alans — and Attila drew off to meet them.

The two armies joined battle on the Catalaunian Plains, near Troyes, on 20 June 451, as the day is conventionally reckoned. The Gothic writer Jordanes, our chief witness, tells of savage fighting for a commanding ridge: Theodoric was killed, but his son Thorismund drove on, and Attila was forced back within his circle of wagons.

The Catholic Encyclopedia says the allies 'overcame the Huns and averted the peril that menaced Western civilization.' Attila withdrew beyond the Rhine, to invade Italy the next year — where he destroyed Aquileia but turned back after his famous meeting with Pope Leo the Great — and died in 453.

sources.text: Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (public domain)

events.title: The fall of Fort St. Elmo in the Great Siege of Malta
events.shortBlurb: After a month of savage assault the Ottomans took the ruined fort — but its stand had bled them and bought time for Christendom…
body: In May 1565 Suleiman the Magnificent sent a great armada, more than forty thousand men, to erase the Knights of St. John from Malta, their home since 1530. The Grand Master Jean Parisot de la Valette, a veteran of seventy years, had some six to eight thousand defenders behind the walls of Birgu, Senglea, and the little star-fort of St. Elmo guarding the harbor mouths.

The Turkish commanders, Mustafa Pasha and Piyale Pasha, expected St. Elmo to fall in days. Instead a few hundred knights and soldiers held its crumbling works from late May until 23 June 1565, when the last defenders died almost to a man. The victory cost the Ottomans dearly — by some reckonings eight thousand men, among them the famed corsair Dragut, mortally wounded before the walls.

That month of blood bought the time Malta needed: the main fortresses held until a relief force from Sicily came in September and the siege was raised. The Catholic Encyclopedia ranks La Valette's defense as high as Lepanto among the feats of Christian chivalry; his new city, Valletta, still bears his name.

events.title: The first Grand Lodge of Freemasonry is founded
events.shortBlurb: Four London lodges united on the feast of St. John the Baptist — the beginning of a fraternity the Church would soon condemn…
body: Freemasonry in its modern, speculative form — a moral system veiled in allegory rather than a craft of working masons — begins, as the Catholic Encyclopedia puts it, with the foundation of the Grand Lodge of England on 24 June 1717.

That day, the feast of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, patron of the masons, four old London lodges met at the Goose and Gridiron ale-house by St. Paul's Churchyard and elected Anthony Sayer their first Grand Master. The organization was completed a few years later with Anderson's Book of Constitutions of 1723 and the three degrees of apprentice, fellow, and master; from 1721 the new fraternity spread rapidly over Europe and America.

The Church moved early against it: in 1738 Clement XII, by the bull In Eminenti, forbade Catholics under pain of excommunication to join or favor the Masons, judging its secret oaths and naturalistic religion incompatible with the faith — a judgment confirmed by Benedict XIV and often restated since.

events.title: The Augsburg Confession is read before Charles V
events.shortBlurb: Melanchthon's statement of the Lutheran faith was read aloud to the emperor at Augsburg — and the schism stood confessed…
body: Charles V summoned the estates of the Empire to Augsburg in 1530, hoping to end the religious quarrel and unite Germany against the Turks. The Lutheran princes answered with a confession of their faith, drafted by Philip Melanchthon from earlier articles and approved by Luther, who, under the imperial ban, could only follow events from Coburg Castle.

On 25 June 1530 the Confession, signed by seven German princes — Elector John of Saxony and Philip of Hesse among them — and by the envoys of Nuremberg and Reutlingen, was presented to the emperor in Latin and German, the German text read aloud before the assembled estates in the chapel of the episcopal palace.

Catholic theologians replied with the Confutatio, read in August, which Melanchthon answered in his Apology of the following year. As the Catholic Encyclopedia observes, the diet showed that the restoration of religious unity was not to be effected. The Unaltered Augsburg Confession of 1580 remains the charter of Lutheran belief.

events.title: The consecration of Pope St. Agatho
events.shortBlurb: A Sicilian, a centenarian by tradition, ascended Peter's chair — to hear an English bishop's appeal and end the Monothelite quarrel…
body: Agatho, a Sicilian of Palermo long serving as treasurer of the Roman Church, succeeded Pope Donus and was consecrated on 27 June 678; there is good authority, the Catholic Encyclopedia says, that he was then more than a hundred years old, though later scholarship has doubted the tale.

Soon after, Wilfrid of York arrived to plead against his uncanonical deposition — the first appeal of an English bishop to the Holy See. At a Lateran synod Agatho judged the case, confirming the division of the great northern diocese but requiring that Wilfrid himself name the new bishops.

His chief work was the Sixth Ecumenical Council. Answering the Emperor Constantine IV, Agatho held synods through the West and sent legates with his letter confessing two wills in Christ; the council opened at Constantinople on 7 November 680 with the papal legates presiding, condemned Monothelitism, and named even Pope Honorius among the heretics. The decrees reached Rome only after Agatho's death on 10 January 681.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 January

events.title: The election of Charles V as emperor
events.shortBlurb: A Habsburg not yet twenty was chosen emperor at Frankfurt, joining Spain, the Netherlands, Austria, and the Empire under one crown…
body: The death of the Emperor Maximilian I in January 1519 opened a contest for the imperial crown between the young King Charles of Spain — already lord of the Netherlands, Naples, and the new world beyond the Atlantic — and Francis I of France, with Henry VIII of England a hopeful third.

On 28 June 1519 the electors at Frankfurt chose Charles. In spite of the opposition of Rome and France, the Catholic Encyclopedia notes, he was everywhere received as emperor elect; not yet twenty, he had laid the foundation of a universal monarchy, and was crowned at Aachen the following year.

His election set the stage of the Reformation age: before him Luther stood at Worms in 1521, to him the Augsburg Confession was read in 1530, and his wars — with France, with the Lutherans, with the Turk — filled four decades. Weary at last, he divided his inheritance between his son Philip and his brother Ferdinand, and died in retirement at the monastery of Yuste in 1558.

events.title: The consecration of Westminster Cathedral
events.shortBlurb: Sixty years after the restoration of the English hierarchy, the great Byzantine cathedral of Westminster was consecrated…
body: Cardinal Herbert Vaughan, third Archbishop of Westminster, vowed to give the restored English hierarchy a worthy mother church. The foundation stone was laid on the feast of SS. Peter and Paul, 29 June 1895, and John Francis Bentley raised it in brick and Byzantine splendor, deliberately refusing to rival the Gothic of neighboring Westminster Abbey. The cathedral opened in 1903.

Canon law forbade consecration while debt burdened the fabric, and Vaughan's death that year slowed the appeal. His successor, Cardinal Francis Bourne, pressed on until, on the last day of April 1910, the building stood free of debt.

The consecration unfolded over three days, 27 to 29 June 1910: the exposition of the relics, then on 28 June the anointing of the cathedral's thirteen altars with a Mass of Dedication, and on the feast of SS. Peter and Paul a final Mass sung by the archbishop before the Lord Mayor of London. The cathedral's own chronicle called it an epoch in the history of the Catholic Church in England.

events.title: The Credo of the People of God
events.shortBlurb: Closing the Year of Faith, Paul VI professed a creed for an age of doubt before the tomb of the Apostles…
body: Pope Paul VI had proclaimed a Year of Faith to mark the nineteenth centenary of the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul. On 30 June 1968, at the solemn liturgy that closed it, he fulfilled, as he said, the mandate given to Peter — to confirm his brethren in the faith — by pronouncing a new profession of faith, the motu proprio Solemni Hac Liturgia, known ever since as the Credo of the People of God.

The pope knew the hour: he spoke of a 'disquiet' agitating modern quarters of the Church, and of Catholics 'seized by a kind of passion for change and novelty.' His creed was not a dogmatic definition, he said, but the creed of Nicaea and of the Church's immortal tradition, repeated in substance with developments called for by the spiritual condition of the time.

It confesses, article by article, the Trinity and the Incarnation, Mary ever Virgin and Mother of the Church, original sin transmitted 'not by imitation, but by propagation,' the Mass as the sacrifice of Calvary made present, and the change of the bread and wine into the body and blood of the Lord — a change 'very appropriately called by the Church transubstantiation.'

sources.text: Apostolic Letter Solemni Hac Liturgia (Credo of the People of God), Pope Paul VI (vatican.va)

events.title: The death of St. Swithun
events.shortBlurb: The humble bishop of Winchester was laid, at his own wish, in the open churchyard where the rain might fall upon his grave…
body: St. Swithun was one of the two trusted counsellors of Egbert, King of the West Saxons, who raised him to the see of Winchester about the year 852 and is said to have committed to him the schooling of his son Ethelwulf. The Catholic Encyclopedia, reckoning his death on 2 July 862 — some later authorities give 863 — preserves little of his episcopate, for his fame rests less on deeds than on the humility of his end.

He asked to be buried not within his minster but in the open ground of the churchyard, where the feet of passers-by might tread above him and the rain from the eaves fall upon his grave. There his body rested until 15 July 971, when Bishop Æthelwold translated his relics into the church and raised a shrine in his honor.

From that translation grew his patronage of Winchester Cathedral and the weather-lore that made his name a proverb: St. Swithun's day, if thou dost rain, for forty days it will remain. His shrine, one of the great pilgrim goals of medieval England, was broken up in 1538, when the cult of the saints was swept away; a modern memorial now marks its place.

events.title: The founding of Quebec
events.shortBlurb: Samuel de Champlain laid the foundation of the Habitation de Québec, the cradle of the Church in Canada…
body: On 3 July 1608 Samuel de Champlain, lieutenant of Pierre Dugua de Monts, laid the foundation of the Habitation de Québec on the strand below Cape Diamond, where the St. Lawrence narrows — kebec, in the Algonquin tongue. Around that modest dwelling of wood arose the village of Quebec, the first permanent French settlement in Canada and the cradle of the Church in New France.

Champlain, whom the Catholic Encyclopedia calls the Father of New France, had written that he longed above all to see the lily flourish in those lands together with the only religion catholic, Apostolic and Roman. He brought over the Franciscan Recollects in 1615, who began the missions to the Montagnais and the Hurons; the Jesuits followed in 1625.

The little colony surrendered to the English Kirke brothers in 1629 and was restored to France by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1632; Champlain died in its fort on Christmas Day, 1635. In 1659 François de Laval arrived as vicar apostolic, and in 1674 Clement X erected Quebec into a diocese depending solely on Rome — the mother see of Canada, from which the Church spread across the continent.

events.title: The election of Pope Celestine V
events.shortBlurb: After a vacancy of more than two years the cardinals chose an aged hermit, who would reign five months and then resign…
body: When Nicholas IV died in April 1292, the cardinals, divided between the Colonna and the Orsini, could not agree upon a successor, and the see of Peter stood vacant for twenty-seven months. At Perugia, on 5 July 1294, at the cry of the aged Cardinal Latino Malabranca, they elected the Benedictine hermit Pietro da Morrone, an aged ascetic of the Abruzzi near eighty, whose little congregation of hermits had been confirmed at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274.

The new pope, who took the name Celestine V, was crowned on 29 August before the basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio at L'Aquila, which he himself had built; his was the last papal election held without the forms of a conclave. Utterly without experience of affairs, he fell under the direction of Charles II of Naples and soon longed for his cell.

Advised by Cardinal Benedetto Caetani that a pope might lawfully resign, he issued a constitution affirming the right and laid down the office on 13 December 1294, after a reign of five months. He died a prisoner of his successor Boniface VIII on 19 May 1296, and Clement V numbered him among the saints in 1313.

events.title: The rehabilitation of St. Joan of Arc
events.shortBlurb: Twenty-five years after the stake at Rouen, a court of the Church annulled the sentence that had condemned the Maid…
body: Joan of Arc was burned in the Old Market of Rouen on 30 May 1431, condemned as a relapsed heretic by Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, sitting in the English interest. Her mother, Isabelle Romée, never ceased to plead her innocence, and after Charles VII recovered Rouen in 1449 the cause was reopened: Guillaume Bouillé held a first inquiry in 1450, and the inquisitor Jean Bréhal a fuller one in 1452.

At the petition of Isabelle and of Bréhal, Pope Callixtus III authorized a solemn revision, which opened at Notre-Dame de Paris on 7 November 1455. The judges heard a hundred and fifteen witnesses who had known Joan or served at her trial.

On 7 July 1456, in the archiepiscopal palace at Rouen, the court pronounced its sentence: the trial, the abjuration, and the condemnation of 1431 were declared tainted with corruption, cozenage, calumny, fraud, malice, iniquity, and manifest errors of fact as well as of law, and were annulled with all their effects. A cross was ordered to be raised on the place where she died. The Maid was beatified in 1909 and canonized on 16 May 1920.

events.title: The death of Pope Eugene III
events.shortBlurb: The first Cistercian pope, the disciple of St. Bernard who summoned Europe to the Second Crusade, died far from his own rebellious city…
body: On the day Pope Lucius II died, 15 February 1145, the cardinals withdrew to St. Cæsarius' cloister on the Appian Way and unanimously chose a man outside their body: Bernard of Pisa, abbot of Tre Fontane, the first monk of Cîteaux to sit in the chair of Peter. He took the name Eugene III.

His eight years were spent in conflict with the Roman commune, which drove him from the city; he found refuge at Viterbo, in France, and at Tivoli. When Edessa fell to the Saracens in 1144, Eugene addressed a stirring appeal to the chivalry of Europe and commissioned his old master, St. Bernard of Clairvaux, to preach what became the Second Crusade; Bernard answered with the treatise De consideratione, written for this pope.

Eugene held reforming synods, above all at Reims in 1148, and that year excommunicated Arnold of Brescia, the firebrand of the Roman revolt. He died at Tivoli, whither he had gone to escape the summer heats, on 8 July 1153, and was buried before the high altar of St. Peter's; Bernard followed him to the grave within six weeks, and Pius IX confirmed his cult in 1872.

events.title: The birth of John Calvin
events.shortBlurb: At Noyon in Picardy was born the man who would give the Reformation its most systematic form…
body: John Calvin was born at Noyon in Picardy on 10 July 1509, the son of Gérard Cauvin, a notary of the cathedral chapter and secretary to the bishop. Sent to Paris, then to Orléans and Bourges for the study of law, he drank in the new learning and the writings of Luther, and by 1533 had broken with the Church of his baptism.

In 1536, at Basel, he published the first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion, the most systematic statement the Reformation produced, and in the same year was detained at Geneva to organize its reform. Driven out in 1538, he was recalled in 1541, and until his death on 27 May 1564 he guided the city's doctrine and discipline, making Geneva the school and fortress of the Reformed churches.

From Geneva his influence reached France, the Netherlands, Scotland, and England; the burning of the Spanish scholar Michael Servetus there in 1553 remains the shadow upon his name. The Church answered his system at the Council of Trent, which defined against the Reformers the doctrines of the sacraments, of tradition, and of the sacrifice of the Mass.

events.title: Clement VII’s sentence against Henry VIII
events.shortBlurb: Clement VII annulled the divorce of Henry VIII and pronounced him excommunicate, suspending the sentence for a last space of repentance…
body: By the spring of 1533 Henry VIII had resolved the King's great matter without Rome: in January he secretly married Anne Boleyn; on 23 May Thomas Cranmer, the new Archbishop of Canterbury, declared his marriage to Catherine of Aragon null from the beginning; and on 1 June Anne was crowned queen at Westminster.

When word reached Rome, Pope Clement VII struck back. By a brief dated 11 July 1533 he declared Cranmer's sentences void and Henry's marriage to Catherine alone valid, pronounced that the king had incurred the greater excommunication, yet suspended the declaration of the sentence until the end of September, offering him a last space to take back his true wife.

Henry did not yield. The definitive sentence for the validity of Catherine's marriage was given on 23 March 1534, and Parliament answered that November with the Act of Supremacy, naming the king supreme head on earth of the Church of England. The breach with Rome, so long threatened, was complete; within two years Fisher and More had sealed with their blood the truth the sentence had defended.

events.title: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy
events.shortBlurb: The Constituent Assembly redrew the Church of France without the pope, and sowed the schism of juror and refractory…
body: Having seized the goods of the Church in November 1789 and suppressed the monastic orders the following February, the National Constituent Assembly turned to the clergy itself. After debate opened on 1 June, it passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy on 12 July 1790.

The law remade the Church upon the map of the state: dioceses were conformed to the eighty-three departments, some fifty episcopal sees suppressed, the title of archbishop abolished; bishops and parish priests were to be chosen by civil electoral assemblies, open even to Protestant and Jewish voters; no confirmation might be sought from the pope, and all appeals to Rome were forbidden. The clergy became salaried officers of the nation.

Louis XVI promulgated the Constitution on 24 August, writing to the pope that he did so with death in his soul. In November the Assembly imposed an oath to the Constitution on every bishop and priest; of some one hundred and thirty bishops only four took it. Pius VI solemnly condemned the whole work on 13 April 1791, and the Church of France split into the jurors of the Constitutional Church and the refractory priests, whose fidelity was answered with deportation and, in the Terror, with death.

events.title: The Great Fire of Rome
events.shortBlurb: Rome burned for a week; and to still the rumor against himself, Nero fastened the crime upon the Christians…
body: In the night between 18 and 19 July of the year 64 fire broke out among the shops by the Circus Maximus and ran through Rome. It raged for six days and seven nights, Tacitus records, was checked, and burst out afresh; of the city's fourteen districts, three were leveled, seven left in ruins, only four unharmed.

Rumor laid the fire at the emperor's door: it was said that Nero sang the burning of Troy while the city burned. To kill the report, Tacitus writes, Nero fastened the guilt on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace, and inflicted the most exquisite tortures upon them. A vast multitude were convicted, not so much of arson as of hatred of the human race: they were crucified, sewn in the skins of beasts to be torn by dogs, or burned as lamps in the emperor's gardens.

So began the first persecution of the Church by the Roman state. Christian tradition reckons among its victims the princes of the apostles themselves, St. Peter crucified and St. Paul beheaded under Nero; and the blood of those martyrs, as Tertullian would write, proved the seed of the Church.

events.title: The death of Pope Leo XIII
events.shortBlurb: The author of Rerum novarum, then the oldest man ever to sit in Peter's chair, ended a twenty-five-year pontificate…
body: Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci, born at Carpineto Romano on 2 March 1810, had been for thirty-two years Archbishop of Perugia when, on 20 February 1878, the conclave chose him to succeed Pius IX; expected to prove a transitional pope, he reigned instead for a quarter of a century.

Leo XIII opened the Vatican Archives to the scholars of the world, restored the study of St. Thomas Aquinas with the encyclical Aeterni Patris in 1879, and on 15 May 1891 issued Rerum novarum, the charter of the Church's social teaching, condemning both the rapacity of unbridled capital and the remedy of socialism. He wrote eleven encyclicals on the Rosary, sought reunion with the separated churches of the East, and lived to be the first pope filmed and the first whose voice was recorded.

He died in the Vatican on 20 July 1903, aged ninety-three years and one hundred and forty days — the oldest of the popes in history. He was buried in St. Peter's, and in 1924 his body was translated to the basilica of St. John Lateran, his cathedral as Bishop of Rome. The conclave that followed him raised Cardinal Sarto, the Patriarch of Venice, to the see of Peter as Pius X.

events.title: The sack of Béziers
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of St. Mary Magdalen, the crusaders against the Albigenses stormed Béziers and slew its people…
body: In 1208 the papal legate Peter of Castelnau was murdered in the lands of Count Raymond VI of Toulouse, and Innocent III summoned the barons of the north to a crusade against the Albigensian heresy of Languedoc. The host that gathered in 1209 marched under the legate Arnold Amalric, Abbot of Cîteaux.

Its first blow fell upon the young Viscount Raymond-Roger Trencavel. On 22 July 1209, the feast of St. Mary Magdalen, the crusaders stormed his city of Béziers; the townsfolk who had refused to yield up the heretics were put to the sword without distinction, in the streets and in the churches where they had taken sanctuary, and the city burned. The legate's own letter to the pope reckoned the slain at near twenty thousand, a figure modern historians judge beyond belief.

The sack is remembered through the words the Cistercian Caesarius of Heisterbach, writing a generation later, put in the legate's mouth: Kill them all; God will know His own. The Catholic Encyclopedia judges they were never spoken. Carcassonne surrendered within weeks, and the war went on to devastate the Midi for twenty years.

events.title: The abdication of Mary Queen of Scots
events.shortBlurb: In her island prison at Loch Leven the Catholic queen of the Scots was compelled to resign her crown to her infant son…
body: The Scotland to which Mary Stuart returned from France in 1561 was already lost to the old faith: the year before, the Reformation Parliament had abolished the Mass and the pope's authority, and the young Catholic queen ruled a realm governed by Calvinist lords and the preaching of John Knox.

Her own hand undid her. Her husband Lord Darnley was murdered at Kirk o' Field on 10 February 1567; within three months she married the Earl of Bothwell, whom the world accused of the deed. The confederate lords rose, met her forces at Carberry Hill on 15 June 1567, and shut her in the island castle of Loch Leven. There, on 24 July 1567, threatened with death if she refused, she signed the instruments of abdication in favor of her year-old son, who was crowned as James VI, with her half-brother the Earl of Moray as regent.

She escaped in May 1568, was beaten at Langside, and fled across the Solway into England — to nineteen years of captivity, the hope of Catholic plots, and the block at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587. Her fall sealed the Protestant settlement in Scotland; her son would one day join the crowns of Scotland and England.

events.title: The martyrdom of Fr. Jacques Hamel
events.shortBlurb: An eighty-five-year-old priest was slain at the altar during morning Mass in Normandy, and the Church numbered him among the martyrs…
body: On the morning of 26 July 2016, Fr. Jacques Hamel, an eighty-five-year-old auxiliary priest, was celebrating Mass in the church of Saint-Étienne at Saint-Étienne-du-Rouvray, near Rouen, when two young men who had pledged themselves to the Islamic State burst in with knives. Before the five faithful present — among them three religious sisters — they seized the priest at the altar and cut his throat; one parishioner was gravely wounded before the police shot the two attackers dead.

The killing, claimed by the Islamic State, struck the Church as World Youth Day opened in Kraków. Speaking of it with the pilgrims of Rouen at a Mass at Santa Marta on 14 September, the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, Pope Francis said that in the long chain of Christian martyrs, which begins with Jesus Christ Himself, the Church now reaches our dear Jacques: he is a martyr, and martyrs are blessed.

Dispensing with the five years the law requires, Pope Francis allowed the Archdiocese of Rouen to open the cause of Fr. Hamel's beatification in April 2017. His tomb, and the little church where he died saying Mass, have become places of pilgrimage.

sources.text: In-flight press conference of Pope Francis returning from World Youth Day in Kraków, 31 July 2016 (vatican.va)
Agenzia Fides, “Father Jacques is part of the chain of Christian martyrs which began with Jesus Christ” (fides.org)

events.title: The Battle of Bouvines
events.shortBlurb: On a Sunday in Flanders, Philip Augustus broke the emperor Otto IV and his allies, and remade the map of western Europe…
body: In 1214 King John of England and the emperor Otto IV — excommunicated by Innocent III for seizing the lands of the pope's ward, the young Frederick of Sicily — joined with Ferrand of Flanders, Renaud of Boulogne, and William Longespée, Earl of Salisbury, to crush Philip Augustus of France between two armies: John's in Poitou, Otto's in the north.

John's thrust broke at La Roche-aux-Moines before Prince Louis; and on Sunday, 27 July 1214, by a little bridge over the Marcq at Bouvines near Tournai, Philip met the northern army and destroyed it. Ferrand and Renaud were led off in chains, Longespée struck down and taken, and Otto fled, his cause lost. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls Bouvines the first French national victory.

Its consequences reached every throne of the West. Otto sank to his wrecked inheritance, and Frederick II, the pope's Hohenstaufen ward, was crowned at Aachen in July 1215; John was brought by his barons to Runnymede in June 1215 to seal Magna Carta. That November Innocent III opened the Fourth Lateran Council, the greatest assembly of the medieval Church, over a Christendom Bouvines had reordered.

events.title: The accession of the Emperor Justinian
events.shortBlurb: On the death of his uncle Justin I, Justinian became sole emperor of the Romans, beginning the reign that codified the law and warred to restore the empire…
body: On 1 August 527 the Emperor Justin I died at Constantinople, and his nephew Justinian, already crowned Augustus and co-emperor the previous April, succeeded him as sole ruler of the Roman Empire in the East. Born Petrus Sabbatius about 482 at Tauresium in Illyricum, he had long been the chief power of his uncle's reign; his consort Theodora had been crowned with him.

The thirty-eight years of his rule were the most brilliant of the later empire. His jurists under Tribonian gathered the law into the Corpus Juris Civilis — the Codex of 529, the Digest and the Institutes of 533, and the later Novels — which gave the canons of the first four general councils the force of law and fixed Roman jurisprudence for a thousand years. His generals Belisarius and Narses recovered Africa from the Vandals in 533 and Italy from the Goths in a twenty-year war.

He ruled the Church as he ruled the state, and not gently: the Fifth General Council, held at Constantinople in 553, sat under his hand and condemned the Three Chapters, while Pope Vigilius, kept in the city against his will, was brought to assent. When the Nika riot of 532 left the church of the Holy Wisdom in ashes, Justinian rebuilt it as the great church of Christendom. He died on 14 November 565.

events.title: Mary Tudor enters London in triumph
events.shortBlurb: Proclaimed queen against the nine days' reign of Lady Jane Grey, Mary Tudor rode into her capital to begin the Catholic restoration of England…
body: Edward VI died at Greenwich on 6 July 1553, and by his device the crown was settled upon his cousin Lady Jane Grey, proclaimed on 10 July. The country would not have her: the eastern counties rose for the Lady Mary, Edward's Catholic half-sister, and on 19 July the council in London proclaimed her queen. The Duke of Northumberland, the author of the device, was taken at Cambridge.

On 3 August 1553 Mary made her entry into London, riding with her sister Elizabeth from Aldgate to the Tower through streets hung for her welcome. At the Tower gate the prisoners of the late reign knelt to greet her — the aged Duke of Norfolk, Bishop Stephen Gardiner of Winchester, and Edward Courtenay, son of the Marquis of Exeter — and she raised them up and kissed them, and set them free. Northumberland went to the block on 22 August; the Lady Jane she meant to spare.

She was crowned at Westminster by Gardiner on 1 October. In the five years of her reign the Latin service was restored, the old heresy laws revived, and England reconciled to the Holy See; the fires kindled for the Protestants at Smithfield fixed her in the memory of their churches as Bloody Mary, a name her Catholic subjects did not use.

events.title: The election of Pope St. Pius X
events.shortBlurb: After the Austrian emperor's veto struck down the leading candidate, the cardinals chose the Patriarch of Venice, Giuseppe Sarto, who took the name Pius X…
body: Leo XIII died on 20 July 1903, and sixty-two cardinals entered the conclave at the end of that month. The favourite was his Secretary of State, Cardinal Mariano Rampolla, who took twenty-four votes on the first ballot; the Patriarch of Venice, Cardinal Giuseppe Sarto, had five.

On the second day of the conclave Cardinal Jan Puzyna of Kraków rose and, in the name of the Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria, pronounced the formal exclusion of Rampolla — the jus exclusivae by which the Catholic sovereigns still claimed a voice in papal elections. The cardinals protested the intrusion and went on with their ballots, but Rampolla's strength ebbed away, and on 4 August 1903, on the seventh ballot, Sarto was elected. He took the name Pius X, with the motto Instaurare omnia in Christo, 'to restore all things in Christ'.

He was crowned on 9 August. Among the first acts of his pontificate, by the constitution Commissum nobis of 20 January 1904, he forbade any such veto in conclaves to come under pain of excommunication; no secular power has openly intervened in a papal election since.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. Pius X (vatican.va)

events.title: St. Oswald falls at Maserfield
events.shortBlurb: The king who had brought Aidan and the monks of Iona to Northumbria was slain by the pagan Penda of Mercia, and numbered at once among the martyrs…
body: Oswald, son of King Æthelfrith of Bernicia, had spent his youth in exile among the Irish monks of Iona and there been baptized. Returning, he overthrew the British king Cadwallon at the Heavenfield near the Roman Wall, in 634 by the common reckoning, setting up with his own hands a wooden cross before the battle; and he sent to Iona for a bishop. In 635 Aidan came, and Oswald gave him the island of Lindisfarne for his see, translating the Irishman's preaching for his thegns until the English speech came to him.

For eight years he ruled Northumbria, the strongest of the English kings, whom Bede numbers among those who held the lordship of the southern nations. On 5 August, in 642 as the chronicle reckons, he met Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, in battle at the place called Maserfield — Oswestry, Oswald's Tree, as the English came to name it — and was slain there, dying, Bede tells, with a prayer for the souls of his soldiers, which passed into a proverb.

Penda set his head and arms upon stakes. His brother Oswiu recovered them: the head was laid at Lindisfarne, the arms at Bamburgh, where his right hand, Bede records, remained uncorrupted. Miracles were told of the very soil where he fell, and the dead king was venerated as a martyr from that day.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 August

events.title: The death of St. Cajetan
events.shortBlurb: Gaetano of Thiene, co-founder of the Theatines and father of the clerks regular, died at Naples, worn out with labour and with grief for the city he loved…
body: Gaetano dei Conti di Thiene was born at Vicenza in October 1480, took the doctorate in both laws at Padua, and served Pope Julius II in the Roman curia before his ordination in 1516. In Rome he gave himself to the Oratory of Divine Love, a company of priests and laymen seeking the reform of the Church from within, and founded hospitals for the incurably sick at Vicenza and Venice.

On 3 May 1524, with Gian Pietro Carafa, Bishop of Chieti and afterwards Pope Paul IV, he founded at Rome the Congregation of Clerics Regular, called Theatines from Carafa's see — priests bound to common life and evangelical poverty, trusting in providence for their bread and forbidden to beg. Clement VII approved the order that June. It was the first of the congregations of clerks regular, the model of the Jesuits and the Barnabites that followed. In the sack of Rome in 1527 the little company was tortured and scattered, and made its way to Venice.

Sent to Naples in 1533, Cajetan laboured there fourteen years, preaching, hearing confessions, and founding a charitable bank against usury that grew into the Banco di Napoli. Worn with toil, and grieved by the factions of the city, he died there on 7 August 1547. He was canonized by Clement X on 12 April 1671.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 August

events.title: The death of the Emperor Henry IV
events.shortBlurb: The emperor who had stood in the snow at Canossa and warred for thirty years with the reformed papacy died an excommunicate fugitive at Liège…
body: Henry IV, king of the Germans from the age of six and emperor from 1084, spent his reign in the long quarrel over the investiture of bishops. Excommunicated by Gregory VII in 1076, he won absolution in the snow at Canossa the next January; then set up the antipope Clement III, took Rome in 1084, and was crowned by his creature in St. Peter's, while Gregory died in exile at Salerno.

His last sorrows came from his own house. His son Henry, crowned to secure the succession, turned against him, and at Ingelheim in December 1105 compelled the old emperor to resign the throne. Henry escaped his keepers, found loyalty at Liège and Cologne, and in the spring of 1106 worsted his son's forces near Visé; but his strength was gone, and at Liège, on 7 August 1106, he died, aged fifty-five, the ban of the Church still upon him.

Even his grave was contested. The faithful of Speyer bore his body home, but the excommunicate emperor was laid in an unconsecrated chapel outside the cathedral, and only in 1111, the ban lifted, did his son have him entombed in the cathedral beside his fathers. The conflict he had fought was settled eleven years after his death, at the Concordat of Worms of 1122.

events.title: The Robber Council of Ephesus
events.shortBlurb: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria and backed by soldiers, the Second Council of Ephesus absolved Eutyches and broke Flavian of Constantinople…
body: The monk Eutyches, condemned by Flavian of Constantinople and his home synod in November 448 for teaching that after the union Christ had but one nature, found a patron in Dioscorus, Cyril's successor at Alexandria, and a court at his back. Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus, and there, on 8 August 449, some one hundred and thirty bishops assembled, with Dioscorus presiding by imperial command.

The bishops who had sat in judgment on Eutyches were denied their votes; the letters of Pope Leo, borne by his legates — among them his dogmatic Tome to Flavian — were never suffered to be read. Eutyches was absolved and restored, while Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, his accuser, were deposed. When resistance was offered, soldiers and a monastic crowd were brought in; bishops were driven to sign a blank paper, and the deacon Hilary, the pope's legate, could only cry Contradicitur — 'it is opposed' — and flee for his life.

Flavian, beaten and sent into exile, died of his usage within days. Leo named the assembly a latrocinium, a den of robbers, and the name has clung to it. Two years later, at Chalcedon in 451, the work was undone, the Tome was read with acclamation, and Dioscorus was deposed.

events.title: The Battle of Adrianople (378)
events.shortBlurb: The Emperor Valens fell with two-thirds of his army before the Goths in Thrace, and with him fell the last Arian patron on the imperial throne…
body: Driven by the Huns, the Goths had begged admission into the empire, and in 376 the Emperor Valens let the Tervingi cross the Danube. The greed of the Roman officers starved them into revolt, and for two years they ravaged Thrace under Fritigern. Valens came up from Antioch and, unwilling to await his nephew Gratian's army from the West, gave battle on 9 August 378 near Adrianople.

The Gothic horse returned upon the Roman flank at the crisis of the day, and the army of the East was destroyed where it stood. Two-thirds of it perished, and the emperor with it; his body was never found. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who had marched in such armies, could find no Roman disaster to set beside it since Cannae.

Valens was the last Arian to hold the throne: baptized by the Arian Eudoxus, he had used his power against the Catholic faith in the East, driving its bishops into exile. The dead man's dominions fell to Gratian, who in January 379 called the Spaniard Theodosius to be Augustus; and Theodosius, within thirteen months, published at Thessalonica the edict that named the Catholic communion the faith of the empire.

events.title: The death of St. Flavian of Constantinople
events.shortBlurb: Deposed and beaten by the soldiers and monks of the Robber Council, the patriarch who had condemned Eutyches died of his usage in exile three days later…
body: Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople from 446, was the first to strike at the teaching of the archimandrite Eutyches, that after the incarnation there is in Christ but one nature. At his synod at Constantinople in November 448 Eutyches was condemned and cast out of his monastery; and it was to Flavian that Leo the Great addressed his dogmatic letter, the Tome, which the fathers at Chalcedon would receive as the faith of Peter.

At the council which Theodosius II gathered at Ephesus on 8 August 449, Dioscorus of Alexandria sat as president, Leo's letters were refused a reading, and Flavian was set at the bar as a criminal. Sentence of deposition was pronounced upon him amid the violence of soldiers and monks; the old man, clinging to the altar, was so handled that his strength was broken. He was sent into exile to Hypaepa in Lydia, and there, on 11 August by the ancient reckoning, he died of what he had suffered.

Rome kept him among the martyrs. When Theodosius died the next year, his sister Pulcheria had the body brought back to Constantinople with more honour, says the chronicler, than a triumph; and at Chalcedon in 451 his name was restored with praise as a confessor of the faith he had died for.

events.title: The death of Pope Innocent XI
events.shortBlurb: Benedetto Odescalchi, the frugal and inflexible pope who withstood Louis XIV and filled the war chest of the Holy League against the Turk, died at Rome…
body: Benedetto Odescalchi was born at Como in 1611, served the curia under Urban VIII, and was made cardinal in 1645. Elected pope on 21 September 1676 against the wish of Louis XIV, he took the name Innocent XI, cut the debts of the Apostolic Camera by rigid economy, and lived as plainly as he ruled.

His pontificate was one long resistance to the Most Christian King. He condemned the Four Articles of the Gallican clergy assembled in 1682; in the quarrel of the régale he refused institution to bishops who had taken part in that assembly, so that by 1688 more than thirty French sees stood vacant; and when the ambassador Lavardin entered Rome with seven hundred armed men to uphold the right of asylum, Innocent excommunicated him, and Louis answered by seizing Avignon. In the same years he condemned sixty-five lax propositions of the casuists and the quietism of Molinos.

The money his thrift gathered he poured into the war against the Ottoman: the subsidies he sent to the Emperor and to John Sobieski of Poland armed the Holy League that raised the siege of Vienna in 1683, recovered Buda in 1686, and took Belgrade in 1688. He died at Rome on 12 August 1689, and was beatified by Pius XII in 1956.

events.title: The encyclical Humani Generis
events.shortBlurb: Pius XII warned against new opinions in philosophy, Scripture, and theology, and ruled how far the question of human evolution might be discussed…
body: On 12 August 1950, addressing the bishops of the world, Pius XII published the encyclical Humani Generis, 'concerning some false opinions threatening to undermine the foundations of Catholic doctrine'. In that same year he would define the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

The encyclical warned against the fashion that would make dogma a mere symbol, against false irenicism that blurred revealed truth for the sake of reunion, and against the exegesis that emptied the first chapters of Genesis of history. On the question then agitating the schools, it did not forbid research and discussion of evolution touching the origin of the human body from pre-existing and living matter; but it required that souls be held immediately created by God, and it judged that the faithful could not embrace polygenism, which cannot be reconciled with the doctrine of original sin actually committed by one Adam.

Its cautions were felt as a check upon the nouvelle théologie stirring in France, and in the years that followed some teachers were withdrawn from their chairs. Several of the theologians so restrained were heard with honour at the Second Vatican Council, and one of them, Henri de Lubac, died a cardinal.

sources.text: Encyclical Humani Generis of Pope Pius XII, 12 August 1950 (vatican.va)

events.title: The election of Pope Paschal II
events.shortBlurb: A fortnight after Urban II died unknowing that Jerusalem had fallen, Cardinal Rainerius was chosen pope, to carry on the crusade and the Gregorian reform…
body: Urban II, the pope of Clermont, died at Rome on 29 July 1099, fourteen days after the crusaders had taken Jerusalem; the tidings had not yet reached the West. On 13 August the cardinals chose in his place Rainerius da Bieda, a monk from near Ravenna whom Gregory VII had made cardinal-priest of San Clemente and Urban had sent as legate to Spain. He took the name Paschal II.

His nineteen years were consumed by the same two causes as his master's. He forwarded the crusade, sending help to the new Latin kingdom and blessing the expeditions that followed the first. And he maintained the Gregorian law against lay investiture, coming to terms with Henry I of England and Philip of France in 1107, but finding no peace with the empire.

In 1111 Henry V came down into Italy, seized the pope and his cardinals, and after two months' captivity extorted from the prisoner a concession of investiture. A Lateran council the next year annulled the grant, and Paschal bore with patience the reproaches of stricter churchmen who blamed his weakness. He died at Rome on 21 January 1118; the long quarrel was composed four years after him, at Worms.

events.title: The Union of Krewo and the baptism of Lithuania
events.shortBlurb: At the castle of Krewo, Jogaila of Lithuania pledged his faith and his crown to Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and Europe's last pagan country was won…
body: On 14 August 1385, at the castle of Krewo, Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, set his seal to a solemn undertaking before the envoys of Poland: he would embrace the Catholic faith with his brothers and his people, marry the young Queen Jadwiga, free the Christian captives in his lands, and join his Lithuanian and Ruthenian dominions to the Crown of Poland for ever.

The word was kept. At Kraków on 15 February 1386 he was baptized with the name Władysław, on 18 February he married Jadwiga, and on 4 March he was crowned king. The next year he went up to Vilnius for the baptism of his people: the nobles one by one, the common folk in companies, while the sacred groves were felled and the temples of the old gods thrown down. A bishopric was founded in Vilnius in 1388.

So Lithuania, the last pagan land of Europe, entered the Church not by the sword but by a marriage; and the crusade of the Teutonic Knights, which had fed upon her paganism for a hundred and fifty years, lost its warrant. The union sealed at Krewo endured, through the nearer bond of Horodło in 1413 to the Commonwealth of Lublin in 1569.

events.title: The death of Wenceslaus IV and the Hussite storm
