events.shortBlurb: The news of the Defenestration of Prague struck King Wenceslaus like a blow, and his death within the fortnight opened Bohemia to seventeen years of religious war…
body: Wenceslaus IV, son of the Emperor Charles IV, ruled Bohemia from 1378 and wore the title of King of the Romans until the electors deposed him in 1400. His reign fell in the worst of the Papal Schism, and in his kingdom the reformers preached to crowded churches: at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, Jan Hus denounced the wealth and vices of the clergy in the Czech tongue, and the king, for his own ends, had favoured him.

Hus was burned at Constance in 1415, and Bohemia seethed. On 30 July 1419 a Hussite procession in Prague, stoned from the New Town Hall, stormed it and threw the councillors from the windows to their deaths — the first Defenestration of Prague. The tidings came to Wenceslaus at his hunting seat, and the shock, it was said, struck him down; he died on 16 August 1419, aged fifty-eight, without an heir.

His brother Sigismund, whom the Czechs hated as the betrayer of Hus, claimed the crown, and the kingdom answered with war. Under Jan Žižka and his wagon-forts the Hussites broke every crusade sent against them, until the Compactata of Basel, granting the chalice to the laity, closed the struggle in 1436.

events.title: The Scots Confession and the Scottish Reformation Parliament
events.shortBlurb: In a week that ended a thousand years of the old Church in Scotland, the estates ratified a Protestant confession and then abolished the Mass and the pope's jurisdiction…
body: The regent Mary of Guise died on 11 June 1560, and the Lords of the Congregation, long in arms against her French garrison, made peace by the Treaty of Edinburgh in July. When the Scottish Parliament met at Edinburgh, the preachers were ready: John Knox with five colleagues — the 'six Johns' — had drawn up in four days a Confession of Faith on the Genevan model.

On 17 August 1560 the three estates, after hearing it read article by article, ratified the Confession as 'hailsome and sound doctrine grounded upon the infallible truth of God's word'. A week later, on 24 August, they finished the work: one act abolished the jurisdiction of the pope in Scotland, another repealed the old statutes in favour of the Mass, and a third forbade its celebration under pain of death for the third offence.

The young queen, Mary Stuart, safe in France as the bride of Francis II, refused her ratification, and the settlement stood without her. The Confession of 1560 remained the standard of the Kirk until the Westminster Confession displaced it in 1647; the old Church in Scotland never recovered.

events.title: The death of Pope Alexander VI
events.shortBlurb: Rodrigo Borgia, the ablest and most infamous of the Renaissance popes, died suddenly of fever, and his son's principality in the Romagna died with him…
body: Roderic de Borja was born at Xàtiva near Valencia on 1 January 1431, was made cardinal at twenty-five by his uncle Calixtus III, and for thirty-five years, as vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, served five popes with rare address. In August 1492 he was himself elected pope as Alexander VI, in a conclave tainted by promises and gifts.

His eleven years were spent in statecraft: he faced the French invasion of Charles VIII, excommunicated Savonarola, kept the jubilee of 1500, and by the bull Inter caetera of 1493 drew the line between Spanish and Portuguese discovery in the new world. For his children he was prodigal — Lucrezia in her marriages, Cesare in his carving of a duchy out of the Romagna — and the papal name sank to its lowest repute.

In the hot August of 1503 both father and son sickened after a dinner at a cardinal's villa near Rome. Cesare recovered; the pope died on 18 August, aged seventy-two. Men told of poison then and since, but the likelier cause was the Roman fever. Within months Pius III was dead in his turn and Julius II reigned, who broke Cesare and repaired what the Borgia had made his own.

events.title: The death of Blaise Pascal
events.shortBlurb: Geometer, physicist, and the fiercest pen of Port-Royal, Pascal died in Paris at thirty-nine, leaving in fragments his apology for the Christian religion…
body: Blaise Pascal was born at Clermont in Auvergne on 19 June 1623, a prodigy who wrote on conic sections at sixteen, built a calculating machine, and sent the barometer up the Puy de Dôme to prove the weight of the air. On 23 November 1654 he underwent the night of fire he recorded in his Mémorial, sewn thereafter into his coat, and gave himself to God and to Port-Royal.

For the Jansenists of that house he wrote the eighteen Provincial Letters of 1656 and 1657, published under a borrowed name, which made the casuistry of the Jesuits ridiculous to all France — and were answered by the Index and the bonfire. In his last years he gathered the notes of a defence of the Christian religion, published after his death as the Pensées, with its famous wager.

Frail all his life, he spent his strength in charity as readily as in thought: in 1662 he helped found the carrosses à cinq sols, the first public coaches of Paris, for the poor's benefit. Worn out by sickness of body, he died in Paris on 19 August 1662, two months past his thirty-ninth year, with the words, 'May God never abandon me.'

events.title: The death of Pope St. Pius X
events.shortBlurb: Broken-hearted at the coming of the Great War he could not stop, Pius X died in its first weeks, offering his life for the peace of the world…
body: In the summer of 1914 Giuseppe Sarto was in his eightieth year and the eleventh of his pontificate. The lamps were going out across Europe: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, Germany on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and Britain answered on 4 August, the eleventh anniversary of his election. The news fell upon the old pope like a sentence.

He sickened on the feast of the Assumption, 15 August, and in the early hours of 20 August 1914 he died of heart failure at the Vatican, whispering, it was reported, that he gladly offered his life for the end of the war. By his will his body was left untouched by the embalmers' knives and laid in a simple tomb in the crypt of St. Peter's.

The cardinals who gathered in his stead chose Giacomo della Chiesa, Benedict XV, whose whole pontificate was a plea for the peace his predecessor had not lived to see. Pius X was beatified in 1951 and canonized by Pius XII on 29 May 1954, the first pope so honoured since Pius V.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. Pius X (vatican.va)

events.title: The death of Alexander of Hales
events.shortBlurb: The English master who brought the Sentences into the schools and gave the Franciscans their first chair of theology at Paris died among his friars…
body: Alexander was born at Hales in the west of England about 1185 and went up to Paris, where he was master of arts by 1210 and regent master in theology a decade later, with a canonry at St. Paul's in London and the archdeaconry of Coventry to his name. King Henry III used him on an embassy of peace to France in 1235.

Then, at the height of his fame and past fifty years of age, he did a thing that astonished the schools: about the year 1236 he took the habit of the Friars Minor, and kept his chair. He was the first Franciscan to teach theology in the university, and among his hearers was the young Bonaventure. In his lectures he made the Sentences of Peter Lombard the text of the schools, as it remained for three hundred years.

His pupils called him the Irrefragable Doctor and the monarch of theologians. The great Summa that bears his name he left unfinished, to be completed by his brethren. He died at Paris on 21 August 1245, and the chair he had made illustrious passed, master after master, to the friars of his order.

events.title: The Battle of the Standard
events.shortBlurb: Under a mast bearing a crucifix and the banners of the northern saints, the levies of Archbishop Thurstan broke the invasion of David of Scotland…
body: In the anarchy of King Stephen's reign, David I of Scotland came down into England for the third time in 1138, professing the cause of his niece the Empress Matilda, and wasting the country south over the Tyne and the Tees toward York. Thurstan, the aged Archbishop of York, gathered the levies of the north to meet him.

The armies met on Cowton Moor, two miles north of Northallerton, on 22 August 1138. In the midst of the English host stood a cart, and on it a ship's mast, from which hung a silver crucifix and the banners of St. Peter of York, St. John of Beverley, and St. Wilfrid of Ripon — the standard that gave the battle its name. Thurstan, too old and sick to ride with them, sent Ralph, Bishop of the Orkneys, in his place, who absolved the host in the archbishop's name and promised the kingdom of heaven to those who should fall.

The wild charge of the Galwegians broke upon the dismounted knights and the arrows of the Yorkshire bowmen; the Scots were routed with heavy loss, and David barely brought his remnant back to Carlisle. In late September the papal legate Alberic of Ostia brokered a truce at Carlisle, and the following spring the second Treaty of Durham gave the north its peace.

sources.text: Richard of Hexham, De gestis regis Stephani (c. 1140), ed. R. Howlett, Rolls Series (1886)

events.title: The death of St. Philip Benizi
events.shortBlurb: The Servite general who had hidden in a cave rather than be made pope, and spent his office making peace between the factions of Italy, died at Todi…
body: Philip Benizi was born at Florence on 15 August 1233, studied medicine at Paris and Padua, and after a year's practice laid aside the physician's art for the new order of the Servants of Mary at Monte Senario. Ordained priest, he rose to be prior general in 1267, and governed the Servites for the rest of his life.

When Clement IV died in 1268 and Cardinal Ottobuoni named Philip in the conclave at Viterbo as a candidate for the papacy, he fled to a cave on Monte Senario and hid until Gregory X was chosen. He sat at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274, and in the faction-ridden cities of Italy he went about as a maker of peace; at Forlí, struck in the face by a young hothead named Peregrine Laziosi, he won him to penance and to the order, and to a saint's life.

At the chapter of 1285 his brethren, refusing his resignation, chose him general once more. Travelling, he came to Todi, and there, on the octave of the Assumption, 22 August 1285, he died. He was the first Servite to be canonized, raised to the altars by Clement X on 12 April 1671; his feast is kept on 23 August.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Servants of Mary (Order of Servites)”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 August

events.title: The death of Fray Luis de León
events.shortBlurb: The Augustinian poet and theologian, who had endured five years in the Inquisition's cells for a Spanish Song of Songs, died nine days after his election as provincial…
body: Luis Ponce de León was born at Belmonte in 1527, professed an Augustinian friar at Salamanca at seventeen, and rose to its most famous chairs of theology and Scripture, a Hebraist as well as the first lyric poet of Spain's golden age.

For translating the Song of Songs into Castilian and for questioning the received text of the Vulgate, he was denounced, and in March 1572 the Inquisition shut him in its prison at Valladolid. There, for nearly five years, he waited and wrote. Acquitted at last and restored to his rights, he went back to his chair; and tradition loves to tell, though the tale is not attested, that he resumed his lecture with the words, Dicebamus hesterna die — 'As we were saying yesterday...'

His prose works, the Names of Christ and the Perfect Wife, came out in 1583, and in 1588 he gave Spain the first edition of the writings of St. Teresa of Ávila. Chosen provincial of the Augustinians of Castile at the chapter of Madrigal on 14 August 1591, as he lay sick in bed, he died there nine days later, on 23 August, and was carried to Salamanca for burial, as his epitaph records, in his sixty-third year.

events.title: The death of Theodoric the Great
events.shortBlurb: The Amal king who had given Italy thirty years of peace between Goths and Romans died at Ravenna, and his work died with him…
body: Theodoric the Amal, a hostage at Constantinople in his youth and king of the Ostrogoths from 471, was sent by the Emperor Zeno against Odoacer, and after four years of war murdered his rival with his own hand at a banquet of reconciliation at Ravenna in 493. From that city he ruled Italy for thirty-three years.

An Arian among Catholic subjects, he kept the peace between them, holding that religion cannot be commanded. He governed through Romans — Cassiodorus his secretary, Boethius his master of offices — gave the land law in his Edict, restored its monuments, and left the Church to itself. But the last years darkened: on suspicion of dealings with Constantinople he sent Boethius and the senator Symmachus to their deaths, and Pope John I, come home from the East without the concessions he demanded, was thrown into prison, where he died in May 526.

Theodoric died of dysentery at Ravenna on 30 August that same year, and was laid in the great mausoleum he had built, under a dome of a single stone. His grandson Athalaric, a child, succeeded under the regency of Amalasuntha; and within nine years Justinian's armies landed, to undo the Gothic kingdom in a generation of war.

events.title: The death of St. Aidan of Lindisfarne
events.shortBlurb: The Irish monk whom Oswald brought from Iona, apostle of Northumbria and founder of Lindisfarne, died at Bamburgh, leaning against the wall of his church…
body: When Oswald of Northumbria asked the monks of Iona for a bishop, the first they sent came home in despair of the English temper; Aidan, trained under St. Senan at Scattery Island, answered that the fault lay with the messenger's harshness, not the people's. They sent him instead, and in 635 he was consecrated and set his see on the bare island of Lindisfarne, in sight of the royal fortress of Bamburgh.

For sixteen years he walked the kingdom on foot, the king himself his interpreter at the first, preaching and founding churches and monasteries; his school at Lindisfarne trained English boys for the ministry — Chad, Cedd, and Eata among them. The horse King Oswin gave him he gave to the next beggar he met. When Penda of Mercia heaped fire about Bamburgh, Aidan prayed from his island, Bede says, and the wind turned the flames back on the besiegers.

Oswin was murdered on 20 August 651, and Aidan outlived him by eleven days, dying at Bamburgh on 31 August, in the seventeenth year of his episcopate, leaning against a buttress of the church — a beam that, Bede notes, twice survived the burning of the church itself. He was buried at Lindisfarne, leaving to the English mission the memory, in Bede's phrase, of a pontiff of surpassing mildness.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 August

events.title: The death of Adrian IV, the only English pope
events.shortBlurb: Nicholas Breakspear of Hertfordshire, the only Englishman ever to sit in Peter's chair, died at Anagni, and a disputed succession opened a long schism…
body: Nicholas Breakspear, born about 1100 at Abbots Langley near St. Albans in Hertfordshire, rose from the cloister of St. Rufus to be cardinal-bishop of Albano and the legate who ordered the Church in Scandinavia, erecting Nidaros as its archbishopric. On 4 December 1154 the cardinals chose him pope as Adrian IV, and no other Englishman has sat in Peter's chair since.

His five years were stormy. He crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor in 1155, quarreled with him two years later at Besançon over the word 'benefice,' made peace with the Norman king of Sicily at Benevento, and, by the bull Laudabiliter — a document whose authenticity scholars still dispute — is said to have granted Henry II of England the lordship of Ireland. Rome itself, in the grip of the commune and of Arnold of Brescia, he could hardly hold, and he spent much of his pontificate away from it.

On 1 September 1159, at Anagni, he died suddenly; the chroniclers tell a strange tale of a fly caught in his throat, while later writers suppose a quinsy. Within days the double election of Alexander III and the antipope Victor IV split the Church in a schism of eighteen years, and Adrian was laid in St. Peter's, the one English pope.

events.title: Terror is declared the order of the day
events.shortBlurb: Pressed by the Paris sections, the National Convention made terror the order of the day, and the machinery of the guillotine turned upon the Church…
body: In the summer of 1793 the Republic stood besieged: royalist rebels held the Vendée, federalist revolts burned in the provinces, and the allied armies pressed the frontiers. On 5 September the Paris sections crowded into the National Convention demanding vengeance on the enemies within, and Bertrand Barère, for the Committee of Public Safety, gave the day its watchword: let terror be placed on the order of the day.

The Convention complied. The Law of Suspects followed on 17 September; the revolutionary calendar swept away the Christian week in October; and in November Notre-Dame itself was rededicated as a Temple of Reason. Across France refractory priests were herded to the guillotine or to the prison-hulks of Rochefort, and the Carmelite nuns of Compiègne would mount the scaffold the following July, singing.

By the reckoning of later historians some sixteen thousand official death sentences were pronounced before the fever broke with Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794), and tens of thousands more perished without judgment. The Church that emerged from the Terror was stripped, scattered, and poorer in everything but its martyrs.

events.title: The battle of the Frigidus
events.shortBlurb: On the river Frigidus Theodosius broke the army of the usurper Eugenius, and with it the last armed hope of Roman paganism…
body: When Valentinian II died at Vienne in 392, the Frankish general Arbogast raised to the western throne his secretary Eugenius, a teacher of rhetoric, and with him the pagan party of the senate made its last restoration: the Altar of Victory returned to the curia, and the old gods rode once more with the standards.

Theodosius I marched from the East and met them in the Julian Alps, on the river Frigidus — the Vipava of our maps — on 5 and 6 September 394. The first day cost him dear, his Gothic vanguard falling in thousands; but on the second, the church historians relate, the Bora wind rose and blew into the faces of the westerners, turning their own missiles back upon them.

Eugenius was taken in his tent and beheaded; Arbogast fled to the mountains and two days later fell upon his sword. Theodosius, master now of a world momentarily undivided, died at Milan the following January, leaving the empire to his sons Arcadius and Honorius — and the Frigidus has stood ever since as the last battle fought in the names of the old gods.

events.title: The outrage at Anagni
events.shortBlurb: Agents of Philip the Fair seized Pope Boniface VIII in his own palace at Anagni, a wound from which the medieval papacy never wholly recovered…
body: The quarrel between Boniface VIII and Philip IV of France, kindled over the taxing of clergy, had risen through the bulls Clericis laicos and Ausculta fili to Unam Sanctam (18 November 1302), the boldest claim a pope ever made over kings. In the spring of 1303 Philip's council resolved to bring Boniface to judgment, and his minister Guillaume de Nogaret crossed the Alps to do it.

On 7 September 1303, with Sciarra Colonna and a band of hired horse, Nogaret broke into Anagni, the pope's own city, and surprised him in his palace — one day before the bull Super Petri solio, excommunicating the king, was to be published. The aged pope, robed and seated with the cross before him, offered his neck, in the words the sources give him; that Colonna struck him with a mailed hand, the chroniclers report and the historians repeat with caution.

The townsfolk rose on the third day and freed him, but the blow was mortal. Boniface died at Rome on 11 October, Dante gave the outrage a canto in the Purgatorio, and within six years Clement V had carried the papal residence to Avignon — the seventy years the Church would call its Babylonian captivity.

events.title: The colloquy of Poissy
events.shortBlurb: Catherine de' Medici gathered cardinals and Calvinist ministers at Poissy in the last great attempt to hold France together in one faith…
body: On 9 September 1561, in the refectory of the convent of Poissy, hard by the royal castle of Saint-Germain, the boy king Charles IX took his seat among six cardinals and some forty archbishops and bishops. His mother Catherine de' Medici, with the chancellor Michel de L'Hôpital, had summoned the colloquy to essay what politics had failed of: a peace between the Church and the Reformed.

Theodore Beza, come from Geneva with Peter Martyr Vermigli, spoke for the ministers, and the cardinal of Lorraine answered for the prelates, with Diego Laínez, general of the Jesuits, at his side. Beza's first oration held even his opponents, until he came to the Supper and confessed the body of Christ to be as far from the bread as heaven is from the earth — and the assembly broke in murmurs that were never stilled.

Sessions dragged into October, and a smaller conference afterward, but the Eucharist admitted no middle term. The Edict of January 1562 granted the Huguenots a measured toleration; within weeks the blood shed at Vassy opened the wars of religion that would trouble France for six and thirty years.

events.title: The Council of Agde
events.shortBlurb: Under the tolerance of an Arian king, Caesarius of Arles gathered the bishops of Visigothic Gaul in council at Agde…
body: In 506 the Visigoths ruled the South of Gaul from Toulouse, Arians governing a Catholic people. With the leave of King Alaric II, Caesarius, the young archbishop of Arles, summoned the bishops of the realm to Agde, a little port of the Mediterranean, and there, in the church of St. Andrew on 10 September, five and thirty of them sat down to order the life of the Church.

The council's canons, seven and forty as commonly reckoned, though the medieval collections transmit more, fixed the ages of holy orders — five and twenty for the deacon, thirty for the priest — confirmed the right of asylum at the altar, and bound the clergy to the discipline that Caesarius preached all his life. Passed almost whole into Gratian's Decretum, they became part of the common law of the medieval Church.

The kingdom whose tolerance had sheltered the synod did not long endure: the next year Clovis and the Franks broke Alaric at Vouillé, and Visigothic rule in Gaul shrank to a strip of coast. The canons of Agde outlived the kingdom that permitted them.

events.title: The founding of the abbey of Cluny
events.shortBlurb: William the Pious of Aquitaine gave his hunting ground at Cluny to the apostles Peter and Paul, founding the abbey that would leaven a century…
body: By a charter dated 11 September 910, William I, called the Pious, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne, gave his villa of Cluny in the Mâconnais 'to the Apostles Peter and Paul,' that a regular monastery might rise there under Berno, abbot of Baume. The legend loves to tell that the duke grudged his hunting ground, and that Berno answered: drive out the dogs, and put monks in their place.

The charter's genius lay in its freedom: the new house was to answer to no bishop and no lord, but to the Holy See alone, holding its lands of the apostles. Under a line of great abbots — Odo, Odilo, Hugh, and Peter the Venerable — that liberty drew well over a thousand priories into the congregation of Cluny, and its abbey church, consecrated in 1095, stood for centuries as the largest in Christendom.

Cluny's observance leavened the reform of the eleventh century, and its cloister gave the Church popes, among them Urban II. Suppressed in 1790, the great church was sold and razed in the years of the Revolution; a single transept survives to measure what was lost.

events.title: The death of Philip II of Spain
events.shortBlurb: The most Catholic king died among the Hieronymites of the Escorial, closing the proudest and most burdensome reign of the Spanish century…
body: On 13 September 1598 Philip II of Spain died at San Lorenzo de El Escorial, the palace-monastery he had built in the foothills of the Guadarrama, aged seventy-one, after an illness of fifty-two days borne, the witnesses agree, with terrible patience. He had been king of Spain since 1556, of Naples and Sicily since 1554, of Portugal since 1580, and, by his marriage to Mary Tudor, king-consort of England.

Under him the monarchy touched its zenith and spent itself. His half-brother Don John broke the Turk at Lepanto in 1571; the revolt of the Netherlands outlasted all his generals; the Armada he sent against England in 1588 came home in wreckage; and the royal treasury was declared bankrupt again and again. Through it all he governed as the first servant of the altars — the champion, in the words of the historians, of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.

He was buried the next day beneath the high altar of his basilica, and the crown passed to Philip III. The empire on which the sun never set, as his age first said of it, would spend the following century spending what he had gathered.

events.title: The election of Pope Urban VII
events.shortBlurb: Giovanni Battista Castagna was chosen pope as Urban VII and was dead of malaria before his coronation — the shortest pontificate on record…
body: Sixtus V died on 27 August 1590, and on 15 September the cardinals, swayed by the Spanish faction, elected Giovanni Battista Castagna, who took the name Urban VII. He was a Roman of a Genoese house, sixty-nine years old, a doctor of laws of Bologna who had served the Curia as Referendary of the Signatura, archbishop of Rossano, and Inquisitor General of the Roman Inquisition, and he had been cardinal these seven years.

He was already sick when elected. The malaria of the Roman summer was on him, and on 27 September, twelve days after his election and before he could be crowned, he died toward midnight. His is the shortest pontificate the Church remembers.

He was buried in St. Peter's, whence his remains were later carried to Santa Maria sopra Minerva. The cardinals returned to the Sistine Chapel and in December chose Gregory XIV; the year had seen three men bear the name of pope.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Martin I in exile
events.shortBlurb: Martin I, who would not bend to the emperor's Typos, died an exile at Cherson, the last pope the Church reckons a martyr…
body: Martin I, a Tuscan of Todi, had served as apocrisiarius at Constantinople before the clergy and people of Rome made him pope in July 649 — without waiting, in defiance of custom, for the emperor's mandate. That October he gathered one hundred and five bishops in the Lateran, and in twenty canons they condemned the Monothelite doctrine and the Typos of the Emperor Constans II.

The emperor's answer came slowly but surely. In June 653 the exarch's men arrested the pope in the Lateran basilica itself and shipped him to Constantinople, where a tribunal condemned him for treason; he was stripped of his pallium, flogged in public, and banished to Cherson in the Crimea.

There, on 16 September 655, he died of want and of his wounds, his letters from exile breathing still a dry irony over the price of bread. East and West together venerate him as the last martyr-pope; the doctrine for which he suffered, two wills in the one Christ, was defined at the Sixth Ecumenical Council a generation later, and his companion in confession, St. Maximus, bore the same witness with his own maimed body.

events.title: The battle of Chrysopolis
events.shortBlurb: Constantine's final victory over Licinius on the Bosporus made him master of the whole Roman world — and cleared the road to Nicaea…
body: For a decade after the Edict of Milan (313) the uneasy partnership of Constantine and Licinius wore down to war. Beaten at Adrianople in July 324 and stripped of his fleet in the Hellespont, Licinius abandoned Byzantium and made his last stand on the Asian shore, at Chrysopolis, beneath Chalcedon.

There, on 18 September 324, Constantine broke him. Eusebius, who wrote within living memory, sets the two camps in a parable: the labarum and the ministers of God with the one, Egyptian diviners and soothsayers with the other. The defeated left some five and twenty thousand on the field by the earliest reckoning; Licinius fled to Nicomedia and there surrendered, spared at the prayer of his wife Constantia, the victor's sister — and put to death the next year on a charge of conspiracy.

Constantine stood at last sole Augustus, and the Church entered a new world. Within the year he summoned the bishops to Nicaea; within six he refounded Byzantium as his city, dedicated in 330, on the very strait where the last battle had been won.

events.title: The death of the Emperor Charles V
events.shortBlurb: The emperor who had heard Luther at Worms and seen Trent open died, his crowns resigned, among the friars of Yuste…
body: Charles V, born at Ghent in 1500, lord of lands on which the sun never set, had spent forty years holding together an empire that no man could govern whole: before him Luther at the Diet of Worms in 1521, his unpaid army sacking Rome in 1527, the Protestants heard at Augsburg in 1530, broken at Mühlberg in 1547, and at last conceded a legal peace in 1555.

Weary and gout-ridden, he laid down his crowns one by one — the Netherlands and Spain to his son Philip in 1555 and 1556, the imperial title to his brother Ferdinand, accepted by the electors in February 1558 — and withdrew to the apartments he had prepared beside the Hieronymite monastery of San Jerónimo de Yuste, in the oak-woods of Extremadura.

There, on 21 September 1558, he died, aged fifty-eight, of a malarial fever, amid his books and his Titians, prepared by the friars for his passage; tradition adds that he held to the last a crucifix that had been his mother's. The last emperor crowned by a pope sleeps now in the Escorial, and his two inheritances, Spanish and Austrian, went their separate ways for three hundred years.

events.title: The death of Pope Clement XIV
events.shortBlurb: Ganganelli, the Franciscan pope whom the Bourbon courts pressed to destroy the Jesuits, died at Rome amid rumors the evidence has never sustained…
body: Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio Ganganelli, born at Santarcangelo near Rimini in 1705, a Conventual Franciscan named in religion Lorenzo, rose by learning and modesty to the cardinalate in 1759 and, in May 1769, to the tiara as Clement XIV — chosen after a conclave in which the ambassadors of France and Spain had labored openly.

Those courts, with Naples and Portugal behind them, demanded one thing: the extinction of the Society of Jesus. After four years of resistance and delay, on 21 July 1773, Clement signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, suppressing the Society for the peace of the Church throughout the world.

He outlived the deed by fourteen months, dying at Rome on 22 September 1774 after weeks of wasting illness. That the Jesuits had poisoned him was the whisper of all Europe; no evidence has ever sustained it. He was buried in the church of the Twelve Apostles, and the order he had cut down lay in its grave until Pius VII raised it up again in 1814.

events.title: The Concordat of Worms
events.shortBlurb: At Worms, pope and emperor traded ring and sceptre for peace, closing the half-century Investiture Contest…
body: The struggle begun when Gregory VII forbade lay investiture in 1075 had outlived that pope and the emperor he humbled at Canossa. On 23 September 1122, at Worms on the Rhine, Pope Callixtus II and the Emperor Henry V set their names to the two declarations — the first concordat between the Church and a temporal power — that ended it.

The emperor renounced investiture with ring and crosier, the bestowal of spiritual office by a lay hand, and granted that elections should be canonical and consecration free. The pope conceded that in Germany elections might be held in the emperor's presence, and that the elect should receive the regalia by the touch of the sceptre — in Germany before consecration, in Burgundy and Italy within six months after.

The First Lateran Council ratified the concordat the following March. Its distinction of the spiritual sword from the temporal became the pattern of every later settlement between altar and throne, and the Church had won, at parchment's length, the freedom of her bishops.

events.title: The Second Council of Nicaea opens
events.shortBlurb: Bishops gathered by the Empress Irene opened at Nicaea the seventh and last council both East and West receive, to judge the veneration of images…
body: Sixty years of iconoclasm had divided the Eastern churches when the Empress Irene, regent for her son Constantine VI, and the Patriarch Tarasius summoned a general council — with the blessing of Pope Hadrian I, whose two legates would sign first among its acts. A first attempt at Constantinople in August 786 was scattered by iconoclast soldiers; the fathers were bidden instead to Nicaea, where the first council had sat.

On 24 September 787, in the church of Hagia Sophia there, some three hundred bishops opened the sessions. The assembly of Hieria, which had proscribed the images in 754, was condemned, and the council defined its measure with care: icons are to receive salutation and honorable reverence — never the worship that belongs to God alone.

The last session was held in the Magnaura palace at Constantinople on 23 October. Christendom reckons Nicaea II its Seventh Ecumenical Council, the last received by East and West alike — though a bungled Latin rendering of its decrees moved the scholars of Charlemagne to protest in the Libri Carolini, and such unity was never again so near.

events.title: The Peace of Augsburg
events.shortBlurb: The settlement Ferdinand concluded at Augsburg in his brother's name gave Lutheran princes legal standing — and the Empire sixty-three years of peace…
body: After a generation of religious strife, the diet that opened at Augsburg in February 1555 met an absent emperor: Charles V, spent, had left its conduct to his brother Ferdinand, King of the Romans. On 25 September the peace was published in the emperor's name with the princes of the Augsburg Confession.

Its rule was cuius regio, eius religio: the prince's faith, Catholic or the Lutheranism of Augsburg, should be the faith of his territory, the dissenter free to sell his goods and depart. At Ferdinand's insistence the reservatum ecclesiasticum guarded the lands of any prince-bishop who should turn Protestant, a clause the Protestant estates never accepted; Calvinism and the sects stood outside the peace altogether.

Within weeks Charles resigned the Netherlands and Spain, and the imperial crown followed. The settlement the old emperor had shunned to sign held the German peace for sixty-three years — until a defenestration at Prague in 1618 opened the Thirty Years' War and taught Europe how much the peace of Augsburg had left undone.

events.title: The battle of the Maritsa
events.shortBlurb: In a night attack on the Maritsa the Ottomans destroyed the army of the Serbian lords, and the Balkans lay open before them…
body: Since Adrianople had fallen to them about 1361, the Ottoman Turks had pressed into the Balkans. In 1371 the despot Jovan Uglješa and his brother Vukašin, king of Prilep — the two greatest lords of the crumbling Serbian empire of Dušan — gathered a host the chronicles swell to seventy thousand and marched to drive them from Europe.

The Ottoman commander Lala Şahin Pasha had a fraction of their numbers. On the night of 26 September 1371, by the river Maritsa near the village of Chernomen, his men fell upon the Christian camp as it feasted, and the rout was utter: both brothers died on the field, and the victors named the battle Sırp Sındığı, the destruction of the Serbs.

Macedonia and the southern Balkans lay open. Within the year the last Nemanjić emperor, Uroš V, died childless; the Emperor John V of Constantinople became the sultan's tributary; and the road ran on through Kosovo in 1389 and Nicopolis in 1396 to the fall of the imperial city itself in 1453.

events.title: The death of Pope John Paul I
events.shortBlurb: Albino Luciani, the smiling pope of thirty-three days, died in the night in the Apostolic Palace, and 1978 became the year of three popes…
body: Albino Luciani, born in 1912 at Forno di Canale in the Veneto, had been bishop of Vittorio Veneto and then patriarch of Venice before the conclave of 26 August 1978 elected him pope. He was the first to join two names — John Paul, for the two popes he honored — and the first to refuse the tiara, taking a simple inauguration on 3 September.

In the night of 28 September, thirty-three days after his election, he died suddenly in his apartment in the Apostolic Palace; he was found lifeless in his bed at first light of the 29th, and the Holy See reckons his death to the 28th. The medical reconstruction concludes an acute myocardial infarction, and the conspiracy theories that flourished in the absence of an autopsy have collapsed under the evidence since published.

The world mourned 'the smiling pope' and laid him in the Vatican grottoes; in October the cardinals gave the Church John Paul II. His cause advanced quietly, and on 4 September 2022 Pope Francis beatified him in St. Peter's Square.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope John Paul I (vatican.va)

events.title: Frederick II is excommunicated
events.shortBlurb: Gregory IX put the ban of the Church on the emperor who would not sail — who then won Jerusalem back while excommunicate…
body: Frederick II, the Hohenstaufen wonder of the world, had vowed at his imperial coronation in 1220 to lead a crusade, and at San Germano in 1225 had sworn it again, this time under penalty of excommunication. When at last he embarked at Brindisi in the September of 1227, only to put back within days with sickness raging in the fleet, Gregory IX would hear no excuses.

On 29 September 1227 the pope pronounced him excommunicate. The sentence did not hold him: on 18 June 1228 Frederick sailed for the East under the ban, and by treaty with the Sultan al-Kamil, concluded at Jaffa in February 1229, he recovered Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Nazareth without striking a blow — taking the crown of Jerusalem in the church of the Holy Sepulchre on 18 March, in a city lying under interdict.

Reconciled with the pope in 1230, he warred with the papacy on and off for the rest of his reign, was excommunicated again, and was deposed at the Council of Lyons in 1245. He died in 1250, and the chroniclers could not decide whether to mourn a persecutor of the Church or a wonder of the world.

events.title: The coronation of Mary I
events.shortBlurb: Crowned at Westminster by the Bishop of Winchester, Mary Tudor became the first queen of England anointed in her own right…
body: When Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, the Duke of Northumberland's devise set aside the king's half-sisters for Lady Jane Grey, proclaimed on 10 July. The country would not have her; within nine days Mary's cause had prevailed, and on 3 August she entered London in triumph.

On Sunday 1 October 1553 she was crowned in Westminster Abbey by Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — the Archbishop of Canterbury being a prisoner in the Tower. It was done, the old account notes, in spite of the excommunication that still lay upon the country; the conduits at Cornhill and Cheapside ran with wine.

She was the first woman anointed queen of England in her own right. Within two years Parliament had restored the old worship and received Cardinal Pole as legate, reconciling the realm to the Apostolic See. The restoration lasted barely five years, and is remembered more for the fires of Smithfield than for the coronation pomp.

events.title: The fall of Jerusalem to Saladin
events.shortBlurb: Eighty-eight years after the crusaders took it, Jerusalem opened its gates to Saladin, and the Latin kingdom was left a coastal remnant…
body: On 4 July 1187, at the horns of Hattin above Tiberias, Saladin destroyed the army of the Latin kingdom, taking King Guy and the relic of the True Cross. City after city then surrendered — Acre, Jaffa, Beirut, Ascalon — until Jerusalem itself, crowded with refugees, stood alone under Balian of Ibelin.

After a short siege Balian obtained terms, and on 2 October 1187, the anniversary, it was noted, of the Prophet's night journey, the city opened its gates. The Latin dominion over Jerusalem had lasted eighty-eight years. Unlike the conquerors of 1099, Saladin forbade a general massacre: the inhabitants were ransomed at ten dinars a man, though thousands who could not pay were led into captivity.

The shock summoned the Third Crusade; Richard of England and Philip of France recovered a strip of coast but never the city. Save for a brief treaty interlude in the thirteenth century, Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands for more than seven centuries.

events.title: Paul VI before the United Nations
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of St. Francis, Paul VI crossed the Atlantic for a one-day visit to plead before the nations: no more war, war never again…
body: On 4 October 1965, the feast of St. Francis of Assisi, Paul VI landed in New York — the first pope to set foot in the Western Hemisphere, and the first ever to visit the United States. "Greetings to you, America," he said at the airport; "the first pope to set foot on your land blesses you with all his heart."

Greeted by Secretary-General U Thant, he addressed the General Assembly in French, in the organization's twentieth year. "No more war, war never again," he pleaded; "it is peace, peace, that has to guide the destiny of the nations of all mankind." The whole journey lasted fourteen hours and ended with Mass at Yankee Stadium.

In Rome the Second Vatican Council was then holding its fourth and last session; two months later, on 8 December 1965, the pope closed it. His one-day pilgrimage for peace set a pattern: his successors have returned to the same rostrum to speak for the Church before the family of nations.

sources.text: Paul VI, Address to the United Nations Organization, 4 October 1965 (vatican.va)

events.title: The Fourth Council of Constantinople opens
events.shortBlurb: Legates of Pope Hadrian II opened in Hagia Sophia the council the West would number as the eighth general synod, called to end the affair of Photius…
body: The patriarch Ignatius, deposed and exiled years before, had been restored by the new emperor Basil the Macedonian; the intruded Photius, who had gone so far as to pronounce the deposition of Pope Nicholas I in 867, was confined to a monastery. Both emperor and patriarch asked Rome for a general council, and Hadrian II sent three legates to preside in his name.

On 5 October 869 the council opened in the cathedral of Holy Wisdom, the pope's legates in the first seats. The fathers were never many — little more than a hundred bishops in all — and over ten sessions, the last on 28 February 870, they reconciled the penitent, heard a silent and unyielding Photius, renewed his condemnation, and subscribed the old formula of Hormisdas binding its signers to the Apostolic See.

Western canonists number this as the eighth ecumenical council, though the East has not received it into her synodal books. Within a decade Ignatius was dead and Photius reigned again in his place, and a further council in 879 undid much of what the council of 869 had decreed.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Constantinople, Fourth Ecumenical Council of”

events.title: The death of William Tyndale
events.shortBlurb: Strangled and burned at Vilvoorde for giving England the Scriptures in her own tongue, Tyndale left a translation that underlies the English Bible to this day…
body: Tyndale, a priest formed at Oxford and Cambridge, held that the plowboy should know the Scripture as well as the prelate. Driven abroad, he translated the New Testament from the Greek and began printing it at Cologne in 1525; stopped there, he finished the work at Worms, and in the summer of 1526 three thousand copies were smuggled into England.

For a decade he lived in hiding on the Continent, adding the Pentateuch and Jonah to his work, while the bishops burned his books and the king's agents hunted him. Betrayed at Antwerp by a false friend, he was held in the castle of Vilvoorde near Brussels and condemned for heresy.

On 6 October 1536, by the reckoning of his earliest biographers, he was strangled at the stake and his body burned, crying — so the martyrologist Foxe records — "Lord, open the King of England's eyes." Within three years an English Bible stood in every parish church; and his renderings, revised but never replaced, still form the bone and sinew of the English versions.

events.title: The Council of Chalcedon opens
events.shortBlurb: The largest assembly of bishops the ancient Church had yet seen gathered in the church of St. Euphemia to confess one Christ in two natures…
body: The emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria had summoned the bishops to Nicaea, then brought them nearer the capital, to Chalcedon on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus. There, on 8 October 451, in the church of the martyr St. Euphemia, the fourth general council opened — some five or six hundred bishops, nearly all from the East, the greatest number any council had yet gathered.

The legates of St. Leo the Great presided, imperial commissioners ordering the outer business. The acts of the Robber Synod of Ephesus were read; Dioscorus of Alexandria, its author, was removed from his seat and later deposed; and Leo's letter to Flavian, the Tome, was acclaimed with the cry that Peter had spoken through Leo.

In its Definition the council confessed one and the same Christ, Son and Lord, in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation. The sessions ran to 1 November; Marcian himself attended the sixth, on 25 October. One canon, the twenty-eighth, exalting the see of Constantinople, Rome would never accept.

events.title: The death of Pope Pius XII
events.shortBlurb: Eugenio Pacelli, who had guided the Church through world war and defined the Assumption, died at Castel Gandolfo after nineteen years as pope…
body: Eugenio Pacelli was born in Rome on 2 March 1876, and on his sixty-third birthday, 2 March 1939, was elected pope, taking the name Pius XII. Within months Europe was at war, and his pontificate was bound up with the war years: his first encyclical, Summi Pontificatus, and his radio appeal of August 1939 warned of the gathering storm.

His nineteen years saw the definition of the Assumption of Our Lady, proclaimed on 1 November 1950 in the bull Munificentissimus Deus, and a great quickening of the Church's liturgical and scholarly life; his wartime silences and charities alike have been debated ever since.

Stricken by a stroke at his summer residence, he died at Castel Gandolfo in the small hours of 9 October 1958, and was buried in the grottoes of St. Peter's. Nineteen days later the conclave chose the Patriarch of Venice, who took the name John XXIII — and within months astonished the world by summoning a council.

events.title: The Battle of Tours
events.shortBlurb: Charles, Mayor of the Palace, broke the advance of the armies of al-Andalus between Tours and Poitiers, and won the name of the Hammer…
body: Twenty years after the conquest of Spain, Abd al-Rahman, governor of al-Andalus, crossed the Pyrenees with a great host, defeated Duke Eudes of Aquitaine, and drove north toward the Loire, pillaging as he went. Eudes turned for help to his old rival Charles, Mayor of the Palace in Austrasia.

In October 732 — the day is variously reckoned the 10th or the 25th of the month — the two armies met on the road between Tours and Poitiers. The Frankish foot stood like a wall, the chroniclers say; Abd al-Rahman was slain, and by nightfall his army was in flight, leaving its plunder and its tents.

The old Catholic judgment calls it one of the great events in the history of the world; later ages named the victor Martellus, the Hammer. Whether one battle or a season of campaigning turned the tide, the armies of the caliphate never again struck so deep into Gaul, and Charles's grandson would be crowned at Rome as Charlemagne.

events.title: The Battle of Hastings
events.shortBlurb: On Senlac Hill near Hastings, King Harold fell with his brothers, and William of Normandy's victory began the remaking of England and her Church…
body: Harold had been king nine months. On 25 September 1066 he destroyed the invading Norsemen at Stamford Bridge; three days later William of Normandy landed at Pevensey, carrying — the Norman writers say — a banner blessed by Pope Alexander II. Forced marches brought Harold south to meet him with a weary army.

The battle was fought on 14 October 1066 on the hill of Senlac, seven miles from Hastings, and lasted from morning to dusk. The old account remarks the temper of the two camps the night before: the Normans prayed and prepared for Communion while the English caroused. By nightfall Harold and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine lay dead, and with them the flower of the English thegnhood.

William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day. The Conquest remade the English Church as well as the realm: Stigand was deposed and Lanfranc of Bec came to Canterbury, councils reformed the clergy, and new cathedrals rose in the Norman manner. On the battlefield itself William raised Battle Abbey, its high altar over the spot where Harold fell.

events.title: The Nobel Peace Prize for Mother Teresa
events.shortBlurb: The Norwegian committee's choice fell on the nun of Calcutta, who received the world's most famous prize in the name of the poorest of the poor…
body: On 17 October 1979 the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that the Peace Prize would go to Mother Teresa of Calcutta, "for work undertaken in the struggle to overcome poverty and distress, which also constitutes a threat to peace."

She was born Gonxha Agnes Bojaxhiu at Skopje in 1910, had gone to India as a Loreto sister, and in 1946, on the train to Darjeeling, received what she called her "call within a call." The congregation she founded, the Missionaries of Charity, established at Calcutta on 7 October 1950, served the dying and the destitute of the city's streets.

At Oslo on 10 December she asked that the money for the customary banquet be given to the poor, and received the prize, as her own words had it, "for the glory of God and in the name of the poor." She died in 1997; John Paul II beatified her in 2003, and she was enrolled among the saints in 2016.

events.title: The revocation of the Edict of Nantes
events.shortBlurb: By the Edict of Fontainebleau Louis XIV revoked the toleration of 1598, silenced the Reformed churches, and scattered the Huguenots across the world…
body: For fourscore and seven years the Edict of Nantes, granted by Henry IV in 1598, had given the Reformed of France a measured toleration. Under Louis XIV the measure was steadily withdrawn, church by church and office by office, until on 18 October 1685 the king signed at Fontainebleau the edict that revoked his grandfather's grant altogether.

Public worship was forbidden to the Protestants, their churches razed, their ministers ordered from the realm within fifteen days; parents were commanded to have their children baptized and schooled as Catholics; and emigration was banned for men on pain of the galleys, for women of prison.

The blow was applauded in France — Vauban and Saint-Simon were nearly alone in deploring it — yet it scattered a multitude: Vauban reckoned a hundred thousand Frenchmen lost to the kingdom, with sixty million livres, nine thousand sailors, and the best of her officers gone to her enemies. The proscribed worship lived on in secret assemblies "in the desert," and flared into the Camisard war of the Cévennes in 1702.

events.title: The marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella
events.shortBlurb: In a private house at Valladolid the heirs of Aragon and Castile were wed in secret, joining the crowns from which a united Spain would rise…
body: Isabella was eighteen, the chosen heiress of Castile; Ferdinand seventeen, heir of Aragon. Their marriage had been long negotiated against the will of her brother King Henry, and was therefore done in secret: the princess slipped away from the court, and Ferdinand crossed Castile disguised as a muleteer with a handful of companions.

On the morning of 19 October 1469, in the house of Juan de Vivero at Valladolid, the Archbishop of Toledo married them. They stood within the forbidden degrees of kinship, and the dispensation shown that day — a bull in the name of a pope already dead — was of doubtful warrant until a true one came from Rome. There was no pomp: money had to be borrowed for the wedding feast.

From that union the two crowns moved as one. Isabella succeeded to Castile in 1474, Ferdinand to Aragon in 1479; together they took Granada in 1492, sent Columbus across the Ocean Sea in the same year, and were styled by the pope the Catholic Monarchs. Their grandson would reign as the Emperor Charles V.

events.title: The Crusaders before Antioch
events.shortBlurb: Two years after Clermont, the host of the First Crusade crossed the Taurus and sat down before the walls of Antioch for its most terrible siege…
body: The armies that answered Urban II at Clermont fared better than the poor pilgrims who went before them. In June 1097 they took Nicaea; on the first of July they routed the Turks at Dorylaeum; then, through a burning summer, they crossed the length of Asia Minor.

On 20 October 1097 they came before Antioch, the ancient city of the disciples, girdled — the old account numbers them — by a wall with four hundred and fifty towers, and provisioned for a long defense by its governor Yaghi-Siyan. Too strong to storm and too large to surround, the city held the crusaders before it for more than seven months of hunger, desertion, and winter rain.

Antioch fell at last on the night of 2-3 June 1098, betrayed by the captain of a single tower; and within days the besiegers were themselves besieged by the relieving army of Kerbogha of Mosul, whom they defeated on 28 June. The way to Jerusalem lay open, though the host did not take it until the next year.

events.title: The destruction of the People's Crusade
events.shortBlurb: The unarmed thousands who had set out for Jerusalem under Peter the Hermit marched into a Turkish ambush, and the People's Crusade ended in a day…
body: Before the princes had gathered their armies, the preaching of the crusade moved the poor. Tens of thousands followed Peter the Hermit and the knight Walter the Pennyless across Europe to Constantinople in the summer of 1096, plundering as they came; the emperor Alexius, to be rid of them, ferried them across the Bosphorus into Turkish territory.

There the host fell to quarreling along national lines. A German band that had seized the castle of Xerigordos was starved into surrender and destroyed; and when rumor came that the same men had taken Nicaea itself, the main body would wait no longer for Peter, who had gone back to Constantinople for supplies.

On the morning of 21 October 1096 the whole multitude, leaving women and children in the camp, marched out toward Nicaea and into the ambush of Kilij Arslan's Turks near Civetot. It was less a battle than a slaughter; Walter fell, pierced by seven arrows, and only a few thousand, rescued by Byzantine ships, returned to tell the tale. The princes' crusade, when it came, marched under discipline — and fared otherwise.

events.title: The death of Charles Martel
events.shortBlurb: The Hammer of Tours died at Quierzy, having shielded Boniface's mission and raised the Frankish power his grandson Charlemagne would crown…
body: Charles was the natural son of Pepin of Herstal, and had fought his way from prison to the mastery of the Frankish realm, ruling as Mayor of the Palace while the later Merovingian kings reigned in name. For a quarter century he campaigned without rest — against Frisians, Saxons, Bavarians, Alemanni, and the Moslem hosts of Spain.

His name in history rests on the October day of 732 when he broke the army of Abd al-Rahman between Tours and Poitiers. But the Church knew him also as the shield of her missionaries: St. Boniface worked under his protection from 723, and wrote that without it he could neither govern his flock nor defend his clergy; under Charles the Bavarian Church was ordered into the dioceses of Salzburg, Regensburg, Freising, and Passau.

He died at Quierzy on the Oise on 22 October 741 — some of the older authorities say the 21st — and was buried with the kings at Saint-Denis, though later ages, for his seizure of Church lands, made him the subject of a fearful legend of damnation. His realm he divided between his sons Carloman and Pepin; his grandson was Charlemagne.

events.title: The Irish rising of 1641
events.shortBlurb: On an October night the Ulster Irish rose for faith and land, beginning eleven years of war that ended at Drogheda and Wexford…
body: The grievances were old: the plantation of Ulster had settled Scottish and English colonists on confiscated lands, the penal laws pressed upon the Catholic gentry, and rumor ran that the Puritan Parliament meant worse. In the autumn of 1641 the dispossessed lords of the north conspired to seize the strong places of Ireland in one night.

The stroke fell on the night of 22-23 October 1641. Sir Phelim O'Neill took the fort of Charlemont by surprise and proclaimed that he rose for the king and the defense of religion and liberty; but the sister plot against Dublin Castle was betrayed on the very eve, and the capital held. Within a week the rising had spread through eight counties of Ulster.

What followed defies easy telling: thousands of settlers were killed or driven out — the numbers were wildly swollen in the English pamphlets, and are contested still — and the Catholic gentry of the Pale joined the northern men to form the Confederation of Kilkenny in 1642. The wars ran eleven years, until Cromwell landed at Dublin in 1649.

events.title: The consecration of Chartres Cathedral
events.shortBlurb: Rebuilt in a generation after the great fire, Notre-Dame de Chartres was consecrated in the presence of St. Louis, her windows already the wonder of Christendom…
body: When fire gutted the Romanesque cathedral of Chartres in 1194, the town's despair turned to hope when the relic of the Virgin's veil — brought from Aachen by Charles the Bald about 876 — was found unharmed. Kings, guilds, and peasants gave or dragged stone, and in little more than a generation the new church rose, the most perfectly Gothic of all cathedrals.

The consecration came in October 1260 — the 24th by the common reckoning, though some authorities give the 17th — and St. Louis is believed to have attended. The royal house had given richly: the upper windows were the gift of the king, of St. Ferdinand, and of the queen mother Blanche of Castile, who had died in 1252.

Her glass is her glory: the old count numbers near four thousand figures in her windows. Kings came to her as pilgrims — Henry III of France eighteen times, Charles V of France twice, and barefoot; and Henry IV, barred from Reims, was crowned at Chartres in 1594. The Revolution spared her, and two wars; she stands as she was consecrated.

events.title: The abdication of Charles V
events.shortBlurb: In the great hall at Brussels the emperor on whom the sun never set laid down his crowns, leaning on the shoulder of William the Silent…
body: He had ruled an empire of which it was said that the sun never set: Spain and the Indies, the Low Countries, Naples and Milan, Austria and the Empire itself. Worn by gout and by forty years of war against France, the Turk, and the Reformation, Charles V resolved to end his days in a cloister.

On 25 October 1555, in the great hall of the Coudenberg palace at Brussels where forty years before he had been declared of age, he resigned the Netherlands to his son Philip before the States General. Leaning on the shoulder of the young William of Orange — later called the Silent — the emperor numbered his journeys: ten to the Low Countries, nine to Germany, seven to Spain, seven to Italy, four to France, two to England, two to Africa. "My life has been one long journey."

In January 1556 he resigned Spain and the Indies; in August, the imperial crown to his brother Ferdinand, though the electors did not accept the resignation until 1558. He withdrew to the monastery of Yuste in Estremadura, and died there on 21 September 1558, holding the cross his wife Isabella had held in death.

events.title: The death of Alfred the Great
events.shortBlurb: The king who saved Christian Wessex from the Danes, and taught his people to read again, died at Winchester, the only English king called the Great…
body: Alfred was born at Wantage in 849, the fifth son of King Ethelwulf, and came to the throne of Wessex in 871 with the Danish host at the gates. In 878, driven to the marshes of Athelney, he rallied, broke the Danes at Ethandun, and stood godfather at the font to their king Guthrum.

The peace he won he used for the Church's repair. Lamenting that learning had perished from England, he gathered scholars and himself translated into the English tongue Gregory the Great's Pastoral Rule and Dialogues, Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, Orosius's history of the world, and Bede's Ecclesiastical History; his reign saw the beginnings of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and a code of laws prefaced with the law of God.

He died on 26 October 899, not yet fifty-one, and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. Posterity has named him alone of English kings "the Great"; the old writers called him England's darling and the shepherd of his people.

events.title: The Assisi Day of Prayer for Peace
events.shortBlurb: At John Paul II's invitation the leaders of the world's religions kept a day of fasting and prayer for peace in the city of St. Francis…
body: In the autumn of 1986, with the cold war still upon the world, John Paul II invited the leaders of the Christian Churches and of the other great religions to Assisi. On 27 October 1986 some one hundred and sixty of them — Christians of many communions, Jews, Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, and others — kept a day of fasting and pilgrimage in the city of St. Francis.

The pope was careful of the boundaries: the faiths did not pray together as one, but came together to pray, each in its own tongue and place, before gathering in the square of the Lower Basilica. Peace, he told them, is not the product of negotiations and compromises alone; it is the result of prayer. For that one day, it was said, the guns fell silent.

The day gave its name to the "spirit of Assisi," carried on by the Community of Sant'Egidio in yearly meetings of prayer for peace. John Paul II returned to Assisi in January 2002, after the towers fell, and Benedict XVI kept the twenty-fifth anniversary there in 2011.

sources.text: John Paul II, Address to the representatives of the Churches and world religions, Assisi, 27 October 1986 (vatican.va)

events.title: The execution of Conradin
events.shortBlurb: The last of the Hohenstaufen, a boy of sixteen, died on the scaffold at Naples, and the long struggle of the Empire and the papacy entered its last act…
body: Conradin was sixteen, grandson of the Emperor Frederick II, and the last hope of his house. Charles of Anjou, called into Italy by the pope and crowned king of Sicily in St. Peter's on 6 January 1266, had slain King Manfred at Benevento; the boy crossed the Alps to claim his inheritance and was received with wild joy, even in Rome.

On 23 August 1268 Charles destroyed his army at Tagliacozzo. Conradin fled, was betrayed into Angevin hands, and on 29 October 1268 was beheaded with his young companion Frederick of Baden on the market-place of Naples. Pope Clement IV had foretold that the gallant youth was being led "like a lamb to the slaughter"; the later tale that the pope counselled his death, the old Catholic historians themselves reject as a fable.

With Conradin the male line of the Hohenstaufen ended, and the Angevin star stood high — but the vengeance of Sicily was preparing. Clement died a month later, on 29 November, and the cardinals then gave the Church the longest vacancy of her history, nearly three years without a pope.

events.title: The Battle of Río Salado
events.shortBlurb: Beside Tarifa the kings of Castile and Portugal broke the last great African invasion of Spain, in a battle the pope had blessed as a crusade…
body: Abu al-Hasan, the Marinid sultan of Morocco, crossed the Strait of Gibraltar with the largest African army Spain had seen in a century, and, joined by Yusuf I of Granada, laid siege to Tarifa, the gateway of the Peninsula. Benedict XII blessed the campaign against them as a crusade, and Alfonso XI of Castile and Afonso IV of Portugal made common cause.

On 30 October 1340 the allies gave battle on the banks of the little river Salado, outside Tarifa. A relic of the True Cross, the chronicles tell, was borne before the Christian host; the fighting lasted from mid-morning to noon, when the Portuguese charge broke the Granadan wing and the whole African army dissolved in flight toward the sea.

It was the last time a great army from Africa disputed the soil of Spain: from that day, the old history says, the Spanish Moslems were confined to the kingdom of Granada, which endured until 1492. Alfonso took the name "the Avenger," and the victory is numbered with Las Navas de Tolosa among the decisive days of the Reconquest.

events.title: The death of Blessed Frances d'Amboise
events.shortBlurb: The widowed Duchess of Brittany, who had planted the first Carmel of nuns in France, laid down her rule and died in her own cloister at Nantes…
body: Born about 1427 at the castle of Thouars, Frances was the daughter of Louis d'Amboise, Viscount of Thouars. Betrothed as a small child to Peter, a younger son of John V, Duke of Brittany, she was married at fifteen in 1442. When Peter came to rule as Peter II in 1450, the pair were crowned in the cathedral of Rennes, and her charity so marked his short reign that chroniclers called it "the time of the blessed duchess."

Widowed and childless in 1457, she withstood the pressure of her family and of King Louis XI, who wished her to marry again, and turned instead to God. With Blessed John Soreth, prior general of the Carmelites, she founded in 1463 at Bondon near Vannes the first convent of Carmelite nuns in France, called "The Three Maries," its first sisters brought from Liège. She took the habit in 1468, was elected prioress in 1473, and later made a second foundation at Nantes.

She died on 4 November 1485 near Nantes and was long venerated as the foundress of the French Carmel. Pope Pius IX confirmed her cult in 1863, and her feast is kept on 4 November; images show her in the Carmelite habit with an ermine cloak to recall her rank.

events.title: The first Catholic diocese in the United States
events.shortBlurb: By the brief Ex hac apostolicae, Pope Pius VI made Baltimore the first see of the young republic and gave John Carroll to its scattered Catholics…
body: After the American Revolution the Catholics of the new United States had no bishop of their own. The clergy of Maryland and Pennsylvania, unwilling to remain a mere mission under the Congregation of Propaganda, petitioned Rome for a diocesan bishop, and Pope Pius VI took the unusual step of allowing them, for that first time only, to elect their candidate. Father John Carroll, a former Jesuit who had lived at Baltimore since 1786, was chosen by twenty-four of the twenty-six votes.

On 6 November 1789, by the pontifical brief Ex hac apostolicae, the pope erected the Diocese of Baltimore as the first in the United States, a see that then embraced the whole nation. Carroll was consecrated a bishop on 15 August 1790 in the chapel of Lulworth Castle in Dorset, England, by Charles Walmesley, vicar apostolic of the Western District.

Carroll had already helped found Georgetown in 1789; he held the first American diocesan synod in 1791, invited the English Dominicans, and established the Visitation nuns. In 1808 Pius VII raised Baltimore to a metropolitan archdiocese with the new suffragan sees of Bardstown, Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, so that the Church in the republic had its own hierarchy.

events.title: The Bolshevik Revolution and the war on religion
events.shortBlurb: The seizure of Petrograd opened one of the longest and bloodiest persecutions the Christian East had ever endured…
body: On 7 November 1917 — 25 October by the Old-Style calendar Russia then kept — Lenin's Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government and stormed the Winter Palace in Petrograd. Within weeks the new regime turned against religion, decreeing in January 1918 the separation of Church and State and the seizure of ecclesiastical property, and setting in motion decades of official atheism.

The Russian Orthodox Church, which had only that same year restored the Moscow patriarchate under Patriarch Tikhon, saw its monasteries closed, its clergy imprisoned or shot, and its faithful driven underground; Tikhon publicly anathematized the persecutors. The Catholics of the former empire, both Latin and Eastern-rite, shared in the suffering, their bishops and priests among the martyrs and prisoners of the coming years.

The Holy See watched with alarm as the persecution spread with Soviet power. Pope Pius XI, who had served as nuncio in the region, condemned atheistic communism in the 1937 encyclical Divini Redemptoris, warning that it sought "to destroy the social order and to undermine the very foundations of Christian civilization."

sources.text: Pope Pius XI, encyclical Divini Redemptoris (19 March 1937), vatican.va

events.title: The death of Blessed John Duns Scotus
events.shortBlurb: The Subtle Doctor, who had forged the classic defense of Our Lady's Immaculate Conception, died suddenly at Cologne…
body: Born about 1266 at Duns in the Scottish Borders, John Duns Scotus entered the Friars Minor and studied and taught at Oxford, Paris, and Cologne. The keenness of his mind won him the title Doctor Subtilis, the Subtle Doctor, and later ages ranked him with Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, and William of Ockham among the great theologians of the medieval schools.

His most celebrated achievement was the classic defense of the Immaculate Conception. Where others feared it derogated from Christ's universal redemption, Scotus argued that the most perfect Redeemer would preserve his Mother from original sin from the first instant of her being — a redemption more excellent, not less. The maxim later attached to his school, "potuit, decuit, ergo fecit" (God could do it, it was fitting, therefore he did it), summed up the case that Pius IX would define as dogma in 1854.

Transferred to the Franciscan studium at Cologne about 1307, he died there unexpectedly on 8 November 1308 and was buried in the Minorite church. His sarcophagus bears the verse "Scotia me genuit, Anglia me suscepit, Gallia me docuit, Colonia me tenet." Pope John Paul II beatified him in 1993.

events.title: The founding of the Redemptorists
events.shortBlurb: St. Alphonsus Liguori gathered a handful of missioners at Scala to preach Christ to the most abandoned poor, choosing for the day the feast of the Lateran…
body: Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, a Neapolitan advocate turned priest, had been stirred by the plight of the herdsmen and country folk of the hills above the Amalfi coast, who lived almost without knowledge of the Gospel. Resting at Scala in 1730 near the sanctuary of Santa Maria dei Monti, he conceived a company wholly given to preaching missions among the most forsaken.

On 9 November 1732, in the humble oratory of a convent at Scala, with Bishop Tommaso Falcoia presiding at the Mass of the Holy Spirit, Alphonsus and a few companions founded the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer — the Redemptorists — under the motto "Copiosa apud eum redemptio," "with him is plentiful redemption." He was thirty-six, and the little band numbered fewer than ten. He chose the day deliberately, for it is the feast of the Dedication of the Lateran, the mother church of the world, a sign of the mission's universal reach.

Among the early members was St. Gerard Majella. Pope Benedict XIV gave the congregation formal approval on 25 February 1749. Alphonsus himself became a bishop and a moral theologian of the first rank, and was later named a Doctor of the Church.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Alphonsus Maria de' Liguori”

events.title: The death of Cnut the Great
events.shortBlurb: The Danish king of a North Sea empire, who had walked to Rome as a pilgrim and bargained there for his people, died at Shaftesbury…
body: Cnut, son of Sweyn Forkbeard, became king of England in 1016, of Denmark about 1018, and of Norway in 1028, ruling a broad North Sea realm. Though he had won it by the sword, he governed as a Christian king, bringing internal peace, repairing the churches his armies had once plundered, and endowing monasteries with lands and relics.

At Easter 1027 he journeyed to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II, and there, in the presence of Pope John XIX, he negotiated on behalf of his subjects: reduced tolls and safe passage for English and Danish pilgrims and merchants on the road to Rome, and relief from the heavy fees demanded of English archbishops when they came to receive the pallium. His letter of 1027, sent home from abroad, records these things in his own words.

He died on 12 November 1035 at Shaftesbury in Dorset — "on the second of the Ides of November," says the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle — and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His empire did not long outlive him, dividing among his sons.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Nicholas the Great
events.shortBlurb: The last of the three popes surnamed "the Great," who upheld the see of Peter against kings and patriarchs alike, died at Rome…
body: Nicholas I was elected bishop of Rome on 24 April 858, consecrated the same day in St. Peter's in the presence of the Emperor Louis II. Of the whole roll of popes, only three bear in the Annuario the title "the Great" — Leo I, Gregory I, and Nicholas — and he earned it as the most forceful pontiff of the Carolingian age.

He upheld the indissolubility of marriage against Lothair II of Lorraine, who sought to put away his wife Teutberga; he defended the rights of bishops such as Rothad of Soissons against their metropolitans; and he resisted Photius, whose irregular elevation at Constantinople foreshadowed the later schism between East and West. In all these causes he asserted the primacy and the judicial authority of the Roman see over the whole Church.

In Rome he rebuilt and endowed churches and encouraged religious life, keeping himself to a spirit of Christian asceticism. He died on 13 November 867, greatly esteemed by his contemporaries; his cult was reaffirmed by Urban VIII in 1630, and his feast is kept on 13 November.

events.title: The healing of the Western Schism
events.shortBlurb: With the consecration of Oddo Colonna as bishop, the Council of Constance sealed the end of the forty-year schism that had rent Latin Christendom…
body: For nearly forty years, since 1378, the Latin Church had been torn among rival claimants to the papacy, until at times three men wore the tiara and Christendom scarcely knew whom to obey. The Council of Constance, opened on 5 November 1414, set itself to end the scandal: it deposed John XXIII and Benedict XIII and received the freely-given resignation of the Roman claimant Gregory XII.

On 11 November 1417 the cardinals and the deputies of the five nations, meeting in conclave, unanimously elected Oddo Colonna, who took the name Martin V in honor of St. Martin of Tours, whose feast fell that day. Being then only a subdeacon, he was ordained deacon on the 12th, priest on the 13th, and consecrated bishop on 14 November 1417 at Constance; he was crowned pope on the 21st.

Recognized by the Church as a whole, Martin V brought the schism to an end and set about restoring the papacy and the Papal States. He soon condemned the conciliarist claim that a general council stands above the pope, forbidding appeal from the pope's judgment in matters of faith, and the long wound of Avignon and the three obediences was at last closed.

events.title: The Battle of the Winwaed
events.shortBlurb: By a rain-swollen river in the north, the Christian Oswiu overthrew the pagan Penda, and, Bede says, heathen Mercia turned to Christ…
body: Penda of Mercia, the last great pagan king among the English, had slain the Christian kings Edwin of Northumbria at Hatfield in 633 and Oswald at Maserfield in 642. In 655 he invaded Bernicia at the head of a great confederate host and besieged Bamburgh, threatening to undo the Christian ascendancy of the north.

Oswiu of Bernicia, offering treasure for peace in vain, vowed that if God granted him victory he would dedicate his infant daughter Ælfflæd to perpetual virginity and give twelve estates for the founding of monasteries. On 15 November 655, in the district of Loidis near Leeds, by the river Winwæd swollen with heavy rain, the armies met. Penda and some thirty allied leaders fell, and Bede records that "many more were drowned in the flight than destroyed by the sword."

Bede reckoned the battle the effective end of Anglo-Saxon paganism: Mercia and its neighbours received the Christian faith, and Penda's own baptized son Peada ruled the southern part. Oswiu kept his vow, and his daughter entered the monastery of Abbess Hilda, later removed to Whitby. The exact site of the river is disputed.

sources.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book III (public-domain translation)

events.title: The deaths of Mary I and Cardinal Pole
events.shortBlurb: Within twelve hours the last Catholic queen of England and her Archbishop of Canterbury both died, and with them the Marian restoration…
body: Mary I, daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, had in 1554 reconciled England to Rome and, in 1556, installed the papal legate Cardinal Reginald Pole as Archbishop of Canterbury, the last Catholic to hold that see. Together they sought to undo the breach of the Reformation and to rebuild the old religion in the realm.

On 17 November 1558, about seven o'clock in the morning, Mary died at St James's Palace in London during an epidemic of influenza that ravaged the country. That same evening, about seven o'clock, Cardinal Pole — himself long ill at Lambeth Palace and only just informed of the queen's passing — died as well, nearly twelve hours after his sovereign.

The crown passed at once to Mary's half-sister Elizabeth, who would sever England from Rome again within a year. Pole lay in state at Lambeth and was buried on the north side of the Corona at Canterbury Cathedral.
